Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 7, p 1185; Davis: Smith's Anesthesia for Infants and Children, ed 8, p 351; Miller: Miller's Anesthesia, ed 8, pp 2757-2761.

question_text: The anesthesiologist is called to the emergency room by the pediatrician to help manage a 3-year-old boy with a high fever and upper airway obstruction. His mother stated that earlier that afternoon, he com plained of a sore throat and hoarseness. The patient is sitting erect and leaning forward; has inspiratory stri dor, tachypnea, and sternal retractions; and is drooling. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate management of airway obstruction in this patient?
option_b: Awake tracheal intubation in the emergency room or the OR if time permits
option_c: Transfer to the OR, inhalation induction, and tracheal intubation
option_d: Transfer to the OR, IV induction, paralysis with succinylcholine, and tracheal intubation
explanation:
This history is consistent with an acute life-threatening cause of upper airway obstruction called epiglottitis (or more appropriately supraglottitis because other supraglottic structures are involved as well). In the past, more than 75% of cases were caused by Haemophilus influenza type b (Hib). With widespread immunization against H. influenzae, this condition has become much less frequent and the causes now include Haemophilus parainfluenzae, group A streptococci, pneumococci, and staphylococci. This condition is a medical emergency that usually starts out as a severe sore throat and rapidly progresses to the "four Ds" (dysphagia, dysphonia, dyspnea, and drooling). It can progress rapidly and cause death within 6 to 12 hours after the onset of symptoms. The child typically is seen sitting up, appears dyspneic with the mouth open, is drooling, and has a high fever and tachycardia. Inspiratory stridor is a late finding and suggests impending complete upper airway obstruction. When suspected, the anesthesiologist and otolaryngologist should be notified and the child immediately transferred to the OR (with the parent if appropriate) before complete upper airway obstruction ensues. In the OR, anesthesia should be induced with sevoflurane and oxygen with the child in a sitting position. Sevoflurane is less likely to induce laryngospasm than isoflurane or desflurane. IV access should be established as soon as the child is deeply anesthetized. Atropine (0.02 mg/kg) should be administered to block vagally mediated bradycardia induced by direct laryngoscopy. Muscle relaxants are contraindicated because they can cause complete obstruction of the upper airway in these patients. The trachea should be intubated under direct laryngoscopy when the depth of anesthesia is sufficient to blunt laryngeal reflexes.

Reference: Davis: Smith's Anesthesia for Infants and Children, ed 8, pp 811-813;

Hines: Stoelting's Anesthesia and Co-Existing Disease, ed 6, pp 614-615.

question_text: A 60-year-old male patient was undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy. During the surgery, it was observed that there was a sudden decrease in etCO2 to 8 mmHg. SpO2 was 90%. BP dropped to 80/50 mmHg and peak airway pressure was observed to be 18cmH2O. Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
• Venous CO2 gas embolism is a potentially fatal complication of laparoscopy that occurs when large CO2 gas bubbles enter the venous system, circulate to the heart, and result in right ventricular chamber gas lock and a subsequent venous outflow obstruction.
  • Although the consequence of CO2 embolism can be severe, clinically significant occurrence is rare.
  • The etiology of a venous CO2 gas embolism during laparoscopic surgery, and its degree of hemodynamic impact, is likely multifactorial. Direct Veress needle insertion into a vein or solid organ during insufflation could potentially result in CO2 entry into the venous system. Open, transected vessels during laparoscopic surgical dissection may result in sudden gas venous ingress and a CO2 gas embolism. Round ligament transection and broad ligament dissection during laparoscopic hysterectomy have resulted in gas embolisms. The deep dorsal venous complex is a major source of bleeding during radical prostatectomies and a potential source of gas embolism during vessel transection.
  • Vigilance is important for the early detection of a venous CO2 gas embolism. Diagnosis is usually dependent on the constellation of clinical signs associated with gas emboli. The severity and presence of these signs vary widely. Acute tachycardia, cardiac arrhythmias, QRS complex widening, hypotension, hypoxemia, and low-end-tidal CO2 may be seen by monitoring. Physical exam findings may include cyanosis and a "mill wheel" murmur by auscultation. TEE is considered the most sensitive method for detecting gas emboli in the heart.
  • Peak airway pressure of 18CmH2O is a normal value.
  • Airway pressure is not usually affected by carbon dioxide embolism.
  • Pneumothorax, endobronchial intubation and bronchospasm will have increased airway pressures.

question_text: A 5-year-old child with previous uneventful general anaesthesia exposure, was given intravenous succinylcholine for rapid sequence intubation at a dose of 0.5 mg/kg. During intubation, masseteric spasm was noted. Considering the other vital to be normal, what would your first line of management be?
option_a: Switch over to atracurium instead of succinyl choline
option_b: Increase the dose of succinyl choline
option_d: Cool the child by using cooling blanket
explanation:
• The first line of management in this child would be to increase the dose of succinyl choline.
  • High incidence of muscle spasm without any symptoms and signs of malignant hyperthermia frequently results from an inadequate dosage of succinylcholine
  • Succinylcholine dosage for intubation: 1-2mg/kg

Conditions to be ruled out in isolated masseteric spasm:

  • Inadequate dose of succinylcholine (less than the recommended dose of 1 mg/kg)
  • Inadequate time for the onset of succinylcholine action
  • Duchenne muscular dystrophy, myotonia congenita and other muscle disorders
  • Temporomandibular joint dislocation

Confusion-Buster:

  • Although an increase in tone of the masseter muscle is an early indicator of malignant hyperthermia, this finding is not consistently associated with that syndrome
  • The masseteric spasm occurs because of an exaggerated contractile response at the neuromuscular junction and cannot be used to establish a diagnosis of malignant hyperthermia
  • At present, in cases of isolated muscle spasm, there is no indication to change to a "non-triggering" anaesthetic

Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

question_text: Which of the following is the LEAST appropriate technique for induction of general anesthesia in a newborn for surgical repair of TEF?
option_b: Inhalation induction with spontaneous ventilation and tracheal intubation
option_c: Inhalation induction using positive-pressure bag and mask ventilation and tracheal intubation
option_d: Rapid-sequence IV induction and tracheal intubation
explanation:
Anesthesia for patients with EA and TEF can be safely induced with either an intravenous or volatile anesthetic. However, positive-pressure bag and mask ventilation should be avoided because it will force gas into the stomach, potentially making ventilation of the lungs more difficult. A frequently used technique to facilitate correct placement of the endotracheal tube is to advance the tube into a bronchus. While listening over the stomach, slowly withdraw the tube until breath sounds are heard over the stomach. Advance the tube until these sounds become diminished. Bronchoscopy is used by some anesthesiologists to make sure only one fistula is present and to help position the endotracheal tube.

Reference: Davis: Smith's Anesthesia for Infants and Children, ed 8, pp 576-577; Hines: Stoelting's Anesthesia and Co-Existing Disease, ed 6, pp 597-598.

question_text: Most common cause of maternal mortality following general anesthesia is?
explanation:
• The most common causes of maternal mortality associated with general anesthesia are either due to pulmonary aspiration or failed endotracheal intubation
  • General anesthesia has been associated with a 1.7 times greater risk of maternal morbidity and mortality than regional anesthesia
  • Maternal mortality associated with aspiration is → 5-15%
  • Mandelson's syndrome → chemical pneumonitis or aspiration pneumonitis caused by aspiration during anesthesia, especially during pregnancy
  • The risk factors include:
    • Gastric volume is greater than 25 mL(0.4 mL/kg)
    • Gastric pH is less than 2.5

Measures to reduce the incidence of aspiration:

  • Administration of nonparticulate antacids like 30ml sodium citrate 30-45 minutes prior to intubation
    • H2 receptor antagonists like intravenous ranitidine 50mg and/or
    • Metoclopramide 10mg 1-2 hours prior to induction

Reference: E Book of Morgan and Mikhail's Clinical Anaesthesiology 6th Edition Chapter 41 Page No 1456

question_text: While performing direct laryngoscopy, the visualization of vocal cords is graded by:
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Cormack-Lehane Classification:
    • Developed by Cormack and Lehane, this scoring system assesses the visibility of the vocal cords during direct laryngoscopy.
    • Grades:
      • Grade 1: Complete visualization of the entire glottic aperture (vocal cords).
      • Grade 2: Visualization of only the posterior aspects of the glottic aperture.
      • Grade 3: Visualization of the tip of the epiglottis only.
      • Grade 4: No visualization beyond the soft palate.
  • Mallampati (Option A): This classification assesses the airway based on visible structures in the oropharynx and is not specific to laryngoscopy.
  • Wilson's score (Option C): This score is not widely recognized in laryngoscopy assessment.
  • Lemon score (Option D): This is not a recognized scoring system for airway visualization.

Key Takeaways:

  • The Cormack-Lehane classification is essential for evaluating laryngeal views during direct laryngoscopy.
  • Understanding these grades helps in predicting potential difficulties in intubation.

question_text: A 25 year old female has presented with achalasia cardia and planned for Heller myotomy. During the induction of anesthesia, the patient aspirates. The immediate management includes all, except
explanation:
• Patients with esophageal disease have the risk of pulmonary aspiration. In such patients, a rapid-sequence induction should be used.
  • Aspiration leads to Mendelson's syndrome. Steroid and prophylactic antibiotic administration is not indicated as part of management.

Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesia, 6th edition, page no. 579

question_text: A 24 years old female underwent a routine procedure under general anaesthesia with endotracheal intubation after which she had complaint of hoarseness of voice. Which among the following is not a measure to help reduce the incidence of post extubation hoarseness?
option_a: Use of low volume, high pressure cuffs
option_b: Lubrication of tube with lidocaine jelly
option_c: Using a smaller sized endotracheal tube
explanation:
• Hoarseness is commonly seen after intubation.
  • Its incidence may be decreased by using tubes with low pressure cuffs, smaller tubes, and lubrication with lidocaine jelly.
  • Hoarseness increases with difficult and long intubation but not with increased intra-cuff pressure. Hoarseness that is persistent or that develops later in the postoperative period should be investigated.

Reference: Understanding Anaesthesia Equipment (Jerry A. Dorsch, Susan E. Dorsch)

question_text: You have intubated the patient with laryngoscopy. The consultant confirms it with the surest sign on the monitor, ie,
option_d: Feeling the tube against the tracheal rings
explanation:
• Unrecognized esophageal intubation can produce catastrophic results.
  • Prevention of this complication depends on direct visualization of the tip of the ETT passing through the vocal cords, careful auscultation for the presence of bilateral breath sounds and the absence of gastric gurgling while ventilating through the ETT.
  • Detection of CO2 in exhaled gas (the most reliable automated method), chest radiography, airway ultrasonography, or the use of an FOB are the objective methods

Reference: Morgan anaesthesia, edition 6, page no 334

question_text: During the intubation, the endo tracheal tube may become malposition in the following places
explanation:
• Even though it is confirmed that the tube is in the trachea, it may not be correctly positioned.
  • Overly 'deep' insertion usually results in intubation of the right main-stem bronchus because the right bronchus forms a less acute angle with the trachea than the left.
  • In contrast, inadequate insertion depth will position the cuff in the larynx, predisposing the patient to laryngeal trauma.

Reference: Morgan anaesthesia, edition 6, page no 334

question_text: Advantages of the given instrument over conventional laryngoscopy are all except:
option_a: Enables the operator to 'look around the corner'
option_b: More useful in guiding the trainees in laryngoscopy
option_c: Movement of the cervical spine is less
option_d: Endotracheal intubation is easier even without the use of a pre-shaped stylet
explanation:
The advantages of video laryngoscopy over conventional laryngoscopy include:

  1. Enables the operator to 'look around the corner': Video laryngoscopy provides a clear view of the glottis and vocal cords, which can sometimes be challenging with a conventional direct laryngoscopy. It allows the operator to see the airway structures more easily.
  2. More useful in guiding the trainees in laryngoscopy: Video laryngoscopy provides a visual display that can be beneficial for teaching
  3. Movement of the cervical spine is less: Video laryngoscopy often allows for a more neutral position of the patient's cervical spine during intubation. This can be advantageous, especially in patients with potential cervical spine injuries.
  4. The statement, Endotracheal intubation is easier even without the use of a pre-shaped stylet is not true. Video laryngoscopes may require a pre-shaped stylet to facilitate intubation in certain cases.

Reference: Objective anaesthesia review (Atul Kulkarni) 4th edition, pg 519.

question_text: A 40-year-old female is posted for thyroidectomy for multinodular goiter, for which her airway is secured using the following airway device. Immediately following intubation, it was found impossible to ventilate the patient. Which characteristic of the given device can be responsible for this scenario?
option_b: Presence of spirals embedded in the tube
option_c: High incidence of kinking with these tubes
option_d: Elastic recoil leading to accidental extubation
explanation:
• The given image is that of a spiral embedded/armored/flex metallic endotracheal tube.
  • The purpose of the Murphy's eye is to provide an alternate pathway for gas flow if the bevel becomes occluded in an endotracheal tube.
  • Spiral embedded tubes don't have Murphy's eye in them due to presence of the metallic spirals.
  • The absence of a Murphy eye may result in obstruction if the bevel abuts the wall of the trachea.
  • Presence of spirals embedded in the tubes allows non kinking of the tube in case of flexion of the neck and in head and neck surgeries.
  • Elastic recoil of the tube can lead to accidental extubhation and inability to ventilate during change in position intraoperatively. Since in the given scenario it is mentioned immediately post intubation, this answer is less likely, though it can be the second best to option a.

Reference: Understanding Anaesthesia Equipment (Jerry A. Dorsch, Susan E. Dorsch) 5th edition pg 566

question_text: How can we avoid the following complication seen after an intubation, in a pediatric patient.
explanation:
Given image shows a chest x-ray of inadvertent Endobronchial intubation leading to atelectasis in a pediatric patient.

Auscultation may be misleading, as breath sounds can be transmitted to the opposite side of the chest in the presence of bronchial intubation.

Decreases in saturation of pulse oximetry (SpO2) will not always be seen, If the patient is receiving a high oxygen concentration, Monitoring expired CO2 may lead to the discovery of bronchial intubation, but it is not a reliable means to detect this problem. Either an increase or decrease in end-tidal CO2 may be seen.

A fiberscope through the tube is equal in accuracy and faster than a chest x-ray for determining tube position in both adults and pediatric.

Reference: Understanding Anaesthesia Equipment (Jerry A. Dorsch, Susan E. Dorsch) 5th edition pg 594

question_text: What does the given capnograph show?
explanation:
Clefts during phase III of the capnography trace indicate spontaneous breathing efforts during controlled mechanical ventilation also called as curare clefts.

Reference: Miller's anaesthesia 9th edition pg 1311.

question_text: What does the given capnograph show?
explanation:
Increased upslope of phase III occurs during bronchospasm (asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), or partially obstructed endotracheal tube/breathing circuit, giving a "shark fin appearance" to the trace.

Reference: Miller's anaesthesia 9th edition pg 1311.

question_text: Conditions where cricothyrotomy may be indicated include all except
explanation:
Cricothyrotomy should not be used in the presence of laryngeal inflammation or infection.

All others are indications of cricothyroidotomy.

Reference: Understanding Anaesthesia Equipment (Jerry A. Dorsch, Susan E. Dorsch) 5th edition pg 672.

question_text: A healthy 2-year-old male is scheduled to undergo a laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair. His airway was managed uneventfully with mask ventilation, which was  followed by direct laryngoscopy and intubation with a 4.5-mm uncuffed endotracheal tube (ETT). Manual ventilation produces an air leak in the oropharynx beginning at a peak pressure of 20 cm H2O. The best next step in the anesthetic management is to
option_b: Replace the ETT with a smaller-sized uncuffed tube
option_c: Replace the ETT with a larger-sized uncuffed tube
option_d: Replace the ETT with a 4.0-mm cuffed ETT
explanation:
• Correct tube size and appropriate cuff inflation is confirmed by easy passage into the larynx and the development of a gas leak at 15 to 25 cm H2O pressure.(which is acceptable as described in the case as leak above 20 cm of H20)
  • No leak indicates an oversized tube or overinflated cuff that should be replaced or deflated to prevent postoperative edema, whereas an excessive leak may preclude adequate ventilation and contaminate the operating room with anesthetic gases.

Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition, pg 914.

question_text: At what maximum inspiratory pressure should an endotracheal tube leak in a child?
explanation:
In infants and young children, there should be a small air leak around the endotracheal tube at peak inflation pressures of approximately 15 to 25 cm H2O. The leak test can be performed by slowly increasing the airway pressure and listening with a stethoscope over the larynx to hear when a leak develops. An air leak within this pressure range allows for adequate ventilation and reduces the incidence of postintubation croup. The most common cause of postintubation croup is a tight-fitting endotracheal tube without a leak at 30 to 40 cm H2O.

Reference: Davis: Smith's Anesthesia for Infants and Children, ed 8, pp 356-357, 389-390.

question_text: The resistance of the tube shown below is primarily because of:
explanation:
Explanation:

The resistance to airflow (R) in an endotracheal tube is primarily determined by its diameter. According to Hagen-Poiseuille law, the resistance is:

Where:

  • rrr = radius of the tube
  • Resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius, making diameter the most critical factor in determining resistance.
  • Resistance is also directly proportional to the length and viscosity, but these contribute less significantly than diameter.

ETT Size and Length Guidelines:

Additional Points:

  • The cuff of the ETT is positioned 3-4 cm above the carina and 2-2.5 cm below the glottis to prevent injury and ensure proper ventilation.
  • Murphy's eye: A side hole near the tip of the ETT that allows continued ventilation if the end of the tube abuts the tracheal wall.
  • Internal diameter is the standard way to describe ETT size because it determines airflow resistance and suitability for ventilation.

question_text: A 43 year male is undergoing vocal cord growth excision under general anesthesia. During the laser guided ablation of the lesion, the endotracheal tube caught fire. In incidence of airway fire, which of the following steps is least helpful
option_c: Fiber optic endoscopy to look for remnants of tube
option_d: Pour normal saline over the field
explanation:
Airway fires are caused by triad

  • If a fire occurs in an airway during laser surgery, the source should be removed, and mask ventilation with 100% O2 should be initiated. reintubation and bronchoscopy with lavage may be required. Severe damage may require a tracheostomy.

Reference: Oxford handbook of Anesthesia, edition 4, page no 577

question_text: A 56-year-old patient with a history of liver disease and osteomyelitis is anesthetized for tibial débridement. After induction and intubation, the wound is inspected and débrided with a total blood loss of 300 mL. The patient is transported intubated to the recovery room, at which time the systolic blood pressure falls to 50 mm Hg. Heart rate is 120 beats/min, arterial blood gases (ABGs) are Pao2 103, Paco2 45, pH 7.3, with 97% O2 saturation with 100% Fio2. Mixed venous blood gases are Pvo2 60 mm Hg, Pvco2 50, and pH 7.25. Which of the following diagnoses is MOST consistent with this clinical picture?
option_d: Sepsis with acute respiratory distress syndrome
explanation:
All hypotension can be broadly broken down into two main categories: decreased cardiac output and decreased systemic vascular resistance. Flow or cardiac output can be further subdivided into problems related to decreased heart rate (i.e., bradycardia versus problems related to decreases in stroke volume). Normal Po2 in mixed venous blood is 40 mm Hg. Increased mixed venous arterial oxygen levels can be due to many conditions including high cardiac output, sepsis, left-to-right cardiac shunts, impaired peripheral uptake (e.g., cyanide), and decreased oxygen consumption (e.g., hypothermia), as well as sampling error. The other choices in this question all represent conditions whereby cardiac output is diminished and consequently would not be consistent with the data given in the question

Reference: Butterworth: Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology, ed 5, pp 360-361.

question_text: A 54-year-old male hypertensive patient underwent laparoscopic lower anterior resection. His blood pressure in the recovery was 190/80 mm Hg and heart rate was 91 beats per minute. He was maintaining saturation of 100% with oxygen mask of 4 liters. Given that, the reason is the pain, step of management will include the following:
explanation:
• Noxious stimulation from incisional pain, endotracheal intubation, full bladder, or preoperative discontinuation of anti-hypertensive medication, is usually responsible for increased blood pressure in the recovery area.
  • Adequate analgesia preoperatively given with opioids.
  • Mild to moderate elevations can be treated with intravenous labetalol; an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, such as enalapril; or a calcium channel blocker, such as nicardipine.
  • The end point for treatment should be consistent with the patient’s own normal blood pressure.

Reference: Morgan and Mikhail’s clinical anesthesiology, page no 1300

question_text: A number 6 endotracheal tube indicates which size?
explanation:
Endotracheal tube sizes are measured according to the ID. They are available in 0.5-mm ID increments

Reference: Miller: Basics of Anesthesia, ed 6, p 230.

question_text: In endotracheal tube what determines resistance?
explanation:
Explanation:

Resistance to airflow in a tube (like an endotracheal tube) is governed by Poiseuille's Law, which describes the resistance to laminar flow in a cylindrical tube.

Poiseuille's Law:

Resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius. Even a small decrease in diameter (or radius) causes a huge increase in resistance.

For example:

  • Halving the radius increases resistance 16 times.

Explanation for other options:

Curvature (option A): Incorrect. While curvature may affect flow dynamics (especially in turbulent flow), in the case of standard, properly placed endotracheal tubes, the curvature is minimal and has negligible impact on resistance.

Texture (Option C): Incorrect. The internal texture of the tube (whether smooth or rough) could theoretically influence turbulent flow, but modern ETTs are made with smooth internal surfaces to reduce friction. So in clinical practice, texture has minimal effect on resistance compared to diameter.

Length (Option D): Partially true, but not the most important

Resistance does increase with length (as seen in Poiseuille's Law), but:

  • The effect is linear with length.
  • The effect of diameter is exponential (radius4).

So while length matters, diameter is the dominant factor influencing resistance

Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9622621

question_text: A 30-year-old primi with pre-eclampsia is posted for caesarean section. Ideal anaesthetic technique is?
explanation:
• Continuous epidural anesthesia is the first choice for patients with
    • Pre-eclampsia duringlabour
    • Vaginal delivery
    • Caesarean section
  • Pre-eclampsia patients have a risk of severe airway oedema, which makes intubation difficult
  • Thus, continuous epidural anesthesia is advantageous as it avoids the need for intubation
  • Besides, continuous epidural anesthesia can improve uteroplacental perfusion and decrease catecholamine secretion
  • But one major prerequisite for regional anesthesia in preeclamptic patients is normal platelet count and normal coagulation
  • Coagulopathy is a contraindication for regional anesthesia
  • Minimal platelet count for regional anesthesia is 100,000/uL, but some cases can be taken up with a platelet count as low as 70,000/uL

Option A: General anesthesia is indicated in patients with coagulopathy and in severe pre-eclampsia with complications

Option D: Spinal anesthesia can be given in mild pre-eclampsia but hypotension associated with spinal anesthesia limits its use in moderate to severe pre-eclampsia

Hence the best option here would be continuous epidural anesthesia

Reference: E Book of Morgan and Mikhail's Clinical Anaesthesiology 6th Edition Chapter 41 Page No 1456

question_text: Which of the following is the major advantage of spinal anesthetic in the pregnant patient posed for appendicectomy?
option_a: A peripheral neuraxial block minimizes central sensitization to pain
option_b: The level of a spinal anesthesia necessary for an appendectomy is quite low
option_c: Spinals rarely cause headaches in pregnant patients.
option_d: A spinal anesthetic allows for anesthesia without significant plasma concentrations of the anesthetic
explanation:
• Regional anesthesia, when feasible, is preferable to general anesthesia in order to
    • Decrease the risks of pulmonary aspiration
    • Failed intubation
    • Minimize drug exposure to the fetus

Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg. 895.

question_text: High flow nasal oxygen helps in oxygenation of patients in the intensive care. All the following patients can benefit from THRIVE except:
explanation:
Explanation:

It is not suitable for patients with a GCS < 8/15 due to risks associated with airway protection and ventilation needs.

  • High Flow Nasal Oxygen (HFNO):
    • Delivery Method: Administered through specialized nasal cannula.
    • Flow Rate: Achieves flow rates up to 70 L/minwith FiO2 nearing 100%.
    • Indications: Effective for spontaneously breathing patients with respiratory distress.
  • THRIVE Study:
    • Transnasal Humidified Rapid Insufflation Ventilatory Exchange: Research supports HFNO's use in apnoeic patients and during procedures under anaesthesia.
    • Mechanism: Helps prolong apnoeic oxygenation and improves time to desaturation during intubation attempts.
  • Patient Considerations:
    • Spontaneously Breathing: Patients must be able to breathe on their own and protect their airways for HFNO to be beneficial.
    • Cognitive Status: AGlasgow Coma Scale (GCS) < 8/15 indicates severe impairment and inability to protect the airway, making HFNO inappropriate.
  • COPD patients can benefit from HFNO to alleviate hypoxemia and improve ventilation (Option B)
  • HFNO is used to enhance oxygenation and reduce work of breathing in ARDS patients (Option C)
  • HFNO helps in oxygenation and alleviating respiratory distress in pneumonia patients (Option D)

Key Takeaways:

  • HFNO is effective in spontaneously breathing patients with respiratory distress, particularly in conditions like COPD, ARDS, and pneumonia.

question_text: Identify the mask in the image used for patients with COVID-19 infection.
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The non-rebreathing mask (NRBM) is commonly used in COVID-19 patients who require high concentrations of oxygen while minimizing aerosol spread.
  • It delivers 60-90% oxygen through a reservoir bag and one-way valves that prevent rebreathing of exhaled gases.
  • By limiting re-inhalation of carbon dioxide and reducing aerosol dispersion, it becomes especially suitable in infectious respiratory illnesses such as COVID-19.

Non-rebreathing mask:

  • Components: Face mask, reservoir bag, one-way valves.
  • Oxygen delivery range: 10-15 L/min flow rate.
  • Indications: Severe hypoxemia, acute respiratory distress, and pre-oxygenation prior to intubation.
  • Advantages: Provides high FiO2, prevents rebreathing, and reduces aerosol generation compared to nebulizers.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Venturi mask (Option A): Provides a fixed oxygen concentration (24-50%) and is typically used in COPD patients who require controlled FiO2 to avoid CO2 retention. It is not suitable for severe COVID-19 hypoxemia requiring high-flow oxygen.

Hudson mask (Option B): A simple face mask that delivers 40-60% oxygen but lacks a reservoir bag. It cannot deliver as high FiO2 as NRBM and offers less protection against aerosol spread.

Nebulizer (Option C): Used for aerosolized drug delivery. In COVID-19 patients, nebulizers increase the risk of aerosol generation and viral transmission, making them unsafe for oxygen therapy in this setting.

Key Takeaway:

For COVID-19 patients with significant oxygen demand, the non-rebreathing mask is the preferred choice because it delivers a high concentration of oxygen while minimizing the risk of aerosol generation.

question_text: While moving a parturient from the birthing room to the operating room for an emergency cesarean section for a prolapsed umbilical cord, the patient develops cough, wheezing, and stridor and becomes cyanotic. The trachea is intubated, and food is noted in the pharynx. Appropriate treatment in this patient should consist of
option_a: Intravenous lidocaine to suppress the cough
explanation:
Three different aspiration syndromes have been described in the general population: aspiration of particulate matter causing airway obstruction, aspiration of acid fluid causing aspiration pneumonitis (Mendelson syndrome), and aspiration of gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic bacteria causing aspiration pneumonia. Aspiration pneumonia has the highest mortality rate but fortunately occurs only with an associated bowel obstruction, which is rarely a problem in obstetrics. Symptoms of aspiration pneumonitis include coughing, tachypnea, tachycardia, bronchospasm, and hypoxemia. Treatment is supportive and includes the Heimlich maneuver if a large foreign body is lodged in the trachea (which is unlikely in the fasting laboring patient), endotracheal intubation, suctioning the airway to remove particulate material, administration of increased concentrations of oxygen, and application of PEEP to achieve oxygenation goals as needed (prophylactic PEEP does not provide any benefit). Coughing is due to the airway irritation and is most effectively decreased with muscle paralysis. Intravenous lidocaine would not be effective. Use of saline or bicarbonate lavage does not decrease lung damage and can worsen hypoxemia. Glucocorticoids or other anti-inflammatory drugs have not been effective in limiting the inflammation and may increase the risk of secondary bacterial infection.

Reference: Chestnut: Chestnut's Obstetric Anesthesia, ed 5, pp 671-675; Suresh: Shnider and Levinson's Anesthesia for Obstetrics, ed 5, pp 403-405.

question_text: Succinylcholine is contraindicated in?
explanation:
• Succinylcholine has been associated with severe hyperkalaemia in patients with
    • Burn
    • Severe abdominal infections
    • Severe metabolic acidosis
    • Closed head injury
    • Conditions associated with upregulation of extra junctional acetylcholine receptors (e.g., hemiplegia or paraplegia, muscular dystrophies, Guillain-Barre syndrome, and burn)
  • Because of the risk of massive rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia, and death in children with undiagnosed muscle disease, succinylcholine is not recommended for use in children except for emergency tracheal intubation
  • Patients with renal failure are no more susceptible to an exaggerated hyperkalaemia response to succinylcholine than are patients with normal renal function (Option A)

Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

question_text: A 40-year-old male has presented to the emergency department following road traffic accident. He has sustained major injuries and requires airway to be relatively secured and protected. Any of the given muscle relaxant can be used in rapid sequence induction and intubation except
explanation:
All the other given agents can provide for ideal intubation condition following induction rapidly.

  • Atracurium besylate.
  • Non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking drug, first used in 1980.
  • A bis-quaternary nitrogenous plant derivative.
  • Initial dose: 0.3–0.6 mg/kg. Intubation is possible approximately 90 s after a dose of 0.5 mg/kg. Effects last 20–30 min.
  • Supplementary dose: 0.1–0.2 mg/kg. May cause histamine release, usually mild, but severe reactions have been reported at body temperature and pH, undergoes spontaneous Hofmann elimination to laudanosine.
  • Up to 50% ester hydrolysis also occurs. Often considered the drug of choice in renal or hepatic impairment.
  • Its cardio stability, low risk of accumulation and spontaneous reversal are also advantages.
  • Stored at 2–8°C; at room temperature.

Reference: FRCA A TO Z, page no 56

question_text: What is the drug of choice for routine intubation in paediatric patients?
explanation:
• Rocuronium is the drug of choice during routine intubation in paediatric patients due to its faster onset of action and its availability for intramuscular injection
  • Succinylcholine is avoided for routine, elective intubation in children due to its side effects
  • The only indication for intravenous succinylcholine in childrenisrapidsequence induction with a "full" stomach and laryngospasm.
  • The duration of action of vecuronium and pancuroniumàprolonged in children due to immature hepatic function

Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

question_text: A 36-year-old woman with a history of hiatal hernia and acid reflux is undergoing a laparoscopic cholecystectomy under general anesthesia. Induction of general anesthesia and intubation were achieved using propofol and succinylcholine. The patient did not recover from the neuromuscular blockade before the end of surgery; she had 0/4 twitches on the Train-of-four twitch response. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's prolonged paralysis?
option_a: A prolonged effect of the intravenous anesthetic propofol
explanation:
• Succinylcholine is metabolized in the plasma by pseudocholinesterase.
  • Its effect does not usually last more than 10 minutes.
  • In the rare condition of an atypical pseudocholinesterase enzyme, its paralytic effects may be prolonged for hours.

Reference: Stoelting’s pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 5th edition pg 326

question_text: Which of the following agent can be used as sole agent for induction and intubation
explanation:
Sevoflurane is the only agent among the options that can be used as a sole agent for induction and intubation due to its low blood-gas partition coefficient, making it fast-acting with minimal irritation to the airway. It is commonly used for inhalational induction, especially in pediatric patients, due to its non-pungent odor and rapid onset.

Incorrect Options:

  • Isoflurane: It is highly pungent, causing airway irritation, and is not suitable for inhalation induction.
  • Halothane: Though previously used for induction, it has been largely replaced by Sevoflurane due to concerns about hepatotoxicity and a slower onset.
  • Desflurane: It has a very pungent odor and can cause airway irritation and coughing, making it unsuitable for use as a sole induction agent.

Key Takeaway:

Sevoflurane is the preferred inhalational agent for sole induction and intubation due to its rapid action, low airway irritation, and favorable safety profile, especially in pediatric populations.

question_text: A 30-year-old man presents for open reduction and internal fixation of a left radius fracture as an outpatient. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes per day for 12 years. The plan is general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation. Which one of the following agents is most appropriate for him?
explanation:
• Although all agents could be used, sevoflurane would be the preferred choice. Sevoflurane could be used in combination with nitrous oxide

Wrong Answers:

Option A: Isoflurane could also be used, but because of its high blood: gas solubility it may delay emergence, which is undesirable in outpatients

Option B: Desflurane has a lower blood: gas solubility that would provide rapid awakening, but desflurane is irritating to inhale and can cause bronchoconstriction in smokers

Reference: Drugs in Anesthesia and Intensive Care, Edward Scarth, Susan Smith 5th edition

question_text: A road traffic accident victim with HR 120/min and BP 90/30 mm Hg is brought to the emergency bay for urgent limb-salvaging surgery. During rapid sequence intubation, the anesthesiologist must choose an induction agent that preserves cardiovascular stability. Which agent is preferred in this hemodynamically unstable patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Ketamine produces dissociative anesthesia with intense analgesia while maintaining airway reflexes and cardiovascular stability.
  • It increases blood pressure and heart rate by stimulating the sympathetic nervous system and supporting cardiac output, making it the preferred induction agent in hypotensive or shocked patients. (Option A)

Clinical features and drug associations:

  • Ketamine: Increases BP and HR by sympathetic stimulation, preserves airway reflexes,provides analgesia and dissociation, ideal for shock and trauma induction (Option A).
  • Propofol: Causes vasodilation and hypotension, unsuitable for unstable patients.
  • Midazolam: Produces sedation and amnesia but may worsen hypotension.
  • Etomidate: Hemodynamically stable but lacks analgesia and suppresses adrenal steroid synthesis, making it less suitable in trauma.

Key Takeaways:

  • Ketamine is the induction agent of choice in hemodynamically unstable or shocked patients.
  • It increases heart rate, blood pressure, and cardiac output through sympathetic stimulation.
  • It provides analgesia and preserves airway reflexes, beneficial in trauma settings.
  • Agents like propofol, midazolam, and etomidate may worsen hypotension or lack analgesic support.

question_text: An otherwise healthy 14-day-old neonate is transported to the OR well-hydrated for surgery for a bowel obstruction. A rapid-sequence induction is planned. Compared with the adult dose, the dose of succinyl choline administered to this patient should be
option_a: Diminished because of the immature nervous system
option_b: The same as the adult dose
option_c: Decreased because of decreased acetylcholine receptors
option_d: Increased because of a greater volume of distribution
explanation:
Neonates and infants (<2 years of age) require more succinylcholine per body weight than do older children and adults to produce neuromuscular blockade, because the extracellular fluid volume is much greater in neonates and infants. Because the volume of distribution of succinylcholine is greater, the recommended dose of succinylcholine in neonates and infants to provide optimal conditions for tracheal intubation is 2 mg/kg instead of the 1 mg/kg used for adults.

Reference: Davis: Smith's Anesthesia for Infants and Children, ed 8, pp 247, 537; Miller: Miller's Anesthesia, ed 8, p 2771.

question_text: A patient developed hypotension and arrhythmias while a supraclavicular plexus block with 0.5% bupivacaine was being performed. What is the appropriate management?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's presentation of hypotension and arrhythmias during a supraclavicular plexus block with bupivacaine strongly suggests Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST). The most appropriate immediate management is Lipid Infusion, which sequesters the lipophilic local anaesthetic from the target organ.

Local Anaesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST) occurs with accidental intravascular injection or rapid absorption of local anaesthetics.

Toxicity from local anaesthetics primarily affects the cardiovascular and central

nervous systems (CNS).

  1. Cardiovascular: arrhythmia, hypotension, cardiovascular collapse
  2. CNS: oral numbness, dizziness, visual disturbances, seizure, coma

Treatment involves immediate cessation of the local anaesthetic, resuscitation and supportive care, and administration of IV bolus of 20% lipid emulsion to bind the lipophilic local anaesthetic from vital organs.

Explanation of Other Options:

CPR (Option A): It is not the initial treatment for hypotension and arrhythmias caused by the toxicity of local anaesthetics. Indicated if such a patient is pulseless.

Intubation (Option B): An Important supportive measure for airway management and ventilation, but doesn't directly reverse the toxicity of local anaesthetics.

NaHCO3 (Option C): This is an adjunctive therapy used to treat metabolic acidosis, which can occur with severe LAST but doesn't directly reverse the toxicity of local anaesthetics.

Key Takeaways:

Local Anaesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST) should be treated with 20% lipid emulsion, which binds the lipophilic local anaesthetics and helps in their removal from vital organs.

question_text: A 40-year-old man was given spinal anaesthesia by first year anaesthesia resident for inguinal hernia repair. After 5 minutes, patient becomes unconscious, apnoeic with hypotension. Here the apnoea is due to:

explanation:
Explanation:

  • High Spinal Anaesthesia:
    • The condition suggests a high spinal block resulting in:
      • Severe hypotension due to widespread vasodilation.
      • Bradycardia from involvement of T1-T4 fibers. (Option A)
      • Respiratory insufficiency as the block ascends to affect the cervical spinal cord.
  • Apnea Mechanism:
    • Primarily due to hypoperfusion of the medulla from significant hypotension.
    • Less likely to be caused directly by phrenic nerve paralysis.
  • Clinical Considerations:
    • Recognizing symptoms of a total spinal where cranial nerve involvement occurs.
    • Anterior spinal artery syndrome may occur due to prolonged hypotension with elevated intraspinal pressure.
  • Immediate Management:
    • Ensure adequate arterial oxygenation and ventilation.
    • Intubation and mechanical ventilation may be necessary for severe respiratory failure.
    • Intravenous vasopressors and rapid IV fluid administration for hypotension.
    • Atropine for bradycardia; ephedrine or epinephrine may be used to enhance heart rate and blood pressure.
  • Failure to connect oxygen is not a primary cause of unconsciousness and hypotension in this scenario. (Option B)
  • Malingering is unlikely given the abrupt change in the patient's condition. (Option C)

Key Takeaways:

  • High spinal anaesthesia can rapidly lead to severe complications, necessitating prompt intervention.
  • Recognizing signs of medullary hypoperfusion is critical for timely management.
  • Comprehensive monitoring and readiness to support ventilation and circulation are essential during spinal anaesthesia procedures.

question_text: The incidence of each of the following is increased in patients with Down syndrome (trisomy 21) EXCEPT
explanation:
Trisomy 21 or Down syndrome is the most common human chromosomal syndrome seen. An increased incidence of congenital hypothyroidism occurs. About one fourth of children with Down syndrome and many adults have smaller tracheas than predicted and require an endotracheal tube that is one or two sizes smaller. One should avoid unnecessary flexion or extension of the neck during intubation because occipito-atlantoaxial instability occurs in about 15% to 20% of patients. Because subluxation is relatively uncommon, routine neck radiographs for all Down syndrome patients are excessive. More than 40% of Down syndrome children have congenital heart disease (e.g., endocardial cushion defects, ventricular septal defects, tetralogy of Fallot, patent ductus arteriosus). Although some children have hypotonia, an increased incidence of MH has not been reported in these patients.

Reference: Baum: Anesthesia for Genetic, Metabolic, and Dysmorphic Syndromes of Childhood, ed 2, pp 105-107; Hines: Stoelting's Anesthesia and Co-Existing Disease, ed 6, pp 634-635.

question_text: During spontaneous breathing, volatile anesthetics

option_b: Increase Vt and increase respiratory rate
option_c: Decrease Vt and decrease respiratory rate
option_d: Decrease Vt and increase respiratory rate
explanation:
• At concentrations of 1 MAC or less, volatile anesthetics, as well as the inhaled anesthetic N2O, will produce dose-dependent increases in the respiratory rate in spontaneously breathing patients. This trend continues at concentrations greater than 1 MAC for all of the inhaled anesthetics except isoflurane.
  • With the exception of N2O, the evidence suggests that this effect is caused by direct activation of the respiratory center in the CNS rather than by stimulation of pulmonary stretch receptors.
  • Additionally, volatile anesthetics decrease Vt and significantly alter the breathing pattern from the normal awake pattern of intermittent deep breaths separated by varying time intervals to one of rapid, shallow, regular, and rhythmic breathing.

Reference: Miller’s Anesthesia, ed 8, pp 691-692.

question_text: You are an observer for a code BLUE drill. You find the mock patient put in a particular position until the medical resuscitation team arrives. The below position is indicated for:
option_c: Ease of transfer of the patient
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Recovery Position: This position is specifically forunconscious but spontaneously breathingpatients, provided there are no contraindications (e.g., cervical spine injury).
  • Airway Management: It helps maintain a clear airway and allows for drainage of vomitus, secretions, and blood, thereby preventing aspiration.
  • Use in Anaesthesia Recovery: Commonly employed during recovery from anaesthesia to ensure patient safety.
  • Compromise in Positioning: It balances the need for effective airway management with the risks associated with other positions:
    • Prone Position: Better airway drainage but may cause diaphragmatic splinting.
    • Lateral Position: Reduces diaphragmatic splinting but may be less effective for airway management.
  • Flexion of Arms: Typically involves flexing both arms, with the upper hand positioned under the jaw to support the airway.
  • Observation and Flexibility: The position should allow for constant observation of the patient and facilitate easy transition to a supine position when necessary.
  • While the recovery position may aid in oxygenation indirectly by keeping the airway clear, its primary purpose is to prevent aspiration rather than specifically enhance oxygenation (Option B)
  • The recovery position is not primarily designed for ease of transfer; it focuses on airway protection and safety during unconsciousness, which may complicate transfers (Option C)
  • The recovery position clearly serves a specific purpose preventing aspiration(Option D)

Key Takeaways:

  • Primary Purpose: The recovery position primarily aims toprevent aspiration in unconscious patients who are breathing spontaneously.
  • Safety: Ensuring airway protection is crucial during emergencies and post-anaesthesia recovery.
  • Adaptability: The chosen position must consider the patient's specific circumstances, ensuring safety and effective ventilation.

question_text: When do you put a victim in the following position?
option_a: Conscious patient with pulse & breathing present
option_b: Unconscious patient with pulse & breathing present.
option_c: Unconscious patient with pulse present but no breathing
option_d: Unconscious patient without pulse but breathing present.
explanation:
Explanation:

The recovery position is used for an unconscious patient with intact pulse and breathing to maintain airway patency and prevent aspiration.

  • The recovery position is indicated for patients who are unconscious but have spontaneous breathing and a palpable pulse.
  • This position involves turning the person onto their side with the head tilted slightly back to maintain airway openness and promote drainage of secretions (like vomit or saliva), thereby preventing aspiration and airway obstruction.
  • It is a first-aid measure used while waiting for medical help to arrive, especially when there's no indication for CPR.

Explanation of other options:

Conscious patient with pulse & breathing present (Option A): Recovery position is not needed as the patient is alert and can maintain their airway independently.

Unconscious patient with pulse present but no breathing (Option C): This is a case of respiratory arrest-rescue breathing or ventilation support is required, not the recovery position.

Unconscious patient without pulse but breathing present (Option D): This scenario is not physiologically possible, as lack of pulse implies cardiac arrest, and spontaneous breathing would not occur-CPR is indicated, not the recovery position.

question_text: When is the indicated position used during resuscitation?
option_a: Unconsciousness with pulse absent and breathing absent
option_b: Unconsciousness with pulse present and breathing absent
option_c: Unconsciousness with pulse and breathing present
option_d: Unconsciousness with pulse absent and breathing present
explanation:
Explanation:

The recovery position is used in unconscious patients who have spontaneous breathing and circulation to maintain airway patency and prevent aspiration.

  • The recovery position involves placing an unconscious patient on their side with the lower arm extended and the upper leg flexed.
  • This posture helps keep the airway open by preventing the tongue from falling back and allows fluids (such as vomit or secretions) to drain, reducing the risk of aspiration.
  • It is particularly indicated in unconscious patients with intact breathing and pulse, especially when drug or alcohol intoxication is suspected.
  • It ensures better airway maintenance while awaiting definitive care.

Explanation of other options:

Unconsciousness with pulse absent and breathing absent (Option A): Indicates cardiac arrest; immediate CPR is required, not the recovery position.

Unconsciousness with pulse present and breathing absent (Option B): Requires rescue breathing or assisted ventilation to support oxygenation.

Unconsciousness with pulse absent and breathing present (Option D): This is physiologically improbable; if it occurs, immediate reassessment and resuscitation are warranted rather than using the recovery position.

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3161868/

question_text: A 10-month-old infant is undergoing elective repair of a left testicular hydrocele under general anesthesia with isoflurane, nitrous oxide, oxygen, and fentanyl. All of the following are effective and reasonable means of preventing hypothermia in this patient EXCEPT
option_a: Placement of an infrared heater over the operating table and prewarming the OR
option_b: Covering the OR table with a heating blanket
option_c: Wrapping the extremities with sheet wadding and covering the head with a cloth cap
option_d: Ventilating the patient with a Mapleson D circuit at low gas flows (e.g., 50 mL/kg/min)
explanation:
A comprehensive understanding of thermoregulation and a meticulous attention to detail during the anesthetic care of infants are both necessary to minimize intraoperative heat loss. In anesthetized infants, heat loss occurs through the transfer of heat from the patient to the environment in one of four ways: radiation (transfer between objects not in contact), conduction (transfer between objects in contact), convection (transfer to moving molecules such as air and fluid), and evaporation. Of these, radiation and convection account for about 75% of the infant's heat loss. For this reason, placement of an infrared heater over the OR table and prewarming the OR atmosphere are the most effective means of preventing hypothermia in these patients. Covering the OR table with a heating blanket; ventilating the patient with warm, humidified anesthetic gases; wrapping the extremities of the patient with sheet wadding; and covering the patient's head with a cloth or plastic cap can also reduce heat loss and prevent hypothermia. Convective forced-air warmers can help prevent a decrease in body temperature and also have been effective in rewarming hypothermic patients. A Mapleson D breathing circuit is not a circle system and does not preserve heat or moisture. To prevent rebreathing of expired gases, spontaneous breathing flow rates need to be two to three times the minute ventilation, and for controlled ventilation fresh gas flows need to be greater than 90 mL/kg/min. Low flows such as 50 mL/kg/min with Mapleson circuits are inadequate and will result in respiratory acidosis.

Reference: Davis: Smith's Anesthesia for Infants and Children, ed 8, pp 162-165, 294-296; Miller: Miller's Anesthesia, ed 8, pp 1627-1628.

question_text: For a spontaneous breathing patient, the Mapleson A system is the most efficient system. What is the single most important reason for this?
option_a: FGF  is equal to alveolar  ventilation
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Dead Space Gas Reuse:
    • The primary reason for the efficiency of the Mapleson A system is that dead space gas is reused.
    • The spill valve (adjustable pressure relief valve) is located at the patient end, allowing exhaled gas that does not contain carbon dioxide to flow back into the reservoir bag during expiration.
    • As the reservoir bag fills with fresh gas, the exhaled gas that is free of CO2 can be reused in the next breath.
  • Efficiency During Spontaneous Ventilation:
    • Mapleson A is particularly efficient during spontaneous ventilation because it allows for the effective utilization of exhaled gases.
    • During expiration, the exhaled alveolar gas containing CO2 is vented out, while fresh gas is readily available for the next inspiration (Option D).
    • The design ensures that the patient mainly inhales fresh gas, minimizing the risk of CO2 rebreathing.
  • Comparison with Other Systems: The efficiency of Mapleson A is notably different when comparing spontaneous to controlled ventilation, with superior performance in spontaneous breathing.
  • Fresh Gas Flow Rate: A fresh gas inflow rate equal to or greater than the minute ventilation is adequate to prevent CO2 rebreathing (Option A).

Key Takeaways:

  • The Mapleson A system effectively reuses dead space gas, significantly enhancing its efficiency for spontaneous breathing patients.
  • Proper positioning of the spill valve facilitates optimal gas exchange, reducing CO2 rebreathing risks.

    • In pregnancy: perform manual lateral uterine displacement (LUD) to reduce aortocaval compression.
  • Airway (A):
    • Open airway using head-tilt chin-lift(if no trauma) or jaw-thrust (if trauma suspected).
    • Most common cause of obstruction = tongue falling back.
  • Breathing (B):
    • Rescue breaths: 2 after every 30 compressions.
    • Method: mouth-to-mouth or bag-mask, ensuring visible chest rise.
    • Duration: ~1 second per breath.
    • If 2 rescuers are present:ratio 15:2 instead of 30:2.

Explanation of Other Options:

Depth of chest compression up to 5-6 cm (Option A): Correct recommendation; helps generate adequate perfusion.

Allow adequate chest recoil (Option B):Essential for venous return and effective CPR.

Chest compression rate 100-120/min (Option D): Correct rate as per guidelines; ensures adequate cardiac output.

Key Takeaways:

  • Adult CPR ventilation rate: 10-12 breaths/min.
  • Compression-to-ventilation ratio: 30:2 (single rescuer), 15:2 (two rescuers).
  • Depth: 5-6 cm, Rate: 100-120/min, Recoil: mandatory.

question_text: The mask shown below operates based on which of the following mechanisms?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows a High-Flow Venturi Mask, which functions based on Bernoulli's Principle. This principle states that as the velocity of a fluid (in this case, oxygen) increases, the pressure within that fluid decreases.

In this mask, when oxygen flows through a narrow nozzle at high speed, it creates a low-pressure zone that draws in room air through side ports. This process allows the mixing of oxygen with ambient air in precise ratios, delivering a fixed and predictable concentration of oxygen to the patient.

  • It is a high-flow oxygen delivery system.
  • Provides an accurate and consistent FiO2 (fraction of inspired oxygen).
  • Commonly used in patients with COPD or those requiring controlled oxygen therapy.
  • Flow rates typically range from 2 to 15 L/min, depending on the required oxygen concentration.

Explanation for other options:

Bohr Effect (Option A): Refers to the physiological mechanism where hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen decreases in the presence of elevated carbon dioxide levels and lower pH. This promotes oxygen release to body tissues and is crucial in the process of gas exchange.

Boyle's Law (Option B): Describes the inverse relationship between the pressure and volume of a gas when temperature is held constant. As volume increases, pressure decreases, and vice versa.

Mapleson Circuits (Option D): These are semi-closed breathing systems commonly used in anesthesia. They are designed to deliver a mix of oxygen and anesthetic gases while efficiently eliminating carbon dioxide from the patient's exhaled breath.

Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10661642/

question_text: When PEEP-Positive end-expiratory pressure is applied to the airway of a spontaneously breathing patient, it is called:
explanation:
• Positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP),used especially in hypoxemia that is refractory to high level of FiO2,is not a "stand-alone" mode, rather it is applied in conjunction with other ventilator modes.
  • When PEEP is applied to spontaneous breathing patients, the airway pressure is called continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP).

Reference: Clinical Application of Mechanical Ventilation, Fourth Edition by David W. Chang, page no 87

question_text: Which of the following fluorinated anaesthetics dissolve rubber & corrodes metal in vaporizers and breathing systems?
explanation:
• Halothane is a potent, non-inflammable, nontoxic (relatively), colourless liquid with relatively non-pungent(pleasant) vapour
  • It is decomposed by light and stabilised by 0.01% thymol but is stable when stored in amber coloured bottles
  • Although it is decomposed by soda lime, it may be used safely with this mixture
  • The vapour is absorbed by rubber (rubber/gas partition coefficient is 120)
  • It corrodes metals in vaporizers and breathing systems
  • In the presence of moisture, it corrodes aluminium, tin, lead, magnesium and alloys
  • It should be stored in a closed container away from light and heat
  • It is soluble in rubber, and plastics commonly found in anaesthetic circuits
  • This has obvious implications for patients with halothane sensitivity, or who are at risk for malignant hyperthermia, in whom anaesthetic free circuit should be used
  • Halothane is ;arrhythmogenic (as it sensitizes heart to catecholamines at IMAC); bronchodilator (used in asthma), maximum uterine relaxant (not used in pregnancy d/t risk of postpartum haemorrhage), vasodilator & myocardial depressant (1/t BP, JCO & bradycardia)
  • 15-20% of absorbed halothane is metabolized (mostly in liver)
  • It is hepatotoxic and repeated use is contraindicated as it may lead to hepatitis (jaundice)
  • Halothane, Ketamine & Atropine are bronchodilators
  • These agents decrease airway resistance and increase anatomical dead space

Reference: Drugs in Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, Edward Scarth, Susan Smith 5th edition; Stoelting's pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 3th edition

question_text: Which of the following is NOT found in the low pressure circuit on an anesthesia machine?
explanation:
The anesthesia machine, now more properly called the anesthesia workstation, has two main pressure circuits. The higher-pressure circuits consist of the gas supply from the pipelines and tanks, all piping, pressure gauges, pressure reduction regulators, check valves (which prevent backward gas flow), the oxygen pressure sensor shutoff valve (also called the oxygen failure cutoff or fail-safe valve), the oxygen supply failure alarm, and the oxygen flush valve-or, simplistically, everything up to the gas flow control valves and the machine common gas outlet. The low-pressure circuit starts with and includes the gas flow control valves, flowmeters, vaporizers, and vaporizer check valve and goes to the machine common gas outlet. See also figure for explanation to Question 12

Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 7, pp 641-650; Miller: Basics of Anesthesia, ed 6, pp 198-204.

question_text: The most important monitors on the anaesthesia workstation is:
option_b: The Oxygen supply pressure failure alarm
option_d: The Oxygen supply pressure failure cutoff
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Oxygen Analyzer:
    • Continuously monitors the oxygen concentration in the gas mixture delivered to the patient.
    • Critical for evaluating the integrity of the Low-Pressure Circuit, ensuring patient safety.
    • Provides real-time feedback, allowing for immediate corrective actions if oxygen levels drop below safe thresholds.
    • Integral in preventing hypoxia and ensuring adequate oxygen delivery throughout the anaesthetic procedure.
  • N2O/O2 Proportioning System (Option A): Ensures a safe mixture of nitrous oxide and oxygen, preventing hypoxic mixtures but does not provide specific oxygen level measurements.
  • Oxygen Supply Pressure Failure Alarm (Option B): Alerts clinicians to low oxygen supply pressure, which is crucial but does not indicate the actual oxygen concentration being delivered to the patient.
  • Oxygen Supply Pressure Failure Cutoff (Option D): Automatically stops nitrous oxide flow if oxygen supply pressure fails, enhancing safety but lacks the capability to measure oxygen content in the gas mixture.

Key Takeaways:

  • The Oxygen analyzer is vital for continuous monitoring of oxygen levels, ensuring patient safety during anaesthesia.
  • Other monitors assist in maintaining safe operating conditions but do not provide ongoing analysis of the oxygen concentration delivered.
  • The oxygen analyzer's ability to detect issues downstream from the flow control valves makes it an indispensable component of anaesthesia equipment.

question_text: Figure shows the pin index safety system in cylinders. Match the index to the correct gas from the table.
explanation:
• The pin-index system is a safety feature, designed to prevent wrong connection of a cylinder containing one substance to a delivery system of different substance.
  • For example, attaching a nitrous oxide cylinder to the oxygen delivery system would produce 100% N2O, while you may believe you are attempting to give 100% O2. This will cause lethal damage to the patient. To prevent such accidents, PISS (pin-index safety system) was introduced.
  • The system works by having a series of holes drilled into the valve on top of the cylinder in particular positions for each gas - these correspond to pins on the anesthesia machine, which prevent connection unless the pins fit into the respective holes.

Reference: OSCEs in Anesthesia, Page Number-110.

question_text: The Low-pressure circuits include all except
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Low Pressure Circuits (LPC):Encompass components that handle gases at pressures significantly lower than those found in the high-pressure and intermediate-pressure circuits.
    • Include:
      • Flow Meters: Regulate and measure the volume of gases being delivered.
      • Vaporizers: Convert liquid anaesthetic agents into vapor for administration.
      • One-way Outlet Check Valve: Prevents backflow and ensures gas flows in the correct direction towards the patient.
  • Pipeline Sources:
    • Part of the intermediate-pressure circuit, which operates at pressures of 50 to 55 psig (pound-force per square inch).
    • Supplies gases from the central pipeline system to the anaesthesia workstation.
    • Not included in the LPC as it precedes the flow control valves and operates at higher pressures.
  • Flow Meters (Option A): Essential for controlling and measuring gas flow, thus a key component of the LPC.
  • Vaporizers (Option B): Integral for the delivery of anaesthetic agents, functioning within the LPC to mix with carrier gases.
  • One-way Outlet Check Valve (Option C):Critical for ensuring unidirectional gas flow towards the patient, part of the LPC system.

Key Takeaways:

  • The Low-Pressure Circuits focus on components that manage anaesthetic gases at lower pressures.
  • Pipeline sources are categorized under the intermediate-pressure circuit, serving as the supply line to the anaesthesia machine.

question_text: Anaesthesia workstations have:
explanation:
Explanation:

  • E-Cylindersare commonly used in anaesthesia workstations when:
    • Pipeline Supply is Unavailable:They serve as backup when the central gas supply fails.
    • Attachment to Anaesthesia Machine:E-cylinders connect to the machine via the hanger yoke assembly.
  • Hanger Yoke Assembly:
    • Orientation and Support:Holds the cylinder in place.
    • Gas-Tight Seal:Utilizes a Bodok seal to prevent leaks and ensure safe operation.
    • Unidirectional Gas Flow:Ensures gases flow only into the machine, not back to the cylinder.
  • Pin Index Safety System (PISS):
    • Safety Mechanism:Prevents incorrect gas attachment by using a unique pin configuration for each gas type.
    • Prevention of Errors:Essential to avoid potential hazards, such as intraoperative fires, resulting from misidentification of gases.
  • Cylinder Specifications:
    • Internal Volume:Approximately 4.8 liters.
    • Pressurization:Full E-cylinders are pressurized to about 2,000 psig.
    • Gas Capacity:Contains 600 litres of oxygen at 20°C and 1,900 psig or 1,590 litres of nitrous oxide at 745 psig.
  • B Type Cylinders are typically larger and not standard for anaesthesia machines (Option A)
  • C Type Cylinders are not commonly used in clinical settings for anaesthesia (Option B)
  • D Type Cylinders are smaller size, not suitable for the volume of gas required during procedures (Option C)

Key Takeaways:

  • E-type cylindersare integral to anaesthesia workstations, providing essential backup gas supply.
  • PISSenhances safety by preventing gas interchange errors, crucial in maintaining patient safety during anaesthesia.

question_text: The oxygen-flush valve provides which of the following oxygen flows (L/min) to the common gas outlet?
explanation:
The oxygen-flush valve provides gas flow at pipeline pressures of about 45 to 55 psi at 35 to 75 L/min. The high flow of oxygen is provided directly to the common gas outlet, bypassing the flowmeters and vaporizers. One should be careful when using the oxygen-flush valve, as high gas flows at high pressures can cause lung barotrauma in the patient.

Reference: Lippincott's ANESTHESIA REVIEW: 1,001 QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS Paul Sikka, MD, PhD

question_text: Modern vaporizers are
explanation:
Modern vaporizers are agent-specific and temperature-compensated. Also, specific fillers are available for each volatile agent, which prevent filling on the wrong agent. A constant concentration of agent is delivered, unaffected by temperature or flow rates. Temperature compensation is achieved by a metallic strip composed of two different metals, which expands/contracts to deliver a constant concentration of vapor.

Reference: Lippincott's ANESTHESIA REVIEW: 1,001 QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS Paul Sikka, MD, PhD

question_text: A 30 year male patient presents with penetrating injury to the eye. He needs globe repair. His anesthesia management will be
option_c: General anesthesia with depolarizing muscle relaxant
option_d: General anesthesia with non depolarizing muscle relaxant
explanation:
• Repair of the globe will need general anesthesia ,deep plane should be maintained to avoid any coughing or gagging and provide immobile surgical field to the surgeon.
  • Local techniques will not be adequate
  • Use of succinylcholine can cause increased intra ocular pressure and theoretically can cause extrusion of contents. Hence use of non depolarizing muscle relaxants are preferred.

Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anaesthesia, 6th edition, page no. 783

question_text: The correct statement regarding placement of flowmeters:
option_a: Nitrous oxide flowmeter should be downstream among all flowmeters
option_b: Air flowmeter should be downstream among all flowmeters
option_c: Oxygen flowmeter should be downstream among all flowmeters
option_d: Oxygen flowmeter should be upstream among all flowmeters
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Flowmeter Placement:
    • The oxygen flowmeter is ideally placed downstream to prevent hypoxic mixtures.
    • Downstream Positioning:
    • Minimizes risk of hypoxia due to potential leaks in other flowmeters.
    • Ensures that most of the oxygen flow reaches the patient, even if other gases leak.
    • Leak Hazards: Flowmeter leaks can lead to a dangerous hypoxic gas mixture.
    • Nitrous Oxide Flowmeter Issues (Option A): If placed downstream, a leak may allow a large amount of nitrous oxide to flow while oxygen escapes, creating a hypoxic mixture.
    • Flow Rate Ratios: Nitrous oxide and oxygen flow rates are typically set at a 3:1 ratio, making it crucial to prioritize oxygen delivery in case of a leak.
    • Innovations: Newer anaesthesia workstations often use electronic flowmeters, which can help reduce the risk of leaks associated with traditional glass flow tubes.
  • While air flowmeters can be positioned downstream, they should not be prioritized over oxygen placement (Option B)
  • Oxygen flowmeter upstream placement increases the risk of hypoxic mixtures due to leaks from downstream flowmeters (Option D)

Key Takeaways:

  • Oxygen flowmeter placement downstream is critical for patient safety, reducing the risk of hypoxic mixtures.
  • Proper positioning of flowmeters is essential in the anaesthesia machine setup to ensure effective gas delivery.
  • Advancements in technology (like electronic flowmeters) can mitigate risks associated with traditional flowmeter designs.

question_text: Which type of needle is shown in the image?
explanation:
Explanation

The Tuohy needle is characterized by its blunt curved tip and lateral aperture (side hole), designed to guide the epidural catheter into the epidural space. It is primarily used for:

  • Epidural anesthesia, and
  • Pain management procedures such as labor analgesia.

Key features:

  • Blunt curved tip: Minimizes the risk of dural puncture.
  • Side hole: Allows smooth passage of the catheter.
  • Depth markings: Aid in accurate insertion into the epidural space.

The needle is typically 16-18 G and inserted using the loss of resistance technique to identify the epidural space.

Explanation of other options:

Whitacre needle (Option A): A pencil-point spinal needle with a non-cutting tip, designed to reduce the risk of post-dural puncture headache (PDPH).

Sprotte needle (Option B): Another pencil-point spinal needle similar to Whitacre but with a longer lateral opening, allowing smoother cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow.

Quincke-Babcock needle (Option D): A cutting-tip spinal needle that produces a sharp puncture in the dura, increasing the risk of CSF leakage and PDPH. It is commonly used for diagnostic lumbar puncture rather than epidural anaesthesia.

Key takeaways:

  • Tuohy needle: Used for epidural anaesthesia; blunt curved tip prevents dural puncture.
  • Whitacre and Sprotte needles: Used for spinal anaesthesia; non-cutting design reduces PDPH.
  • Quincke-Babcock needle: Cutting type; increases PDPH risk.

question_text: All are true about preoxygenation, except;
option_a: Oxygen is delivered by mask for several minutes prior to anaesthetic induction
option_b: Increasing the duration of apnea without desaturation improves safety
option_c: 100% oxygen must be provided at high flow rates
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Preoxygenation:
    • Purpose: Replaces nitrogen in the lungs with oxygen, increasing the time before desaturation occurs in an apnoeic patient.
    • Benefits:
      • Provides amargin of safetywhile securing the airway and resuming ventilation.
      • Allows for longer apnoea time before haemoglobin desaturation.
  • Distinction from Apnoeic Oxygenation:
    • Apnoeic oxygenationrefers to the physiological process where oxygen diffuses from the oropharynx/nasopharynx into the alveoli during apnoea.
    • Preoxygenationis a preparatory step before induction, whileapnoeic oxygenationis a separate mechanism during apnoea.
  • Oxygen is delivered by mask for several minutes prior to anaesthetic induction (Option A): True; this is a standard practice for effective preoxygenation.
  • Increasing the duration of apnoea without desaturation improves safety (Option B): True; it enhances safety during the induction phase by prolonging the time before desaturation.
  • 100% oxygen must be provided at high flow rates (Option C): True; delivering high-flow 100% oxygen maximizes preoxygenation effectiveness.

Key Takeaways:

  • Preoxygenation is essential for improving patient safety during anaesthesia by delaying hypoxia during airway management.
  • It differs from apnoeic oxygenation, which is a physiological process occurring during apnoea.

question_text: A 53-year old woman was brought to the hospital after she became unconscious in the marriage party. Her ECG shows the following. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
• First Degree Heart Block:
    • Defined by a prolonged PR interval (greater than 0.20 seconds).
    • Every P wave is followed by a QRS complex.
  • Mobitz Type I Heart Block (Wenckebach Phenomenon):
    • The PR interval progressively lengthens until one P wave is not followed by a QRS complex.
    • Exhibits a pattern of dropped beats.
  • Mobitz Type II Heart Block:
    • The PR interval remains constant throughout the cycles.
    • There are intermittent dropped QRS complexes despite consistent PR intervals.
  • Complete Heart Block (Third Degree):
    • There is no relationship between P waves and QRS complexes; atrial and ventricular contractions are independent.

Why Not Other Options

  • A: First degree heart block is characterized by a constant prolonged PR interval without dropped beats.
  • B: Mobitz Type I involves a lengthening PR interval until a beat is dropped, which is not indicated here.
  • D: Complete heart block would show no correlation between P waves and QRS complexes, rather than a constant PR interval.

Key Takeaways:

The most probable diagnosis is Mobitz type II heart block, marked by a constant PR interval with occasional dropped QRS complexes. Recognizing the differences between heart block types is essential for timely management and intervention in cardiac emergencies.

Tags: Neet 2021

Level: Good to know

Reference: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, 26th Edition, Page no. 1199

question_text: A 62-year-old male was brought to the emergency department in an unconscious state. He is having history of coronary artery disease. He was having symptoms of palpitations and dizziness for the past few days. His ECG is showing disordered electrical ventricular activation with no identifiable QRS complexes, no identifiable P-waves and no PR interval. What will be the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
• Ventricular Fibrillation (VF):
    • Characterized by disordered electrical activation of the ventricles.
    • No identifiable QRS complexes are present, indicating chaotic electrical activity.
    • There are no identifiable P-waves and no PR interval, demonstrating a complete lack of organized electrical conduction.
  • Ventricular Tachycardia (VT):
    • Typically features a wide QRS complex with abnormal morphology.
    • There is usually absence of P waves, but the rate is typically greater than 100/min.
  • Polymorphic VT and Torsades de Pointes:
    • These conditions also show a wide QRS complex but differ in rhythm and morphology.
    • Torsades de Pointes specifically involves a pattern of changing morphology with a prolonged QT interval.

Why Not Other Options

  • A: Polymorphic VT shows varying QRS morphology and is organized enough to discern a pattern, which is not seen in this case.
  • C: Monomorphic VT would have identifiable wide QRS complexes and an organized rhythm.
  • D: Torsades de Pointes has a characteristic changing QRS morphology and is usually related to prolonged QT interval.

Key Takeaways:

The most probable diagnosis is ventricular fibrillation, characterized by disordered electrical activity with no identifiable QRS complexes or P-waves. Recognizing these ECG features is crucial for timely intervention in emergency cardiac care.
