question_text: Which skeletal muscle relaxant follows Hoffman elimination?
explanation:
• Atracurium ( Figure 27–4 ) is an intermediate-acting iisoquinolin nondepolarizing muscle relaxant. In addition to hepatic metabolism, atracurium is inactivated by a form of spontaneous breakdown known as Hofmann elimination. The main breakdown products are laudanosine and a related quaternary acid, neither of which possesses neuromuscular blocking properties.
  • Laudanosine is slowly metabolized by the liver and has a longer elimination half-life (ie, 150 minutes). It readily crosses the blood-brain barrier, and high blood concentrations may cause seizures and an increase in the volatile anaesthetic requirement. During surgical anaesthesia, blood levels of laudanosine typically range from 0.2 to 1 mcg/mL however, with prolonged infusions of atracurium in the ICU, laudanosine blood levels may exceed 5 mcg/mL.

Reference

LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12th edition. Chapter 27- Skeletal muscle relaxants by Dr. Marieke Kruidering-Hall,PhD,& Dr. Lundy Campbell, MD. Page no. 467

question_text: A patient was administered succinylcholine and halothane prior to surgery. Soon after, the patient developed sudden muscle rigidity, a core body temperature of 104°F, and elevated pCO<sub>2</sub> levels. Which of the following is the most appropriate medication for management?
explanation:
Explanation:

Malignant hyperthermia is a rare but life-threatening pharmacogenetic disorder of skeletal muscle metabolism.

It is triggered by certain anesthetic agents-especially halothane-and neuromuscular blockers like succinylcholine (SCh).

Pathophysiology:

  • The condition is caused by a hereditary defect in the ryanodine receptor (RyR1) on the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) of skeletal muscles.
  • This defect results in prolonged and uncontrolled calcium release from the SR.
  • Excess intracellular calcium leads to:
    • Sustained muscle contraction
    • Increased metabolism
    • Hyperthermia
    • Lactic acidosis
    • Rhabdomyolysis
    • Hypercapnia (elevated pCO2)

Drug of Choice - Dantrolene:

  • Mechanism: Dantrolene blocks RyR1 calcium channels in skeletal muscle, thereby inhibiting calcium release from the SR.
  • It prevents sustained muscle contraction and reduces metabolic activity, effectively treating malignant hyperthermia.
  • Cardiac and smooth muscles are not significantly affected because they express a different ryanodine receptor subtype (RyR2).

Summary:

  • Triggering agents: Halothane, succinylcholine
  • Mechanism: Uncontrolled calcium release via defective RyR1
  • Clinical features: Muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, elevated pCO2
  • Treatment of choice: Dantrolene, which inhibits RyR1-mediated calcium release in skeletal muscles

Explanation of other options:

Sodium bicarbonate (Option A):

  • Used to treat metabolic acidosis, but it does not stop the underlying muscle rigidity or excessive calcium release.
  • It may be given as a supportive measure but is not the primary treatment.

Lorazepam (Option C):

  • A benzodiazepine used for seizures, anxiety, and muscle relaxation, but it does not address calcium dysregulation in malignant hyperthermia.
  • It does not directly reverse muscle rigidity or lower hyperthermia.

Mannito (Option D): l

  • An osmotic diuretic used for intracranial pressure and acute kidney injury, but it does not treat malignant hyperthermia.
  • Mannitol may help prevent renal failure from rhabdomyolysis but is not the primary treatment.

Key Takeaways:

Dantrolene is the drug of choice for malignant hyperthermia

question_text: Which of the following is not nondepolarizing relaxant agent?
explanation:
• Depolarizing Relaxant Drugs
    • The extremely short duration of action of succinylcholine (5–10 minutes) is due to its rapid hydrolysis by butyrylcholinesterase and pseudo cholinesterase in the liver and plasma, respectively.
    • Plasma cholinesterase metabolism is the predominant pathway for succinylcholine elimination. Since succinylcholine is more rapidly metabolized than mivacurium, its duration of action is shorter than that of mivacurium .
    • The primary metabolite of succinylcholine, succinylmonocholine, is rapidly broken down to succinic acid and choline. Because plasma cholinesterase has an enormous capacity to hydrolyze succinylcholine, only a small percentage of the original intravenous dose ever reaches the neuromuscular junction.
    • In addition, because there is little if any plasma cholinesterase at the motor end plate, a succinylcholine-induced blockade is terminated by its diffusion away from the end plate into extracellular fluid. Therefore, the circulating levels of plasma cholinesterase influence the duration of action of succinylcholine by determining the amount of the drug that reaches the motor end plate.

Reference

LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12th edition. Chapter 27- Skeletal muscle relaxants by Dr. Marieke Kruidering-Hall,PhD,& Dr. Lundy Campbell,MD. Page no. 468

question_text: Reason for preferring Cis-Atracurium over atracurium is:

Cisatracurium

This R-Cis, R-Cis enantiomer of atracurium is nearly 4 times more potent, slower in onset(Option A ruled out), but similar in duration of action.(Option C ruled out)

Like atracurium it undergoes Hofmann elimination(Option D ruled out), but in contrast to the racemate, it is not hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase and hepatic metabolism is limited, so that less of the toxic metabolite is formed.

Most importantly, it does not provoke histamine release and side effects are fewer. Currently, cisatracurium is one of the preferred muscle relaxants, especially for liver/kidney disease patients and for the elderly.

Because plasma cholinesterase has an enormous capacity to hydrolyze succinylcholine, only a small percentage of the original intravenous dose ever reaches the neuromuscular junction.

    • Therefore, the circulating levels of plasma cholinesterase influence the duration of action of succinylcholine by determining the amount of the drug that reaches the motor end plate.

Reference

LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12th edition. Chapter 27- Skeletal muscle relaxants by Dr. Marieke Kruidering-Hall,PhD,& Dr. Lundy Campbell,MD. Page no. 468

question_text: A 45 years old female patient underwent abdominal hysterectomy under general anaesthesia with skeletal muscle relaxant Succinylcholine. Suddenly she develops Muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, rapid onset of tachycardia, hypercapnia, hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis. Which of the following drug should be given to reduce calcium release from Sarcoplasmic reticulum?
explanation:
• Malignant hyperthermia is a heritable genetic disorder of skeletal muscle that occurs in susceptible individuals exposed to volatile anaesthetics while undergoing general anaesthesia . The depolarizing muscle relaxant succinylcholine may also trigger malignant hyperthermia.
    • The malignant hyperthermia syndrome consists of muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, rapid onset of tachycardia and hypercapnia, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis following exposure to one or more triggering agents.
    • Malignant hyperthermia is a rare but important cause of anaesthetic morbidity and mortality. The specific biochemical abnormality is an increase in free cytosolic calcium concentration in skeletal muscle cells.
    • Treatment includes administration of dantrolene (to reduce calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum) and appropriate measures to reduce body temperature and restore electrolyte and acid-base balance

Reference :

LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12th edition. Chapter 25- General Anaesthetics by Dr. Helge Eilers,MD & Dr. Spencer Yost,MD. Page no. 437

question_text:
Adverse effects of depolarizing agents are...
1. Hyperkalemia
2. Hypokalemia
3. Increased intraocular pressure
4. Decreased intraocular pressure
5. Increased intragastric pressure
6. Muscle pain
explanation:
• Hyperkalemia
    • Patients with burns, nerve damage or neuromuscular disease, closed head injury, and other trauma can respond to succinylcholine by releasing potassium into the blood, which, on rare occasions, results in cardiac arrest.
  • Increased Intraocular Pressure
    • Administration of succinylcholine may be associated with the rapid onset of an increase in intraocular pressure (< 60 seconds), peaking at 2–4 minutes, and declining after 5 minutes. The mechanism may involve tonic contraction of myofibrils or transient dilation of ocular choroidal blood vessels. Despite the increase in intraocular pressure, the use of succinylcholine for ophthalmologic operations is not contraindicated unless the anterior chamber is open (“open globe”) due to trauma.
  • Increased Intragastric Pressure
    • In heavily muscled patients, the fasciculations associated with succinylcholine may cause an increase in intragastric pressure ranging from 5 to 40 cm H 2 O, increasing the risk for regurgitation and aspiration of gastric contents. This complication is more likely to occur in patients with delayed gastric emptying (eg, those with diabetes), traumatic injury (eg, an emergency case), eesophage dysfunction, and morbid obesity.
  • Muscle Pain
    • Myalgias are a common postoperative complaint of heavily muscled patients and those who receive large doses (> 1.5 mg/kg) of succinylcholine.

Reference :

LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12th edition. Chapter 27- Skeletal muscle relaxants by Dr. Marieke Kruidering-Hall,PhD,& Dr. Lundy Campbell,MD. Page no. 474

question_text: Not true about priming dose of neuromuscular blockers is?
option_b: Can produce significant muscle paralysis in healthy patient also
option_c: Used to shorten the onset of action
explanation:
• The introduction of short- and intermediate- acting agents has resulted in the greater use of priming doses
  • Theoretically, giving 10% to 15% of the usual intubating dose (Option A)5 min before induction will occupy enough receptors so that paralysis will quickly follow when the balance of relaxant is administered
  • A priming dose does not usually lead to clinically significant paralysis, which requires that 75% to 80% of the receptors be blocked (a neuromuscular margin of safety)
  • Priming can additionally cause measurable deterioration in respiratory function (e.g., decreased forced vital capacity) and may lead to oxygen desaturation in patients with marginal pulmonary reserve
  • These negative side effects are more common in older, sicker patients

question_text: On induction of a patient for a cardiac surgery, large doses of opioid were administered. Following muscle relaxation with a non-depolarizing muscle relaxant, it was found that the patient could not be ventilated by positive pressure by the senior anesthetist. What is the most likely cause for the same?
explanation:
• Rapid IV administration of large doses of an opioid (particularly fentanyl and its derivatives as used in cardiac surgery) can lead to generalized skeletal muscle rigidity
  • This can be severe enough to interfere with manual ventilation
  • Although generally termed chest wall rigidity, evidence supports the conclusion that most of the resistance to ventilation is due to laryngeal musculature contraction
  • Prophylaxis for the stiff chest syndrome.
    • Priming with non-depolarizer.
    • Slow, intermittent, small doses of opioids.
    • Use of inhalational agent
  • Treatment for stiff chest syndrome
    • Neuromuscular blocking agents
    • Naloxone

Reference: Stoelting’s pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 5th edition pg. 223

question_text: The tension which needs to be generated in cardiac muscle fibres before shortening will occur is known as:
explanation:
• The tension which needs to be generated in cardiac muscle fibres before shortening is known as  afterload
  • Preload is the initial length of the cardiac muscle fibre before contraction begins.
  • The volume of blood ejected from the left ventricle with every contraction (ml) is known as stroke volume.
  • The intrinsic ability of cardiac muscle fibres to do work with a given preload and afterload is called contractility.

Reference: Physics, Pharmacology and Physiology for Anaesthetists, Matthew E. Cross, second edition, pg 260.

question_text: Which of the following is correct regarding phase I depolarizing neuromuscular block?
explanation:
• Phase I depolarizing block is preceded by muscle fasciculation
  • During partial neuromuscular block, phase I depolarizing block is characterised by:
    • No fade during repetitive stimulation (tetanic or TOF)
    • No post tetanic facilitation(potentiation)
  • Rapid hydrolysis by butyrylcholinesterase(plasma cholinesterase) terminates phase I depolarizing blockade of succinylcholine
  • Phase II block resembles non-depolarizing block, is characterised by:
    • Fade during repetitive stimulation (tetanic or TOF)
    • Post tetanic facilitation(potentiation)
  • Phase II block can be antagonized by administering a cholinesterase inhibitor like neostigmine

Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

question_text: Mivacurium is short acting due to:
explanation:
• Mivacurium short acting due to rapid hydrolysis by butyrylcholinesterase (aka plasma cholinesterase or pseudocholinesterase)
  • It has an onset of action within 2-3 minutes and a duration of action of 10-20 minutes
  • Patients with atypical pseudocholinesterase→prolonged duration of the block like succinylcholine administration

Note:

  • Shortest acting muscle relaxant-Succinylcholine
  • Shortest acting non-depolarising muscle relaxant - Mivacurium (Gantacurium, if given in options, as it is ultra-short acting)

  • It is a short acting non-depolarizing muscle relaxant due to its metabolism by pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase)

question_text: Which of the following is an incorrect statement concerning rapacuronium?

explanation:

question_text: The Muscle relaxant of choice for renal failure is:
explanation:
• Muscle relaxant of choice for renal failure is Atracurium
  • Atracurium undergoes Hofmann elimination - which is spontaneous non-enzymatic degradation. So renal failure doesn't affect the clearance of atracurium
  • Hence it is the agent of choice in renal failure patients
  • Cis- Atracurium also undergoes Hofmann elimination and is an alternative to atracurium for renal failure patients

Option C & D- Pancuronium and pipecuronium are predominantly eliminated by ultrafiltration by the glomeruli and so the neuromuscular block is prolonged in patients with renal failure

Option A- Vecuronium depends primarily on biliary excretion and secondarily (25%) on renal excretion

Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

question_text: The following are primarily dependent on kidney for excretion except?
explanation:
• Cis-atracurium does not depend on kidney for excretion
  • Cis-atracurium undergoes Hofmann elimination - which is spontaneous non-enzymatic degradation. So renal failure doesn’t affect the clearance of cis atracurium. Hence it is the agent of choice in renal failure patients. Atracurium also undergo Hofmann elimination and so is an alternative to cis atracurium in renal failure
  • Steroidal muscle relaxants are predominantly eliminated by ultrafiltration by the glomeruli before urinary excretion
  • Doxacurium, pancuronium, and pipecuronium are partially excreted by the kidneys, and so the neuromuscular block is prolonged in patients with renal failure(Option B, C & D)

Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

question_text: The following patients are at risk of hyperkalaemia from succinyl choline except?
explanation:

question_text: Muscle relaxant that does not have an active metabolite is?
explanation:
• A small amount of pancuronium (15% to 20%) is metabolized, mainly by deacetylationin the liver(Option A)
  • The metabolites (3-OH, 17-OH, and 3,7-di-OH) are considerably less potent as neuromuscular blockers and are excreted in the urine
  • Accumulation of the 3-OH metabolite is responsible for prolongation of the duration of block induced by pancuronium
  • Vecuronium is metabolized in the liver by deacetylation into three possible metabolites: 3-OH, 17-OH, and 3,17-di-OH vecuronium. The 3-OH metabolite has 80% the neuromuscular blocking potency of vecuronium (Option B)
  • Therefore, during prolonged administration of vecuronium, this metabolite may contribute to prolonged neuromuscular blockade

Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

question_text: Non-depolarizing muscle relaxants are?
explanation:
• Nondepolarizing muscle relaxants bind ACh receptors but are incapable of inducing the conformational change necessary for ion channel opening
  • Because ACh is prevented from binding to its receptors, no end-plate potential develops
  • Neuromuscular blockade occurs even if only one subunit is blocked.
  • Thus, nondepolarizing muscle relaxants function as competitive antagonists.

Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

question_text: Risk factor for postoperative myalgia seen with succinylcholine is?
explanation:
• Postoperative skeletal muscle myalgia, which is particularly prominent in the skeletal muscles of the neck, back, and abdomen, can occur after administration of succinylcholine, especially to young adults undergoing minor surgical procedures that permit early ambulation
  • The exact underlying mechanism of succinylcholine-induced myalgia is not known, but several mechanisms including increased myoplasmic calcium concentrations, degradation of membrane phospholipids, release of free fatty acids, and free radicals are thought to be causative factors

Reference: Yao & Artusio's Anesthesiology: Problem-Oriented Patient Management; Edn 9

question_text: Muscle most resistant to non-depolarizing block is
explanation:
• In general, diaphragm, jaw, larynx & facial muscles (orbicularis oculi) respond & recover from muscle relaxation sooner than the thumb
  • Muscle relaxants cause block in following sequence:
    • Eyelids (ptosis in non-depolarizing & fasciculation in depolarizing is first clinical sign)
    • Imbalance of extra ocular muscles with diplopia (may last for days)
    • Relaxation of muscles of face, jaw, neck & limbs and finally relaxation of abdominal wall &diaphragm (last to be paralyzed)
    • So, head & neck muscles are first affected

Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

question_text: Each of the following statements concerning side effects of succinylcholine when used to paralyze neonates is false
option_c: Dysrhythmias frequently occur following intramuscular injections
explanation:
• Unlike adults, neonates and infants seldom have muscle fasciculations with succinylcholine.
  • The most frequently encountered side effect associated with succinylcholine in neonates and infants is bradycardia, especially when succinylcholine is given intravenously.
  • The incidence of brady dysrhythmias is significantly decreased when the succinylcholine is administered intramuscularly.
  • Other side effects include rhabdomyolysis, myoglobinuria, hyperkalemia, and malignant hyperthermia.

question_text: Which receptor is responsible for the effects of succinylcholine?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Succinylcholine:
    • Type: Depolarizing neuromuscular blocker.
    • Mechanism:
      • Binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors(nAChR) at theneuromuscular junction.
      • Initial effect: Causesdepolarizationof the motor end plate, leading tofasciculations(muscle twitches).
      • Persistent depolarization: Unlike acetylcholine, succinylcholine leads to prolonged depolarization, which results in:
        • Desensitizationof the nAChRs.
        • Inactivationof voltage-gated Na2 channels, preventing further action potentials.
        • Increased K2 permeabilityin the muscle membrane.
    • Result: Failure of action potential generation, leading toneuromuscular blockadeand muscle relaxation.
  • Muscarinic receptor (Option B): Incorrect; muscarinic receptors are primarily involved in parasympathetic functions and are not the target for succinylcholine's action.
  • GABA receptor (Option C): Incorrect; GABA receptors are associated with inhibitory neurotransmission in the central nervous system, unrelated to succinylcholine's mechanism.
  • Dopamine receptor (Option D): Incorrect; dopamine receptors are involved in the central nervous system's reward and motor control pathways, not relevant to succinylcholine's action.

Key Takeaways:

  • Succinylcholineacts throughnicotinic receptors, causing depolarization followed by neuromuscular blockade.
  • Mechanismincludes receptor desensitization and inactivation of sodium channels, leading to muscle relaxation.

question_text: Which drug is used to reverse the muscle relaxant effects of vecuronium when renal function is normal?
explanation:
Explanation:

Sugammadex is a selective binding agent that rapidly and effectively reverses the neuromuscular blockade caused by vecuronium in patients with normal renal function.

  • Vecuronium is a non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker (aminosteroid class) used for muscle relaxation during anesthesia.
  • It works by competitively inhibiting acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction.
  • Sugammadex is a modified gamma-cyclodextrin, specifically designed to encapsulate and inactivate steroid-based neuromuscular blockers like:
    • Vecuronium
    • Rocuronium
  • Upon IV administration, Sugammadex forms a tight 1:1 complex with free vecuronium, rapidly reducing its availability at the receptor sites, thus reversing muscle paralysis.
  • Onset of reversal: Within 2-3 minutes
  • Excretion: Renally cleared; use with caution in renal impairment
  • Advantages: No cholinergic side effects, no need for anticholinergic co-administration

Explanation of other options:

Neostigmine (Option B): An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor traditionally used to reverse non-depolarizing blockers, but it is less effective and slower than sugammadex for vecuronium. Requires co-administration with atropine or glycopyrrolate due to muscarinic effects.

Atropine (Option C): A muscarinic antagonist used to counteract the muscarinic side effects of neostigmine, not used alone to reverse neuromuscular blockade.

Physostigmine (Option D): A cholinesterase inhibitor that crosses the blood-brain barrier and is primarily used to reverse central anticholinergic toxicity, not for neuromuscular blockade reversal.

question_text: While cannulating the internal jugular vein in a patient, you look for a triangle that is formed by:

question_text: 4 hours into a laparotomy surgery, the temperature probe reads a measurement of 28 degrees Celsius. Detrimental effects of hypothermia include all of the following except:

Hypothermia is associated with

question_text: A hemiplegic patient when posted for surgery, which muscle relaxant is to be avoided?

question_text: A 40-year-old male in kidney failure with serum creatinine of 2.1 mg/dl and serum K+ 4.0 Meq/L is posted for surgery. Which of the following muscle relaxants can be used ?
explanation:
• The patient is in renal failure with elevated serum creatinine with normal serum potassium levels. succinyl choline can be safely administered to patients with diminished or absent kidney function provided serum potassium levels are normal.
  • Pancuronium is almost entirely dependent on kidney for excretion (60-90%). Pancuronium has a prolonged elimination half-life in renal failure patients and thus should be used very cautiously.
  • 30% of Vecuronium excretion occurs via the kidney and so its elimination half-life is also prolonged in renal failure.
  • 40-60% of d-tubocurarine is excreted via the kidney and so prolonged effects are seen with renal insufficiency

question_text: A medical representative visits the anesthetic department to provide information to anesthetists on the drug sugammadex. Which statement is true of sugammadex?
option_a: It displaces muscle relaxants from nicotinic receptors, thereby reversing neuromuscular blockade.
option_b: The complex of sugammadex and rocuronium binds to plasma proteins.
option_c: Sugammadex metabolites are found in the urine.
option_d: The recommended dose of sugammadex depends on the level of neuromuscular blockade to be reversed and varies from 2 to 16 mg/kg.
explanation:
• The therapeutic dose of sugammadex depends on the degree of neuromuscular blockade to be reversed and varies from 2 to 16 mg.
  • Option a: Sugammadex binds to neuromuscular blocking agents like rocuronium and vecuronium to form complexes. Formation of these complexes removes drug from the neuromuscular junction, thus reversing neuromuscular blockade.
  • Option b: Both sugammadex and rocuronium will bind to plasma proteins.
  • Option c: In preclinical and clinical studies, renal excretion of the unchanged product of sugammadex has been observed with no metabolites being formed.

Reference : https://anaesthesiology.gr/media/File/pdf/WFSA%20tutorial%20332%20An%20Overview%20of%20Sugammadex.pdf

question_text: 20-year-old man has presented for emergency repair of torsion of the testis. He is it and well but is allergic to suxamethonium. He had lunch 4 hours ago. A modified rapid sequence induction with rocuronium is planned. Which of the following best describes rocuronium?
option_b: Neostigmine is its only reversal agent.
option_c: Does not exhibit fade and post-tetanic potentiation.
explanation:
Both rocuronium and vecuronium are non-depolarizing muscle relaxants.

Option b: Neostigmine displaces the muscle relaxant from the receptor, thus facilitating muscle contraction, whereas the newer reversal ‘sugammadex’ binds to neuromuscular blocking agents like rocuronium and vecuronium to form complexes.

Option c: being non-depolarizing muscle relaxant, rocuronium exhibits fading of train of four and post titanic potentiation.

Option d: it is not known to cause hyperkalemia. Succinylcholine is known to cause hyperkalemia.

Reference: Stoelting’s pharmacology and physiology in anesthetic practice 5th edition pg 328-333.

question_text: You are enrolled in an institutional study comparing neostigmine and sugammadex for reversal of neuromuscular blockade. For cases where sugammadex will be used to assess reversal efficacy, which muscle relaxants should be administered to the study subjects?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Sugammadex is a modified gamma-cyclodextrin specifically designed to reverse neuromuscular blockade produced by vecuronium and rocuronium.
  • It encapsulates these steroidal non-depolarizing agents, forming a water-soluble complex that removes them from the neuromuscular junction, allowing rapid and reliable reversal.
  • Because it works effectively on both rocuronium and vecuronium, either agent may be used in the study protocol. (Option C)

Clinical features and drug associations:

  • Sugammadex: Binds and inactivates rocuronium and vecuronium through encapsulation, provides rapid reversal, minimal muscarinic side effects, primary reversal agent for steroidal non-depolarizing blockers. (Option C)
  • Vecuronium: Steroidal non-depolarizing relaxant reversible by sugammadex, appropriate for study use.
  • Rocuronium: Also reversed rapidly and reliably by sugammadex,suitable for study inclusion.
  • Agents outside these: Not appropriate because sugammadex does not reverse atracurium, cisatracurium, pancuronium, or depolarizing agents.

Key Takeaways:

  • Sugammadex reverses neuromuscular blockade produced specifically by rocuronium and vecuronium.
  • It works by encapsulating these steroidal neuromuscular blockers, rapidly removing them from the neuromuscular junction.
  • This makes either rocuronium or vecuronium appropriate for studies involving sugammadex efficacy.
  • It provides faster and more predictable reversal compared to neostigmine.

question_text: Following administration of a muscle relaxant, the patient develops erythema, flushing and a drop in blood pressure. Which of the following agents is most likely responsible?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given features of erythema, flushing and drop in blood pressure developing after administration of a muscle relaxant point to the use of atracurium.

  • Atracurium is a non-depolarising muscle relaxant with intermediate duration.
  • It undergoes metabolism through plasma esterases and spontaneous degradation in plasma and tissues via Hofmann elimination, producing less-active metabolites.
  • Due to this, it does not show prolonged elimination half-life in patients with renal impairment, making it a suitable choice in such cases.
  • Atracurium can trigger histamine release, potentially causing bronchospasm, hypotension, and increased bronchial and salivary secretions, though the effect is less pronounced than with tubocurarine unless injected rapidly.
  • Cisatracurium, the cis-isomer, is metabolised similarly but is more potent than atracurium and does not cause histamine release. (Option C ruled out)
  • Neuromuscular blocking agents are broadly categorised into depolarising and competitive (non-depolarising) types.
  • Currently, succinylcholine is the only depolarising agent widely used in clinical practice, while several competitive/nondepolarizing agents are available.
  • Their primary applications include aiding endotracheal intubation and providing skeletal muscle relaxation during surgical procedures.
  • Some of the nondepolarizing agents classified according to their duration of action are given in the table below.

Explanation of other options:

Vecuronium (Option A): Vecuronium, a non-depolarising muscle relaxant of intermediate duration, is not commonly associated with histamine release. It undergoes hepatic and renal elimination.

Pancuronium (Option D): Pancuronium, an amino-ester, is a long-acting competitive muscle relaxant that is not frequently associated with histamine release. It exhibits antimuscarinic receptor activity, is eliminated via both the kidneys and liver, and its vagolytic effects can lead to tachycardia, hypertension, and increased cardiac output.

question_text: Which of the following would NOT result in an increase in intraocular pressure?
option_a: Increase in Paco2 from 35 to 40 mm Hg
option_c: Acute rise in venous pressure from coughing
option_d: 100 mg IV succinylcholine in a patient in whom eye muscles have been detached from the globe
explanation:
Normal intraocular pressure is 10 to 22 mm Hg. In general, IV anesthetics, with the possible exception of ketamine, decrease intraocular pressure. In addition, nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers, inhaled anesthetics, narcotics, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, osmotic diuretics, and hypothermia decrease intraocular pressure. However, elevation of Paco2 out of the physiologic range, as seen with hypoventilation as well as arterial hypoxemia, will increase intraocular pressure. Depolarizing neuromuscular blockers, such as succinylcholine, also increase intraocular pressure. This increase in intraocular pressure occurs when succinylcholine is administered IM or IV. Pretreatment with a nondepolarizing muscle relaxant before administering succinylcholine may attenuate the rise in intraocular pressure. The mechanism for the increase in intraocular pressure after succinylcholine use is related to drug-induced cycloplegia rather than contraction of extraocular muscles, as this increase in intraocular pressure will occur even if the intraocular muscles are cut. The greatest increase in intraocular pressure occurs with coughing or vomiting, where the intraocular pressure may increase as much as 35 to 50 mm Hg. The proposed mechanism for the acute increase in intraocular pressure is an increase in venous pressure. There does not appear to be a change in intraocular pressure with changes within normal physiologic ranges in arterial blood pressure or Paco2

Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 7, pp 1375-1376; Miller: Basics of Anesthesia, ed 6, pp 487-488.

question_text: Dose of which of the following muscle relaxant must be calculated on the basis of total body weight of an obese person rather than its ideal weight?
explanation:
• In morbidly obese persons, doses of
    • Atracurium
    • Cisatracurium
    • Succinyl choline
    • Mivacurium
    • Neostigmine
    • Midazolam (initiation dose)
    • Propofol (maintenance dose) are calculated based on total body weight (TBW)
  • Dose of Fentanyl, Alfentanyl or Sufentanil are calculated based on total body weight (TBW) or corrected weight (i.e. IBW + 0.4 x excess weight;)
  • Pancuronium, Vecuronium, Rocuronium, Remifentanil, Morphine, Paracetamol, Propofol (induction dose) and Midazolam(continuous dose) are calculated based on ideal body weight (IBW)

Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

question_text: Which of the following muscle relaxant can cause pain on IV injection Site
explanation:
• Rocuronium is desacetoxy analogue of vecuronium with a low potency (1/6 - 1/8 of vecuronium) and so rapid onset of action (because potency and speed of onset are inversely related)
  • It is the fastest (most rapid) acting nondepolarizing muscle relaxant (75 sec), which is slightly slower than depolarizing muscle relaxant succinylcholine &non-depolarizing rapacuronium only
  • Rocuronium injection can cause pain on injection site, which may be decreased by alkalinizing the solution
  • Other painful injections include Etomidate, Propofol, Methohexital and Thiopental
  • Rocuronium would clearly be the best choice of nondepolarizing Muscle relaxants for rapid sequence induction, because of its:
    • Rapid onset of action
    • Short duration of action
    • Minimal cardiovascular S/E
  • Rocuronium is also suitable for rapid sequence induction but at cost of much longer duration of action

Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

question_text: Muscle relaxant which can cause seizures:
explanation:
• Atracurium can cause seizure due to accumulation of its metabolite, Laudanosine
  • Laudanosine, a tertiary amine, is a breakdown product of Atracurium’s Hofmann elimination
  • It has CNS stimulating properties, can cross Blood brain barrier and can result in precipitation of seizures
  • But this is significant only with large doses and hepatic failure
  • Cisatracurium is a stereoisomer of atracurium which results in lesser laudanosine production than atracurium

Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

question_text: Among the non-depolarizing muscle relaxants, a few exhibit vagolytic properties. They are
explanation: Reference: FRCA A to Z, edition 5, page no 408

question_text: MH and neuroleptic malignant syndrome share each of the following characteristics EXCEPT
option_d: Flaccid paralysis after administration of vecuronium
explanation:
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a potentially fatal disease that affects 0.5% to 1% of all patients being treated with neuroleptic (antipsychotic) drugs. The syndrome develops gradually over 1 to 3 days in young males and is characterized by the following:

  1. Hyperthermia,
  2. Skeletal muscle rigidity,
  3. Autonomic instability manifested by changes in blood pressure and heart rate, and
  4. Fluctuating levels of consciousness.

The mortality from neuroleptic malignant syndrome is 20% to 30%. Liver transaminases and creatine phosphokinase levels are often elevated in these patients. Treatment includes supportive care and administration of dantrolene. This disease may mimic MH because of its many similarities. One difference between neuroleptic malignant syndrome and MH is the fact that nondepolarizing muscle relaxants such as vecuronium or cisatracurium will cause flaccid paralysis in patients with neuroleptic malignant syndrome but not in patients with MH.

Reference: Hines: Stoelting's Anesthesia and Co-Existing Disease, ed 6, pp 540, 635-640.

question_text: What percentage of a term newborn's total body weight consists of water?
explanation:
The body compartment volumes change with age. Muscle contains about 75% water, whereas adipose tissue contains only 10% water. Overall, total body water decreases with age mainly due to a decrease in extracellular fluid, whereas the muscle and fat content increases. The fraction of total body weight that consists of water is 80% in premature newborns, 75% in term newborns, and 60% in 6-month old infants and in adults. These alterations in body composition have implications for the volume of distribution and redistribution of drugs.

Reference: Davis: Smith's Anesthesia for Infants and Children, ed 8, p 123; Miller: Miller's Anesthesia, ed 8, pp 2763-2764.

question_text: Dibucaine number refers to
explanation:
• Pseudocholinesterase deficiency causes prolonged residual paralysis at normal Sch dose (1-2 mg/kg) whereas, phase 2 non-depolarization blockade occurs after administration of →higher doses >6 (7-10) mg/kg
  • Scoline apnoea is prolonged residual paralysis after administration of succinyl choline (suxamethonium)
  • It can be seen in patients with hereditary (inherited) atypical pseudocholinesteraseenzyme (homozygous >>> heterozygous)and phase II (non-depolarizing) block.
  • Decreased level of normal pseudocholinesterase (not choline esterase) enzyme would usually not result in prolonged apnoea unless the surgery was very short. In other words, in contrast to doubling or tripling of blockade duration seen in patients with heterozygous atypical enzyme or patients with low (normal/typical) enzyme levels, patients with homozygous atypical enzyme→ will have a very prolonged blockade (4-8 hrs) following Sch administration
  • Prolonged apnoea after suxamethonium is best managed by providing mechanical ventilation, maintaining anaesthesia and continuous monitoring until muscle function returns to normal
  • It has reduced mortality to very low levels. Transfusion of fresh frozen plasma (as it provides pseudocholinesterase) & purified pseudo cholinesterase is beneficial & can antagonize the block but is not recommended as its infectious risks outweigh its potential benefits i.e. Mivacurium

Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

question_text: In a patient who is having a neuromuscular disease, myasthenia graves, what is true in regards to muscle relaxants
explanation:
• Myasthenia gravis. Autoimmune disease characterized by weakness and increased fatigability of skeletal muscle.
  • Caused by an immune response in which IgG autoantibodies are produced against the acetylcholine receptors of the neuromuscular junction postsynaptic membrane.
  • Peri-operatively: there is increased sensitivity to non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs and relative resistance to suxamethonium with increased tendency to develop dual block.
  • Tracheal intubation and IPPV are usually performed without neuromuscular blocking drugs, using e.g., propofol and/or a volatile agent.

Reference: FRCA A TO Z, page no 392

question_text: When performing a rapid-sequence induction (RSI) for an emergency caesarean delivery, which of the following muscle relaxants is desirable to use after the IV induction agent is administered?
explanation:
• When performing an RSI for a caesarean section, the patient is preoxygenated, and after you ascertain that intubation should be easy, you inject your IV induction agents (e.g., propofol, ketamine, or etomidate) followed by a paralytic drug to facilitate oral endotracheal intubation.
  • Thiopental is another IV general anesthetic that can be used.
  • Paralysis to optimize tracheal intubation conditions can be obtained with either succinylcholine (30-45 seconds) or rocuronium (< 60 seconds).
  • Vecuronium can also be used but is less desirable because it has a slower onset of action of 144 seconds.
  • Atracurium is the least desirable of the listed drugs due to the significant histamine release, resultant hypotension, and slow onset of action.
  • Although cis-atracurium has little histamine release, it has a very slow onset of action and is not recommended for an RSI induction if succinylcholine, rocuronium, or vecuronium is available.

Reference: Miller's Anesthesia, 8th Edition, Page Number-2345.

question_text: Which of the following muscle relaxants is eliminated by renal excretion?
explanation:
• The duration of action of neuromuscular blocking drugs is related to the dose administered, as well as how the drug is metabolized or handled in the body.
  • Succinylcholine normally is rapidly metabolized by plasma cholinesterase and has an ultrashort duration of action.
  • The intermediate-duration neuromuscular blockers atracurium and cis-atracurium undergo chemical breakdown in the plasma (Hofmann elimination), as well as ester hydrolysis.
  • Vecuronium and rocuronium also have intermediate duration of actions and undergo primarily hepatic metabolism and biliary excretion with limited renal excretion (10%-25%).
  • Only the long-duration neuromuscular blocker Pancuronium is primarily excreted in the urine (80%).
  • In patients with renal failure, the duration of action of neuromuscular blockers is not prolonged with atracurium or cis-atracurium; is slightly prolonged with vecuronium and rocuronium; and is markedly prolonged with d-tubocurarine, Pancuronium, doxacurium, and pipecuronium.
  • Of the long-duration drugs, 80% of Pancuronium, 70% of doxacurium, and 70% of pipecuronium are renally excreted unchanged in the urine.
  • d-tubocurarine has a little more liver excretion and a little less renal elimination compared with Pancuronium.

Reference: Miller’s Anesthesia, ed 8, pp 975–977.

question_text: Which of the following drugs is used to reverse the muscle relaxation caused by vecuronium?
explanation:
Explanation:

Vecuronium is a non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker that competitively antagonizes acetylcholine (ACh) at the nicotinic receptors in the neuromuscular junction, preventing depolarization.

Neostigmine is an anticholinesterase. It inhibits acetylcholinesterase, leading to increased ACh concentration at the neuromuscular junction, which outcompetes vecuronium and reverses its effect.

Reversal with neostigmine is usually combined with an antimuscarinic agent (e.g., atropine or glycopyrrolate) to counteract muscarinic side effects like bradycardia, salivation, or bronchospasm.

Explanation of Other Options:

Atropine (Option B): Used along with neostigmine to prevent muscarinic side effects; it does not reverse neuromuscular blockade by itself.

Dantrolene sodium (Option C): Used in malignant hyperthermia; acts on ryanodine receptors to reduce calcium release, not to reverse vecuronium.

Baclofen (Option D): A GABA-B agonist, used as a muscle relaxant in spasticity, not in anesthesia reversal.

Key Takeaways:

  • Neostigmine is the classical reversal agent for vecuronium.
  • Must be given with atropine/glycopyrrolate.
  • Sugammadex is another modern reversal agent, but specifically for amino steroid NMBs (rocuronium, vecuronium).

question_text: You are administering anesthesia for a cervical spine procedure, and the surgeon has indicated that she plans to monitor somatosensory-evoked potentials (SSEPs) and motor-evoked potentials (MEPs). Your anesthetic plan includes avoidance of long- acting muscle relaxants in addition to avoiding the use of
option_a: Dexmedetomidine to smooth out the anesthetic delivery
option_b: Continuous propofol infusion as anesthesia maintenance
option_c: Half MAC of nitrous oxide to supplement the inhalation agent
option_d: 1 MAC or higher of sevoflurane as needed for maintenance anesthesia
explanation:
• EPs are altered by many variables other than neural damage.
  • In general, intravenous anesthetic techniques (with or without nitrous oxide) cause minimal changes, whereas volatile agents (halothane, sevoflurane, desflurane, and isoflurane) are best avoided or used at a constant low concentration.

Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 130.

question_text: Succinyl choline is contraindicated in all except?
explanation:
• Succinyl choline is not contraindicated in liver failure
  • Even though in liver failure, the amount of butyryl cholinesterase will decrease (to 20% of normal) leading to prolonged neuromuscular blockade, it is still not a major concern
  • Succinyl choline is contraindicated in head injury (transient rise in ICP), burns patient and muscle dystrophies like Duchenne muscular dystrophy due to the risk of dangerous hyperkalaemia

Relative Contraindications of Succinylcholine:

  • Burn injury
  • Massive trauma
  • Severe intraabdominal infection
  • Spinal cord injury
  • Encephalitis
  • Stroke
  • Guillain-Barre syndrome
  • Severe Parkinson’s disease
  • Tetanus
  • Prolonged total body immobilization
  • Ruptured cerebral aneurysm
  • Polyneuropathy
  • Closed head injury
  • Haemorrhagic shock with metabolic acidosis
  • Myopathies (e.g., Duchenne’s dystrophy)

Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

question_text: In a patient who is having a neuromuscular condition, chronic denervation injury, what is true in regards to muscle relaxants
explanation:
• Denervation hypersensitivity.
  • Increased sensitivity of denervated skeletal muscle to acetylcholine.
  • Develops approximately 4–5 days after denervation, and is due to proliferation of extra-junctional acetylcholine receptors over the entire muscle membrane, instead of being restricted to the neuromuscular junction.
  • Thought to be the mechanism underlying the exaggerated hyperkalemic response to suxamethonium seen after peripheral nerve injuries.
  • Its cause is unclear.
  • Also occurs in smooth muscle.

Reference: FRCA A TO Z, page no 178

question_text: A 30-year male patient presents with penetrating injury to the eye. He needs globe repair. His anesthesia management will be
option_d: General anesthesia with non-depolarization muscle relaxant
explanation:
• Repair of the globe will need general anesthesia, deep plane should be maintained to avoid any coughing or gagging and provide immobile surgical field to the surgeon.
  • Local techniques will not be adequate.
  • Use of succinylcholine can cause increased intra ocular pressure and theoretically can cause extrusion of contents.
  • Hence use of non-depolarizing muscle relaxants is preferred.

Reference: Morgan and Mikhail’s clinical anesthesia, 6th edition, page no . 783

question_text: A 50-year-old male who is a case of pleomorphic adenoma is posted for superficial parotidectomy. Muscle relaxant of choice is?
explanation:
• Muscle relaxants are avoided during parotid surgeries.
  • Most common surgery for pleomorphic adenoma is superficial parotidectomy with facial nerve dissection.
  • The surgeon may request the omission of NMBs during neck dissection, thyroidectomy, or parotidectomy to allow nerve identification (e.g., spinal accessory, facial nerves) by direct nerve stimulation and thereby facilitate their preservation.

Reference: Morgan and mikhail’s clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition pg 793.

question_text: A 28 years old female, a case of severe preeclampsia, has been administered magnesium sulphate in the labor room, following which decision has been taken to opt for an emergency LSCS due to fetal bradycardia. All drug doses have to be reduced after administering magnesium sulphate except
explanation:
• Magnesium enhances the effects of other CNs depressants and NMB agents; 30–50% of the normal dose of non-depolarizing relaxants should be used to maintain neuromuscular blockade in the presence of magnesium sulfate.
  • Acute administration of magnesium sulfate prior to the use of suxamethonium appears to prevent potassium release and may reduce the incidence and severity of muscle pains.
  • It does not affect local anesthetic doses.

Reference: Drugs in Anesthesia and Intensive Care, Edward Scarth, Susan Smith 5th edition pg 235

question_text: Regarding acute pain, all of the following statements are true except:
option_a: It is caused by noxious stimulation due to injury, a disease process, or the abnormal function of muscle or viscera
option_c: Four physiological processes are involved: transduction, transmission, modulation, and perception
option_d: It is associated with a systemic neuroendocrine stress response
explanation:
• Acute pain can be Nociceptive and Neuropathic
  • Nociceptive pain is caused by activation or sensitization of peripheral nociceptors, specialized receptors that transduce noxious stimuli.
  • Acute pain is almost always nociceptive. Nociceptive pain serves to detect, localize, and limit tissue damage.
  • All other statements given above regarding acute pain are true.

Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 1050.

question_text: A patient in the pain clinic complaints of tight, band-like pain in the bilateral frontal region. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Migraine headaches are typically described as throbbing or pounding and are usually unilateral.

Trigeminal neuralgia (or tic douloureux) is classically unilateral and usually located in the V2 or V3 distribution of the trigeminal nerve. It has an electric shock quality.

Cluster headaches are classically unilateral and periorbital, described as a burning or drilling sensation that may awaken the patient from sleep.

Tension headaches are classically described as tight, band-like pain or discomfort that is often associated with neck muscle tightness. The headache may be frontal, temporal, or occipital, and is more often bilateral than unilateral.

Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 1073, 1074.

question_text: After administering antibiotic in a patient under general anesthesia, patient had delayed recovery from muscle relaxants. Which antibiotic must have been administered from among the following?
explanation:
• Aminoglycoside antibiotics potentiate the effects of NDMRs (Non-depolarizing Neuromuscular blocker)
  • While penicillin, cephalosporins, erythromycin, and tetracycline are devoid of neuromuscular effects
  • Gentamicin belongs to aminoglycoside family, and thus augments the effects of NDMRs

Reference: Stoeltings pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 5th edition pg. 332

question_text: Which of the following is capable of triggering malignant hyperthermia
explanation:
• Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is a life-threatening hypermetabolic state of skeletal muscle that is triggered by the volatile inhaled anesthetics—isoflurane, desflurane, and sevoflurane—and by the depolarizing muscle relaxant succinylcholine.
  • Malignant hyperthermia presents as an increase in carbon dioxide production, acidosis, cardiac arrhythmias, muscle rigidity, and hyperthermia.
  • Death can occur if the MH crisis is not managed appropriately and early in the course of the episode.
  • The mainstay of treatment is I.V. dantrolene.

Reference: stoelting’s anesthesia and coexisting diseases sixth edition pg 635

question_text: On induction of anesthesia and muscle relaxation by succinylcholine, a patient shows recovery from succinylcholine after 25 mins. He was found to have dibucaine number 55. Which variant of pseudocholinesterase genotype would this patient be having?
explanation:
• Dibucaine number reflects the quality of the cholinesterase enzyme circulating in the plasma.
  • In case of the usual typical butyrylcholinesterase genotype (E1uE1u), the dibucaine number is 70 or higher, whereas in individuals homozygous for the atypical gene, the dibucaine number is less than 30.
  • In individuals with the heterozygous atypical variant (E1uE1a), the dibucaine number is in the range of 40 to 60.
  • In individuals with the homozygous atypical genotype (E1aE1a), the neuromuscular block induced by succinylcholine or mivacurium is prolonged to 4 to 8 hours, and in individuals with the heterozygous atypical genotype (E1uE1a), the period of neuromuscular block induced by succinylcholine or mivacurium is about 1.5 to 2 times that seen in individuals with the usual genotype (E1uE1u).

Reference: stoeltings pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 5th edition pg 326

question_text: A patient with Guillain Barre syndrome has been posted for a surgery under general anesthesia. Which of the following is contraindicated?
explanation:
Succinylcholine has been associated with severe hyperkalemia in patients with burns, severe abdominal infections, severe metabolic acidosis, closed head injury, or conditions associated with upregulation of extra-junctional acetylcholine receptors (e.g., hemiplegia or paraplegia, muscular dystrophies, Guillain-Barré syndrome)

Reference: Stoelting’s pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 5th edition pg 327.

question_text: Dibucain number refers to ?
explanation: Ans. is 'a' i.e., Ach chlinestrase activity derangement Dibucain number : Dibucain (a local anaesthetic) inhibits 80% of normal pseudocholinesterase and 20% of atypical (non-functional) pseudocholinesterase. Therefore normal dibucain number is 70- 80%. Dibucain number is used to measure the activity of atypical pseudocholinesterase.

question_text: A 54-year-old male patient is admitted for TIPSS (trans jugular intrahepatic Porto systemic shunt) procedure. He is an alcoholic, known case of chronic Liver disease and hepatorenal syndrome. The plan is to give general anesthesia. The muscle relaxant of choice will be
explanation:
• Atracurium has Two modes of metabolism:
  • Ester hydrolysis (60% of dose) in plasma by non-specific esterases to laudanosine, a quaternary acid and alcohol.
  • Hofmann degradation, i.e., spontaneous breakdown to laudanosine and monoacrylate. This occurs at body temp and pH. Acidosis and cold slow the rate of degradation.

Others metabolism: Vecuronium- liver, Rocuronium- duration of action prolonged in liver/ renal disease.

Reference: FRCA A TO Z, page no 56

question_text: A 22-year-old parturient is anesthetized for an emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy. She is in the twenty-fourth week of gestation and receives general sevoflurane anesthesia and has received rocuronium for muscle relaxation. Just before emergence, muscle relaxation is reversed with glycopyrrolate and neostigmine. Three minutes later, the fetal heart rate falls to 88 beats/min. The most likely cause of this is
explanation:
Atropine and scopolamine cross the placenta easily, whereas glycopyrrolate is poorly transferred across the placenta. Although neostigmine crosses the placenta poorly, enough does cross the placenta and can cause fetal bradycardia in utero. That is why it is better to reverse muscle relaxants in pregnant patients for nondelivery surgery with neostigmine and atropine

Reference: Butterworth: Morgan & Mikhail';s Clinical Anesthesiology, ed 5, p 229.

question_text: In a patient with compartment syndrome, which of the following signs would be the last to appear?
explanation:
Whenever perfusion to an extremity is inadequate (e.g., trauma or poor perfusion), hypoxic edema develops, producing swelling. When this occurs in a compartment, tissue pressures rise, decreasing capillary perfusion. Symptoms of compartment syndrome include extreme pain unrelieved by analgesics, paresthesias, paralysis, and pallor. Extensive rhabdomyolysis may develop as well as permanent nerve and muscle injury in the compartment. Because the problem is at the tissue level, pulses and capillary refill may still be present. Treatment includes fasciotomy to relieve the elevated pressure

Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 7, p 1514; Miller: Miller's Anesthesia, ed 8, p 2450.

question_text: Which is the shortest acting muscle relaxant?
explanation:
• Suxamethonium is the shortest acting muscle relaxant
  • It has a rapid onset (30-60 s) and short duration of action (typically less than 10 min) due to rapid hydrolysis by butyrylcholinesterase (aka plasma cholinesterase or pseudocholinesterase)
  • It is used in anaesthesia as a skeletal muscle relaxant to facilitate tracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation surgical procedures
  • Suxamethonium is recognised as a potential triggering agent in individuals susceptible to malignant hyperthermia and therefore the use of Suxamethonium is contraindicated in patients with a personal or family history of this condition
  • Ultra short acting (<10 minutes)
    • Gantacurium
  • Short-acting (10-20 minutes)
    • Mivacurium
  • Intermediate-acting (20-50 minutes)
    • Atracurium
    • Cisatracurium
    • Vecuronium
    • Rocuronium
  • Long-acting (>50 minutes)
    • Pancuronium
    • Pipecuronium
    • Doxacurium
    • Metocurine
    • d-tubocurarine

Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

question_text:
Choose the correct option for the given statements:
Assertion: Some muscles reflect respiratory muscle response better than others
Reason: All muscle groups demonstrate equal sensitivities to muscle relaxants.
option_a: Both assertion and reason are false.
option_b: Assertion is true but reason is false.
option_c: Both assertion and reason are true, and reason is correct for assertion.
option_d: Both assertion and reason are true, but reason is not correct for assertion
explanation:
• When monitoring neuromuscular blockade, it is important to realize that different muscle groups demonstrate different sensitivities to muscle relaxants.
  • Some muscles reflect respiratory muscle response better than others.

Reference: Fundamentals of anaesthesia 4th edition, Ted Lin, Tim Smith and Colin Pinnock, chapter 45, pg 881.

question_text: All of the following statements are correct about the following image except:
option_a: Red box is known as post tetanic potentiation
option_b: Post tetanic count >5 indicates profound neuromuscular blockade
option_c: Post tetanic count of >15 is equivalent to two twitches in TOF
option_d: Post tetanic potentiation is seen in presence of non-depolarizing agent
explanation:
• Intense muscle blockade can completely abolish the response to a train of four.
  • Tetanic stimulation increases the mobilization of ACh in the presynaptic membrane.
  • Subsequent electrical stimulation uses twitches at 1-second intervals, releasing supra-normal concentrations of ACh sufficient to overcome the effect of non-depolarizing relaxants. This is called POST TETANIC POTENTIATION.
  • PTC < 5 indicates profound neuromuscular blockade.
  • A PTC > 15 is at least equivalent to two twitches of a TOF, and at this level, successful pharmacological reversal of the remaining muscle blockade is possible.
  • Post tetanic potentiation is seen in presence of non-depolarizing agent and phase II block with succinylcholine.

Reference: Fundamentals of anaesthesia 4th edition, Ted Lin, Tim Smith and Colin Pinnock, chapter 45, pg 883.

question_text: Muscle relaxant which is excreted exclusively by kidney (so C/I in renal failure) and most sensitive to patients of myasthenia gravis
explanation:
• Galamine is totally (exclusively) excreted by kidney, so is contraindicated in renal failure
  • In myasthenia gravis, Isoflurane(1st) &Propofol(2nd), are anaesthesia of choice
  • It is resistant to depolarizing MRg. Sch & sensitive to non-depolarizingMuscle relaxants e.g. Galamine
  • Muscle relaxants of choice in Myasthenia gravis are→Atracurium (1st in 1/10 dose), Cisatracurium (2nd) &Mivacurium or Rapacurium.

Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

question_text: 28-year-old trauma patient sustained a fracture and spinal cord transection at the T9 level. Having spent a long time on the ITU, he is currently in community rehabilitation. He is unable to walk and mobilizes in a wheelchair. He has developed sepsis from an infected pressure sore on his coccygeal area and needs urgent debridement. An exaggerated response to depolarizing muscle relaxants in this patient would be due to which one of the following?
explanation:
• Extra-junctional nicotinic receptors proliferate in denervation injuries and in burns patients and are located along the muscle membrane.
  • The worry in these circumstances is that when these extra-junctional acetylcholine receptors are stimulated by depolarizing muscle relaxants, a massive efflux of potassium will ensue from the muscle cell – enough to precipitate a cardiac arrest.
  • Option a: Pre-junctional receptors are present on the pre-junctional neuromuscular membrane and have a role in ‘fade' phenomena seen with nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade.
  • Option c: Nicotinic post-junctional receptors are present at the post-junctional membrane of the neuromuscular junction and are necessary for normal neuromuscular transmission to occur.
  • Option d: Antibodies to acetylcholine receptors are seen in myasthenia gravis.

Reference: Anaesthesia UK. he neuromuscular junction. http://www.frca.co.uk/article. aspx?articleid=228

question_text: The Laudanosine is a metabolite of?
explanation:
• Laudanosine, a tertiary amine, is a breakdown product of Atracurium’s Hofmann Elimination
  • Laudanosine has CNS stimulating properties and can result in precipitation of seizures
  • But this is significant only with large doses and hepatic failure as it is metabolized by liver and excreted in urine and bile
  • Cis-atracurium also produces laudanosine but is about five times lesser than atracurium

Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

question_text: Cause of convulsions seen with prolonged infusion of atracurium is?
explanation:
• Atracurium has been designed to undergo spontaneous degradation at physiologic temperature and pH by a mechanism called Hofmann elimination, yielding →laudanosine (a tertiary amine) and a monoquaternary acrylate as metabolites
  • Laudanosine easily crosses the blood-brain barrier, and it has central nervous system stimulating properties and seizure activity in people with decreased seizure potential

Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

question_text: Reversal of neuromuscular blockade is accomplished with all except?
explanation:
• Anticholinergic drugs like Glycopyrrolate and Atropine are used only to attenuate the undesirable muscarinic effects of anticholinesterase reversal agents
  • Reversal agents commonly used in clinical practice:
    • Cholinesterase inhibitors: Neostigmine (most common), edrophonium, and pyridostigmine
    • Sugammadex, a cyclodextrin, is the first selective relaxant binding agent for rocuronium and vecuronium
    • L-Cysteine causes inactivation of gantacurium

Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

question_text: Sugammadex is used for the reversal of:
explanation:
• Sugammadex is a cyclodextrin
  • It is the first selective relaxant binding agent
  • It exerts its reversal effect by forming tight complexes in a 1:1 ratio with Steroidal nondepolarizing agents(rocuronium > vecuronium >> pancuronium)
  • Sugammadex is essentially eliminated unchanged via the kidneys

Reference: Morgan and mikhail's clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition

question_text: Which neuromuscular blocking agent undergoes Hofmann elimination?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Atracurium undergoes Hofmann elimination, a chemical process in which the drug is spontaneously degraded at physiological pH and temperature.
  • This elimination pathway is organ-independent, making atracurium suitable for patients with renal or hepatic impairment.
  • Although atracurium can be safely used in liver failure, caution is advised in renal failure because its metabolite laudanosine can accumulate, potentially increasing the risk of seizures.
  • Cisatracurium, a related agent, has a lower risk of toxicity due to the absence of significant laudanosine production.

Neuromuscular Blocking Agents Undergoing Hofmann Elimination:

Explanation of Other Options:

Pancuronium, Rocuronium, and Vecuronium (Options A, B & C) are primarily metabolized by hepatic and renal pathways and do not undergo Hofmann elimination.

Hence, these agents are less suitable for patients with organ dysfunction.

question_text: Trigger free anesthesia is a concept that avoids:
explanation:
Management of known cases Malignant hyperthermia (MH).

  • Pretreatment with oral dantrolene is now thought to be unnecessary.
  • Sedative premedication is sometimes given to reduce 'stress', but this is controversial.
  • Avoidance of known triggering agents: volatile agents and suxamethonium.
  • N2O is considered safe.
  • Many other drugs have been implicated at some time, but the above are the only definite triggers.
  • TIVA is a useful technique.
  • Local anesthetic techniques may be used, but MH may still occur.
  • All local anesthetic agents are considered as safe as each other.
  • New breathing system, flushed with fresh gas for 10-20 min, has been suggested as being adequate.
  • Routine monitoring should include core temperature.

Reference: FRCA A to Z, edition 5, page no 367

question_text: Trismus after administration of succinylcholine IV signals the onset of MH in what percentage of patients?
explanation:
Trismus (masseter spasm) is characterized by rigidity of the jaw muscles while the limb muscles remain flaccid after administration of succinylcholine. Trismus may herald the onset of MH in some patients but may be due to a number of other causes and may occur in normal patients. It previously had been believed that 50% of patients who experience trismus after administration of succinylcholine would go on to develop MH. Recent evidence suggests, however, that the incidence is less. If masseter spasm occurs in a patient after administration of succinylcholine, the most conservative course would be to cancel the operation. If cancellation of the operation is not feasible, then a nontriggering anesthetic should be used, and the anesthesiologist should pay close attention for any signs of MH.

Reference: Miller: Miller's Anesthesia, ed 8, p 1296.

question_text: Select the TRUE statement
option_a: Dibucaine is an ester-type local anesthetic
option_b: A dibucaine number of 20 is normal
option_c: The dibucaine number represents the quantity of normal pseudocholinesterase
explanation:
• Dibucaine is an amide-type local anesthetic that inhibits normal pseudocholinesterase by approximately 80%.
  • In patients who are heterozygous for atypical pseudocholinesterase, enzyme activity is inhibited by 40% to 60%.
  • In patients who are homozygous for atypical pseudocholinesterase, enzyme activity is inhibited by only 20%.
  • The dibucaine number is a qualitative assessment of pseudocholinesterase.
  • Quantitative as well as qualitative determination of enzyme activity should be carried out in any patient who is suspected of having a pseudocholinesterase abnormality.

question_text: During general anesthesia, which nerve is most commonly monitored using a peripheral nerve stimulator to assess the degree of neuromuscular blockade?

question_text:
Assertion(A): Dantrolene sodium is indicated in the treatment of malignant hyperthermia
Reason(R): Dantrolene inhibits muscle contraction by preventing calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
option_a: Both Assertion(A) and Reason(R) are true, but Reason(R) does not explain Assertion(A)
option_b: Both Assertion(A) and Reason(R) are true, and Reason(R) explains Assertion(A)
option_c: Both Assertion(A) and Reason(R) are not true
option_d: Both Assertion(A) and Reason(R) are not true, but Reason(R) explains Assertion(A)
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Dantrolene is the definitive treatment for malignant hyperthermia, a hypermetabolic crisis caused by uncontrolled calcium release inside skeletal muscle.
  • The Reason correctly describes how dantrolene works by blocking calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, reversing muscle rigidity and the excessive metabolic activity that defines malignant hyperthermia.
  • Therefore, both statements are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion.
  • Mechanism: Dantrolene acts on the ryanodine receptor to prevent calcium release, reducing muscle contraction and metabolic heat production.
  • Indication: First-line therapy for malignant hyperthermia triggered by succinylcholine or volatile anesthetics.
  • Effect: Rapid reversal of hypermetabolism, muscle rigidity, and rising ETCO2 levels. (Supports Assertion and Reason)
  • Early symptoms include rising ETCO2, tachycardia, muscle rigidity, and sudden temperature increase.
  • Supportive care includes active cooling, management of acidosis, and correction of electrolyte disturbances.
  • Monitoring continues in the post-crisis period due to risk of recurrence and renal complications.

Key Takeaways:

  • Dantrolene is the definitive treatment for malignant hyperthermia (MH).
  • It works by inhibiting calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in skeletal muscle.
  • This reduces the hypermetabolic state responsible for rigidity, hypercarbia, and hyperthermia in MH.
  • Prompt administration of dantrolene is crucial to prevent cardiac arrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis, and organ failure.

question_text:
Which of the following sentences are TRUE for inhalational anaesthetic agents?
1. More solubility of gases causes rapid induction of anaesthesia
2. Less solubility of gases causes rapid induction of anaesthesia
3. More solubility of gases causes slow induction of anaesthesia
4. Less solubility of gases causes slow induction of anaesthesia
explanation:
• One of the most important factors influencing the transfer of an anaesthetic from the lungs to the arterial blood is its solubility characteristics The blood: gas partition coefficient is a useful index of solubility and defines the relative affinity of an anaesthetic for the blood compared with that of inspired gas. The partition coefficients for desflurane and nitrous oxide, which are relatively insoluble in blood, are extremely low.
    • When an anaesthetic with low blood solubility diffuses from the lung into the arterial blood, relatively few molecules are required to raise its partial pressure; therefore, the arterial tension rises rapidly. Conversely, for anaesthetics with moderate to high solubility, more molecules dissolve before partial pressure changes significantly, and arterial tension of the gas increases less rapidly. A blood:gas partition coefficient of 0.47 for nitrous oxide means that at equilibrium, the concentration in blood is 0.47 times the concentration in the alveolar space (gas). A larger blood:gas partition coefficient produces a greater uptake of anaesthetic and therefore reduces the time required for F A /F I to approach 1.

Reference

LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12th edition. Chapter 25- General Anaesthetics by Dr. Helge Eilers,MD & Dr. Spencer Yost,MD. Page no. 432

  • Physiologically it causes vasodilation (i.e. hypo-tension) & decreases vascular resistance throughout the body (Option A)

question_text: A patient undergoing surgery is maintained on anesthesia with halothane. During the procedure, the patient suddenly developed hyperthermia and muscle rigidity. Which of the following drugs is most likely implicated in this condition?
explanation:
Suxamethonium (Succinylcholine): This drug is a depolarizing muscle relaxant commonly used in anesthesia. It can lead to a life-threatening condition known as malignant hyperthermia (MH) when used in combination with halothaneanesthesia. MH is characterized by hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, and metabolic acidosis. It results from an abnormal calcium release in muscle cells, and suxamethonium is one of the primary triggers.

Incorrect Answer Explanation:

  • (A) D-curare: Curare is a non-depolarizing muscle relaxant, but it does not cause malignant hyperthermia. It is less likely to cause muscle rigidity and hyperthermia in the presence of halothane.
  • (C) Cisatracurium: This is also a non-depolarizing muscle relaxant, and like other non-depolarizing agents, it does not trigger malignant hyperthermia.
  • (D) Rocuronium: Another non-depolarizing muscle relaxant, rocuronium does not cause malignant hyperthermia. Non-depolarizing agents do not lead to the hyperthermic crisis seen with suxamethonium.

Key Takeaway:
Suxamethonium (Succinylcholine), when used with halothane, can trigger malignant hyperthermia, which is characterized by hyperthermia and muscle rigidity.

explanation:
• Halothane is very well tolerated in the concentrations used for induction and maintenance of anaesthesia, and it causes very little airway irritation
  • Halothane is a potent respiratory depressant (Option A)
  • Although it
    • Increases respiratory rate
    • It also reduces tidal volume
    • Overall effect is a reduction in alveolar minute ventilation
  • Halothane is also a potent bronchodilator(Option D)

question_text: A 5-year-old boy is anesthetized for elective repair of an umbilical hernia. General anesthesia is induced and maintained with sevoflurane, nitrous oxide, and oxygen via an anesthesia mask. At the conclusion of the operation, the patient is taken to the recovery room and subsequently discharged to the outpatient ward. Before discharge, the patient's mother notes that the urine appears dark brown (cola-colored). The most appropriate action at this time would be
option_a: Discharge the patient with instructions to return if urine color does not normalize
option_b: Discharge the patient in 3 hours if no other signs or symptoms are manifested
option_c: Obtain serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) levels and discharge the patient if they are normal
explanation:
Dark brown or cola-colored urine (i.e., myoglobinemia) may be caused by rhabdomyolysis, a possible sign of MH, and this patient should be evaluated. More typical signs and symptoms of MH include tachycardia, tachypnea, hypercarbia, hyperkalemia with peaked T waves, acidosis, increased sympathetic activity, irregular heartbeat, mottled cyanotic skin, profuse sweating, and a late sign of increased temperature (> 1.5° C over 5 minutes or temperature >38.8° C). Supportive laboratory tests for MH include elevated serum creatine phosphokinase (CPK); myoglobin in the serum and urine; increased serum potassium, calcium, and lactate levels; and a metabolic/respiratory acidosis on an arterial blood gas. If the presumed diagnosis is MH, therapy should be initiated.

Reference: Davis: Smith's Anesthesia for Infants and Children, ed 8, pp 1186-1189; Hines: Stoelting's Anesthesia and Co-Existing Disease, ed 6, pp 635-637

question_text: A patient undergoing surgery was administered halothane. Shortly after, the anesthetist observed that the patient developed muscle rigidity and a significant rise in body temperature. Which ion is primarily responsible for these clinical signs?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's symptoms of muscle rigidity and elevated body temperature following halothane administration suggest malignant hyperthermia. This condition is primarily triggered by excessive calcium release. It results from prolonged activation of abnormal ryanodine receptors, which causes an uncontrolled outflow of calcium ions from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the muscle cells. The elevated intracellular calcium leads to continuous muscle contraction and a rapid increase in body temperature.

question_text: A patient in OT was given anaesthesia ( isoflurane, halothane, etc) suddenly developed lung collapse and hypotension. what is the reason for it
explanation:
Pneumothorax:

  • Sudden lung collapse and hypotension during anesthesia are hallmark signs of pneumothorax.
  • Intraoperative pneumothorax can occur due to barotrauma, trauma during intubation, or pre-existing lung pathology exacerbated by positive-pressure ventilation.
  • Hypotension arises from decreased venous return due to increased intrathoracic pressure compressing the heart and major vessels.
  • Diagnosis is confirmed by clinical signs (unilateral decreased breath sounds, hyper-resonance) and imaging (if available). Immediate treatment involves needle decompression or chest tube insertion.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

  1. ARDS (Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome):
    • ARDS typically develops over hours to days, not suddenly during surgery.
    • It presents with severe hypoxemia and diffuse pulmonary infiltrates, but it is not associated with sudden lung collapse or hypotension in this context.
  2. Pleural Effusion:
    • Pleural effusion causes gradual dyspnea and reduced breath sounds but does not lead to sudden lung collapse or hemodynamic instability like hypotension.
  3. Pulmonary Edema:
    • Pulmonary edema presents with frothy pink sputum, bilateral crepitations, and hypoxemia.
    • It does not cause lung collapse or sudden hypotension unless secondary to severe cardiac dysfunction.

Key Takeaway:

Sudden lung collapse and hypotension during anesthesia strongly indicate pneumothorax, which requires urgent recognition and management to prevent life-threatening complications.

question_text: Inhalational agent suitable for neurosurgery is?

question_text: A drug with lowest MAC would have the following characteristic?
explanation:

  • So, lower the MAC value, lower is the concentration of anaesthetic drug required which would imply the drug is more potent.

Example:

  • Methoxy flurane - MAC- 0.2→most potent
  • Other drugs:
    • Desflurane: 6.0
    • Sevoflurane- 2.05
    • Isoflurane- 1.28
    • Halothane - 0.75 (since methoxyflurane is no longer in use, among the commonly used inhalational agents, halothane is the most potent)

question_text: Drug with lowest blood gas partition coefficient is?

  • An inhalational anaesthetic with lower blood gas partition coefficient would have a→higher alveolar concentration which will lead to →faster induction and recovery
  • Blood/gas partition coefficient of anaesthetic gases:
    • Halothane-2.5 → slowest induction
