question_text: All of the following are seen with nitrous oxide except:
option_b: Expansion of air-filled spaces in the body
explanation:
• N2O exhibits the following two effects.
  • The 'concentration effect' implies that the greater the inspired anesthetic concentration, the more rapid the rise in the alveolar concentration.
  • The 'second gas effect' refers to the ability of one gas administered in a high concentration (e.g., N2O) to accelerate the uptake of another gas (e.g., halothane) that is co-administered. sixty-six percent of N2o in oxygen decreases the MAC of halothane to 0.29, of enflurane to 0.6, of isoflurane to 0.5, of sevoflurane to 0.66, and of desflurane to 2.8.
  • Option a: Nitrous oxide is 35 times more soluble than nitrogen in the blood. Because of this physical property of the gas, when N2o is discontinued, the ingress of the gas into the alveoli lowers the alveolar oxygen concentration. This is called fink effect or diffusion hypoxia.
  • Option b: Nitrous oxide is 35 times more soluble than nitrogen in the blood; N2O will therefore cause an increase in the size of air-filled spaces (e.g., pneumothorax, intestines, air cysts in the middle ear) in the body.
  • Option c: 15% of patients receiving N2O will experience nausea and vomiting.

Reference: Drugs in Anesthesia and Intensive Care, Edward Scarth, Susan Smith 5th edition pg 278.

question_text: Factors increasing the MAC are all except?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Factors Decreasing MAC:
    • Hypoxia: Decreases CNS metabolic activity and neurotransmission, leading to a lower MAC. Hypoxia impairs neuronal function and generally decreases the requirement for anaesthetics.

Key Takeaways:

  • Understanding how various factors influence MAC is essential for anesthetic management.
  • Hypoxia is a significant factor that decreases MAC, contrary to the other options, which increase it.

question_text: All the following are seen with Nitrous oxide except:
option_b: Expansion of air-filled spaces in the body
explanation:
• N2O exhibits the following two effects
  • The 'concentration effect' implies that the greater the inspired anesthetic concentration, the more rapid the rise in the alveolar concentration
  • The 'second gas effect' refers to the ability of one gas administered in a high concentration (e.g. N2O) to accelerate the uptake of another gas (e.g. halothane) that is co-administered
  • sixty-six percent of N2O in oxygen decreases the MAC of halothane to 0.29, of enflurane to 0.6, of isoflurane to 0.5, of sevoflurane to 0.66, and of desflurane to 2.8

Option A: Nitrous oxide is 35 times more soluble than nitrogen in the blood. Because of this physical property of the gas, when N2O is discontinued, the ingress of the gas into the alveoli lowers the alveolar oxygen concentration. This is called fink effect or diffusion hypoxia.

Option B: Nitrous oxide is 35 times more soluble than nitrogen in the blood; N2O will therefore cause an increase in the size of air-filled spaces (e.g. pneumothorax, intestines, air cysts in the middle ear) in the body.

question_text: Incidence of halothane hepatitis is?
explanation:
• Halothane hepatitis is rare with an incidence of 1 per 35,000 cases but very fatal, with a mortality of 50-75%.

  • Risk factors for halothane hepatitis:
    • Multiple exposures to halothane at short intervals
    • Middle-aged obese women - because halothane undergo extensive metabolism in obese patients
    • Familial predisposition to halothane
  • Another theory for halothane hepatitis is that it is caused by a hypersensitivity reaction associated with oxidative metabolism of halothane
  • The liver in halothane hepatitis shows centrilobular necrosis
  • In a patient with prior history of halothane hepatitis, inhalational induction agent of choice is Sevoflurane

Reference: Drugs in Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, Edward Scarth, Susan Smith 5th edition; Stoelting's pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 3th edition

question_text: Nitrous oxide is considered a carrier gas and an incomplete anesthetic agent. This is attributed to its property of
explanation:
Second-Gas Effect

  • The second-gas effect reflects the ability of high-volume uptake of one gas (first gas) to accelerate the rate of increase of the Pa of a concurrently administered “companion” gas (second gas).
  • For example, the initial large-volume uptake of nitrous oxide accelerates the uptake of companion (second) gases such as oxygen and volatile anesthetics.
  • This increased uptake of the second gas reflects increased tracheal inflow of all the inhaled gases (first and second gases) and higher concentration of the second gas or gases in a smaller lung volume (concentrating effect) due to the high-volume uptake of the first gas.

Reference: STOELTING’S Pharmacology and Physiology in Anesthetic Practice FIFTH EDITION, page no 104

question_text: If pressure in a full nitrous oxide "E" cylinder is 745 psi at 20°C, the pressure in a half-full cylinder will be about _______ psi:
explanation:
Pressure in a half-full "E" cylinder of nitrous oxide will still be 745 psi. Nitrous oxide is present in the cylinder as a liquid, and therefore, the volume remaining in the cylinder does not reflect the pressure in the cylinder. Capacity of an "E cylinder" of nitrous is about 1590 L. It is not until three-fourth of the gas is consumed (about 400 L remaining) that the pressure in the cylinder begins to fall. Therefore, the reliable way to determine the remaining nitrous oxide in the cylinder is to weigh the cylinder. The empty weight of the cylinder is stamped on the cylinder.

Reference: Lippincott's ANESTHESIA REVIEW: 1,001 QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS Paul Sikka, MD, PhD

question_text: Inhalation anaesthetic which is least blood soluble?
explanation:

  • Blood gas partition coefficient of an inhaled anaesthetic is a measure of its blood solubility
  • Xenon has the lowest blood-gas partition coefficient (0.115) among all inhaled anaesthetics. And so, xenon has the fastest induction and emergence from anaesthesia
  • Methoxyflurane with a blood gas partition coefficient of 12 has the slowest induction and recovery but is not in use currently

question_text: The most nephrotoxic inhaled anaesthetic is?
explanation:

  • The renal toxicity of volatile anaesthetics is due to their metabolic breakdown to free fluoride ions
  • The amount of fluoride ions produced:
    • Methoxyflurane: 50uM
    • Sevoflurane: 20-30 uM
    • Enflurane: 20uM
    • Isoflurane and desflurane: 5uM
  • When compared to methoxyflurane, the lower incidence of nephrotoxicity among the newer inhaled anaesthetics is due to
    • Lesser metabolic breakdown
    • Lower solubility in the kidney which results in lesser amount of intrarenal fluoride which is liberated
    • Due to faster clearance of these fluorides

Reference: Drugs in Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, Edward Scarth, Susan Smith 5th edition; Stoelting's pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 3rd edition

question_text: Which of the following inhalational anesthetic agents has a blood-gas partition coefficient comparable to that of nitrous oxide?
explanation:
Explanation:

The blood-gas partition coefficient determines how quickly an inhalational anesthetic induces anesthesia and how fast recovery occurs.

  • A lower blood-gas partition coefficient means the anesthetic is less soluble in blood, leading to:
    • Faster onset of action
    • Faster recovery
  • Desflurane (~0.42) is very close to Nitrous Oxide (~0.47) → hence similar in terms of rapid onset and recovery.
  • Because of its low solubility, Desflurane allows for tight control over the depth of anesthesia and is often preferred in daycare surgeries for rapid emergence.

Desflurane

Properties:

  • Chemical Nature: Desflurane is a fluorinated ether.
  • Vapor Pressure: High vapor pressure - 681 mm Hg at 20°C.
  • Blood-Gas Partition Coefficient (λb/g): Very low - 42.
  • Similar to Nitrous Oxide (0.47).
  • Clinical Effect:
  • Rapid induction and quick emergence from anesthesia.
  • Ideal for daycare surgeries and short procedures.
  • Requires a Tec 6 vaporizer for precise delivery:
  • Because of its high vapor pressure and low boiling point.
  • Ensures consistent and controlled anesthesia.
  • Reflects the solubility of an inhalational agent in blood.
  • Inversely proportional to speed of onset and recovery:
  • High B/G coefficient → Slow onset & recovery (more soluble in blood).
  • Low B/G coefficient → Fast onset & recovery (less soluble in blood).
  • Desflurane's low B/G value makes it fast-acting and easy to titrate.

Uses :

Desflurane is well-suited for rapid induction and quick recovery because of its low blood solubility; however, it is not recommended for inhalation induction as its pungent odor and tendency to irritate the airways can cause discomfort and coughing.

Contraindication:

It should be avoided in patients with severe hypovolemia, malignant hyperthermia, and intracranial hypertension.

Explanation for other options:

Other incorrect options do not have blood gas partition co-efficient similar to nitrous oxide.

Isoflurane (option A): High blood solubility → slow onset and recovery.

Sevoflurane(Option C): Faster than isoflurane/halothane, but still slower than desflurane.

Halothane (option D): High blood solubility → slow onset and recovery.

question_text: Least potent among the commonly used inhaled anaesthetics is?

• MAC (Minimum alveolar concentration values)

  • MAC is the best measure to estimate the potency of inhalational agents
  • So, higher the MAC value (as in desflurane here)→higher is the concentration of anaesthetic drug required which means→ lower is the potency
  • Desflurane is one-fourth as potent as the other volatile agents, but it is 17 times more potent than nitrous oxide. (MAC VALUE OF NITROUS OXIDE IS 104)
  • Nitrous oxide is the least potent among the inhalational agents

question_text: You discover that and anaesthetic machine with soda-lime absorber and a sevoflurane vapouriser has not been used for the last 2days. However the fresh gas flow was left running at 2Litres/min for the last 48hrs.which of the following is the most appropriate action before using this machine to administer anaesthesia to the first patient on the list?
option_b: Continuously flush the anaesthetic machine for 1 hour and use the workstation
option_c: Change the soda-lime absorber and use the same workstation
option_d: Use high  gas flows for the first hour
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Risk of Carbon Monoxide Production: Desiccated soda lime can degrade inhaled anaesthetics, producing carbon monoxide (CO) and trifluoro methane. These byproducts can reach significant concentrations and interfere with anaesthetic gas monitoring.
  • Duration of Inactivity: Leaving the fresh gas flow running for 48 hours without use can desiccate the absorbent, increasing the risk of CO production. This is particularly dangerous after prolonged disuse, especially over weekends.
  • Safety Measures:
    • Changing the soda lime absorber is critical because:
      • It minimizes the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning, which is more likely when absorbents are desiccated.
      • Carbon monoxide levels can reach dangerously high levels (over 35% carboxyhaemoglobin) due to prolonged contact between absorbent and anaesthetics.
  • Preventive Recommendations: To avoid such complications in the future:
    • Turn off gas flow when the machine is not in use.
    • Regularly change absorbents, especially after long periods of inactivity.
    • Change absorbents whenever colour change indicates
    • Change both canisters in a two-canister system.
    • Consider changing compact canisters more frequently if used.

Key Takeaways:

  • Change the soda lime absorber before use to ensure patient safety.
  • Desiccation of absorbent increases the risk of CO production and potential poisoning.
  • Implementing regular maintenance and monitoring of anaesthetic equipment is crucial for patient safety.

question_text: A patient undergoing surgery is administered succinylcholine for muscle relaxation. After administration, he developed hyperthermia, rigidity, tremors, and tachycardia. What is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The symptoms of hyperthermia, rigidity, tremors, tachycardia after succinylcholine administration are classic for Malignant Hyperthermia. Sodium dantrolene is the Drug of Choice for Malignant Hyperthermia.
  • Dantrolene interferes with muscle contraction by binding the Ryr1 receptor channel and inhibiting calcium ion release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The dose is 2.5 mg/kg intravenously every 5 min until the episode is terminated (upper limit, 10 mg/kg)

Explanation of Other Options:

Neostigmine (Option A)

  • Neostigmine is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used to reverse non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockade (e.g., rocuronium, vecuronium).
  • Does not treat malignant hyperthermia.

Atropine (Option C)

  • Atropine is a muscarinic antagonist used to treat bradycardia or organophosphate poisoning.
  • Does not address the underlying hypermetabolic crisis in MH.

Midazolam (Option D)

  • Midazolam is a benzodiazepine used for sedation, anxiolysis, and seizure control.
  • Does not reverse the muscle rigidity or hyperthermia in MH.

Key takeaways:

Succinylcholine and inhaled general anaesthetics are triggering agents for malignant hyperthermia. Drug of choice for malignant hyperthermia is Dantrolene sodium. It binds to Ryr1 channel, inhibiting the release of Ca2+ from sarcoplasmic reticulum.

question_text:
Assertion(A): Some neuromuscular blocking agents like atracurium and cisatracurium have extrahepatic and extrapulmonary metabolism.
Reason(R): Laudanosine produced during the metabolism has been found to be nephrotoxic in experimental animals.
option_a: Both Assertion(A) and Reason(R) are true, but Reason(R) does not explain Assertion(A)
option_b: Both Assertion(A) and Reason(R) are true, and Reason(R) explains Assertion(A)
option_c: Both Assertion(A) and Reason(R) are not true
option_d: Both Assertion(A) and Reason(R) are not true, but Reason(R) explains Assertion(A)
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Atracurium and cisatracurium undergo metabolism outside the liver and lungs through Hofmann elimination and ester hydrolysis, making their clearance independent of hepatic or renal function. This supports the Assertion.
  • Although laudanosine is a metabolite formed during this process and has shown nephrotoxic potential in experimental animal studies, this toxicity does not explain why these drugs undergo extrahepatic metabolism.
  • Thus both statements are true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion.
  • Atracurium and cisatracurium: Metabolized via Hofmann elimination and ester hydrolysis, independent of hepatic and renal pathways. (Supports Assertion)
  • Laudanosine: A breakdown product associated with CNS excitation and nephrotoxicity in animal models, but unrelated to the rationale for extrahepatic metabolism.
  • Clinical advantage: Safe use in patients with hepatic or renal impairment due to predictable metabolism and lack of accumulation.
  • Hofmann elimination is temperature and pH dependent, providing reliable breakdown across physiologic conditions.
  • Although laudanosine is produced, its clinical toxicity is minimal at usual doses.

Understanding these metabolic pathways guides anesthetic choice in organ dysfunction.

Key Takeaways:

  • Atracurium and cisatracurium undergo extrahepatic and extrapulmonary metabolism, primarily via Hofmann elimination and ester hydrolysis.
  • These pathways make them suitable for patients with hepatic or renal dysfunction, as clearance is independent of major organ function.
  • Laudanosine is a metabolite formed during atracurium breakdown and has experimental nephrotoxic potential, but this does not explain their extrahepatic metabolism.
  • Understanding Hoffmann elimination is essential for choosing neuromuscular blockers in critically ill or organ-impaired patients.

question_text: Neuromuscular blocking agents can cause dyselectrolytemia. This includes depolarizing agents like succinylcholine. Succinylcholine, when administered to patients can increase serum potassium by approximately

question_text: The plasma esterases are involved in the metabolism of many anesthetic agents used. Anomalies in gene coding these enzymes can therefore cause abnormal metabolism of the drugs. In this context dibucaine number is related to which drug
explanation:
Suxamethonium is broken down by plasma cholinesterase.

  • These enzymes are coded for by autosomal genes on chromosome 3. the normal phenotype is eu (usual). a patient with eu:eu will break down suxamethonium rapidly so that its duration of action is around 2–6 minutes.
  • There are several variations of these genes and deviation from the normal means that the resulting enzyme’s activity is decreased. consequently, it takes longer to break down the suxamethonium and its duration of action is increased. the diagnosis and extent of the enzyme abnormality can be made using dibucaine.
  • Dibucaine is a local anesthetic agent that inhibits normal plasma cholinesterase by approximately 80%, but does not inhibit an abnormal enzyme as effectively. a normal number is between 75 and 85, whereas abnormal homozygotes can have numbers as low as 30.

Reference: FRCA A TO Z, page no 136

question_text: A 3-year-old child status post resection of Wilms tumor at age 2 years is receiving doxorubicin (Adria mycin) and cyclophosphamide for metastatic disease. The patient is scheduled for placement of a Hickman catheter for continued chemotherapy. Anesthetic concerns related to this patient's chemotherapeutic treatment include each of the following EXCEPT
explanation:
Wilms tumor, also called nephroblastoma, is a common abdominal malignancy of children. Children commonly present with increasing abdominal girth and have a palpable mass. Peak age of diagnosis is 1 to 3 years. Renal function is usually preserved but hypertension, often mild, is common (60%). Fever, hematuria, and anemia are often present. Treatment consists of surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy. Chemotherapeutic drugs used in this tumor include dactinomycin, doxorubicin (Adriamycin), vincristine, and cyclophosphamide (Cytoxan). Bone marrow suppression (e.g., anemia, thrombocytopenia) can occur with all cytotoxic drugs. Because cardiomyopathy can occur with cyclophosphamide (>100 mg/ m2) and with doxorubicin (>220 mg/m2), preoperative echocardiography should be considered even in asymptomatic patients. Late cardiac dysfunction may develop 7 to 14 years after treatment. Alkylating agents, such as cyclophosphamide, inhibit plasma cholinesterases, which may affect the metabolism of succinylcholine. Pulmonary fibrosis and/or pneumonitis can occur in patients who have received bleomycin (the patient in this case did not receive bleomycin). This pulmonary toxicity may be related to high-inspired oxygen concentrations and excessive fluid administration. Vincristine has several CNS side effects, including peripheral neuropathy, impaired sensorium, and encephalopathy and renal toxicity

Reference: Davis: Smith's Anesthesia for Infants and Children, ed 8, pp 751-754, 1138-1141; Hines: Stoelting's Anesthesia and Co-Existing Disease, ed 6, pp 628-629; Miller: Miller's Anesthesia, ed 8, pp 1216-1217.

question_text: Which of the following is the correct sequence of potency of anesthetic agents?
explanation:
Potency is inversely proportional to MAC i.e. agents with high MAC will have low MAC.

N2O has the highest MAC, hence it is least potent. Methoxyflurane has the lowest MAC, hence it is the most potent.

The potency of inhalational anesthetic agents is measured inversely by their Minimum Alveolar Concentration (MAC).

  • Potencyis inversely proportional to MAC (lower MAC = higher potency).
  • Methoxyflurane has the lowest MAC among these agents, making it the most potent.
  • Nitrous Oxide (N2O) has the highest MAC, making it the least potent.

Sequence Explanation:

  1. Methoxyflurane: Most potent (lowest MAC).
  2. Halothane: Next most potent after Methoxyflurane.
  3. Isoflurane: Less potent than Halothane.
  4. N2O: Least potent (highest MAC).

Key Takeaway:

The potency of anesthetic agents follows the sequence Methoxyflurane > Halothane > Isoflurane > N2O, as determined by their MAC values.

question_text: Which of the following describes the 'second gas effect' in anesthesia?
option_a: Accelerated uptake of a second gas when administered with nitrous oxide
option_b: Increased potency of the second anesthetic agent
option_d: Decrease in the alveolar concentration of the second gas
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Second Gas Effect:
  • Definition: Describes how the presence of a rapidly absorbed gas (likenitrous oxide) enhances the uptake of a second, slower anesthetic gas.
  • Mechanism: Nitrous oxideis taken up quickly by the lungs, which leads to:
  • A decrease inalveolar volume.
  • Increasedpartial pressure gradientfor the second gas.
  • Faster onsetof the second gas's effects, enhancing its uptake and leading to quicker anaesthesia.
  • Increased potency of the second anaesthetic agent (Option B):Incorrect; the second gas effect does not increase the potency of the anaesthetic agent but rather speeds up its uptake.
  • Prolongation of anaesthesia duration (Option C): Incorrect; the second gas effect relates to the onset of action, not the duration of anaesthesia.
  • Decrease in the alveolar concentration of the second gas (Option D): Incorrect; the effect results in increased concentration and uptake, not a decrease.

Key Takeaways:

  • Thesecond gas effectenhances the uptake of a slower anaesthetic gas when used withnitrous oxide, leading tofaster onsetof anaesthesia.
  • It highlights the interplay between inhaled anaesthetic agents, optimizing the efficiency of anaesthesia induction.

question_text: Which of the following is the preferred agent for inhalational induction of anesthesia in children?

Halothane (Option C): Halothane was previously used for pediatric induction but has a slower onset than sevoflurane and carries a rare risk of hepatotoxicity, making it less suitable today.

question_text: A patient is under general anesthesia, and the anesthesiologist reviews the MAC values of volatile anesthetic agents. Which of the following agent-MAC pairs is incorrect?

Explanation:

  • MAC represents the alveolar concentration of an inhaled anesthetic that prevents movement in 50% of patients exposed to a surgical stimulus.
  • It is inversely related to potency, a lower MAC indicates higher potency. Desflurane has an actual MAC of 6%, making it the least potent agent among those listed, so pairing it with 0.75% is incorrect.
  • Isoflurane, sevoflurane, and halothane match their known MAC values.

MAC values and clinical relevance:

  • Isoflurane: MAC 1.2%, moderate potency with stable cardiovascular profile. (Option A)
  • Sevoflurane: MAC 2%, smooth induction, non-pungent, widely used in pediatric practice. (Option B)
  • Halothane: MAC 0.75%, highly potent agent but avoided today due to hepatotoxicity concerns. (Option C)
  • Desflurane: MAC 6%, lowest potency but offers rapid adjustments and fast emergence because of very low blood-gas solubility.

Key Takeaways:

MAC (Minimum Alveolar Concentration) indicates potency: lower MAC = higher potency.

  • Correct MAC values:
    • Isoflurane: 1.2%
    • Sevoflurane: 2%
    • Halothane: 0.75%
    • Desflurane: 6%
  • Desflurane has the highest MAC and is thus the least potent.
  • Halothane has the lowest MAC among the listed agents, making it the most potent.

question_text: A 56-year-old male with known pulmonary bullae is scheduled for lung-conservative surgery. During anesthetic planning, the anesthesiologist must avoid agents that can expand air-filled spaces and increase intrathoracic pressure. Which of the following agents should be avoided?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Nitrous oxide diffuses rapidly into closed or partially closed air-filled spaces because it is significantly more soluble in blood than nitrogen (34 times higher).
  • This leads to expansion of bullae, blebs, or pneumothorax, increasing the risk of rupture and worsening intrathoracic pressure during lung-conservative surgery.
  • Therefore, nitrous oxide must be strictly avoided in such procedures.

Clinical features and drug associations:

  • Nitrous oxide: High solubility compared to nitrogen leading to rapid diffusion into trapped intrathoracic gas, expands bullae and pneumothorax, increasing rupture risk in lung surgery (Option A).
  • Isoflurane: Does not expand closed gas spaces; considered safe for lung procedures (Option B).
  • Sevoflurane: Similar safety profile to isoflurane; no risk of worsening bullae or pneumothorax. (Option C)

Key Takeaways:

  • Nitrous oxide should be avoided during lung-conservative surgery because it diffuses rapidly into air-filled spaces.
  • This can increase the volume or pressure of trapped gas in alveoli, bullae, or pneumothorax.
  • Isoflurane and sevoflurane do not expand air spaces and are safer alternatives.
  • Nitrous oxide's high blood-gas partition ratio compared to nitrogen makes it unsuitable when lung integrity must be preserved.

question_text: Decreased environmental temperature and loss of heat regulation in a patient emphasizes the use of various methods to maintain the body temperature perioperatively. The shown equipment plays a role in maintaining the temperature by means of:
explanation:

  • They work byconvection, circulating warm air around the body, andconduction, transferring heat directly through the patient's skin from the blanket.
  • Prewarming with these blankets helps prevent phase one hypothermia, which is caused by a temperature gradient between the core and peripheral regions.
  • Additional methods to prevent hypothermia include:
    • Heated humidification of inspired gases
    • Warming intravenous fluids, and
    • Increasing ambient operating room temperature.
  • Conduction alone is insufficient; convection also plays a role. (Option A)
  • Convection is important, but conduction also contributes to heat maintenance. (Option B)
  • Prevention of evaporation is not the primary mechanism here. (Option D)

Key Takeaways:

  • Forced-air warming blanketswork through bothconductionandconvectionto maintain body temperature, preventing perioperative hypothermia effectively.

question_text: Faster induction of inhalational agents in neonates is because of?
option_a: Increased FRC compared with older children
option_b: Relatively lesser blood flow to vessel-rich organs
option_c: Blood/gas coefficients of volatile anaesthetics are reduced in neonates
explanation:
• Neonates, infants, and young children have relatively greater alveolar ventilation and reduced FRC compared with older children and adults
  • This greater minute ventilation-to-FRC ratio with relatively greater blood flow to vessel-rich organs contributes to a rapid increase in alveolar anaesthetic concentration and speeds inhalation induction
  • Furthermore, the blood/gas coefficients of volatile anaesthetics are reduced in neonates compared with adults, resulting in even faster induction times and potentially increasing the risk of accidental overdosage

question_text: When is the fetus most susceptible to the effects of teratogenic agents?
explanation:
Organogenesis mainly occurs between the 15th and 56th days (3-8 weeks) of gestation in humans and is the time during which the fetus is most susceptible to teratogenic agents. Although all commonly used anesthetic drugs are teratogenic in some animal species, there is no conclusive evidence to implicate any currently used local anesthetics, IV induction agents, or volatile anesthetic agents in the causation of human congenital anomalies.

Reference: Chestnut: Chestnut's Obstetric Anesthesia, ed 5, pp 360-366; Suresh: Shnider and Levinson's Anesthesia for Obstetrics, ed 5, pp 806-809.

question_text: Which inhalation anesthetic does NOT produce uterine relaxation?
explanation:
All volatile halogenated anesthetic agents (e.g., halothane, enflurane, isoflurane, desflurane, sevoflurane) cause a dose-related relaxation of uterine smooth muscle. With anesthetic concentrations of 0.2 MAC, the decrease in uterine activity is slight, and these agents have been used for inhalation analgesia during labor. At 0.5 MAC, uterine relaxation is more significant, but the uterine response to oxytocin remains intact. Nitrous oxide does not affect uterine activity.

Reference: Chestnut: Chestnut's Obstetric Anesthesia, ed 5, pp 452-454; 575-576; Suresh: Shnider and Levinson's Anesthesia for Obstetrics, ed 5, pp 156-157, 176-177.

question_text: A Tec 5 isoflurane vaporizer is being used at a high altitude location where the atmospheric pressure is 380mmHg. The dial is set to 1%. The clinical effect on the patient is the same as when using it at sea level (with the dial set to 1%). The most likely reason for this is:
option_a: A Tec 5 vaporizer compensates for altitude.
option_b: Partial pressure of isoflurane at the alveolus remains the same.
option_c: Blood-gas solubility of isoflurane remains the same.
option_d: There is no change in the boiling point of isoflurane.
explanation:
• At high altitude the atmospheric pressure decreases.
  • The saturated vapor pressure (SVP) of isoflurane does not change (SVP changes with change in temperature not with change in atmospheric pressure).
  • The concentration delivered by the vaporizer increases because SVP takes up a high proportion of ambient pressure.
  • Hence, at any given dial setting the delivered percentage of inhalational agents will increase with altitude (decrease in barometric pressure); however, its partial pressure will remain constant.
  • The clinical effect of isoflurane is determined by the alveolar partial pressure rather than the concentration delivered by the vaporizer.
  • The partial pressure of isoflurane at the alveolus remains constant.
  • This reflects the partial pressure of isoflurane in the brain.
  • The vaporizer dial setting should remain constant irrespective of altitude to produce the same clinical effect.

Reference:

  1. Carter JA. Provision of anaesthesia in difficult situations and the developing world. In: Ward's anaesthetic equipment, 5th ed. Davey AJ, Diba A, Eds. Philadelphia, USA: Elsevier Saunders, 2005; Chapter 29: 485-98.
  2. Roy PK. Physiological adaptation and anaesthesia at high altitude. Indian Journal of Anaesthesia 2002; 46: 175-81.

question_text: Which among the following inhalational agents has a blood-gas partition coefficient similar to that of nitrous oxide?
explanation:
Explanation:

The inhalational agent with a blood-gas partition coefficient similar to that of nitrous oxide (~0.46) is Desflurane(~0.42).

The solubility of an inhalational agent is indicated by its blood-gas partition coefficient.

A lower blood-gas partition coefficient means the agent is less soluble in blood, leading to faster induction of anaesthesia and faster recovery.

A higher coefficient means more solubility, resulting in slower induction and slower recovery.

The inhalational agents in increasing order of their blood-gas partition coefficients are Desflurane> Nitrous Oxide> Sevoflurane> Isoflurane > Halothane (Option A, C & D ruled out)

Key Takeaways: Desflurane has a blood-gas partition coefficient similar to that of nitrous oxide. The inhalational agents in increasing order of their blood-gas partition coefficients are Desflurane> Nitrous Oxide> Sevoflurane> Isoflurane > Halothane

question_text: In which of the following patients would the mini mum alveolar concentration (MAC) for isoflurane be the greatest?
explanation:
The MAC for isoflurane is greatest at age 3 months. The MAC is lower in preterm neonates compared with term neonates. The low MAC in the newborns may be related to the immaturity of the CNS and/or related to the elevated levels of progesterone and β-endorphins. The increase in MAC in the first few weeks after birth seems to be related to the falling progesterone levels. After age 3 months, the MAC of these volatile anesthetics steadily declines with aging except for a slight increase at puberty. For reasons that are unclear, the MAC for sevoflurane is similar in neonates and infants younger than 1 year (3.2%). The MAC of sevoflurane then decreases with age (1 to 12 years, 2.5%; 40-year-old, 2%).

Reference: Davis: Smith's Anesthesia for Infants and Children, ed 8, pp 190, 556; Hines: Stoelting's Anesthesia and Co-Existing Disease, ed 6, p 587.

question_text: Robinhood phenomenon or reverse cerebral steal phenomenon is seen with which of the following induction agents?
explanation:
• Barbiturates cause → cerebral vasoconstriction leading to → a reduction in the cerebral blood flow
  • Because barbiturate-induced cerebral vasoconstriction occurs only in normal areas, these agents tend to redistribute blood flow from normal to ischemic areas in the brain. The cerebral vasculature in ischemic areas remains maximally dilated because of ischemic vasomotor paralysis
  • Thus, thiopentone sodium causes preferential perfusion of the focal ischemic areas in the brain, which is known as robin hood/ reverse cerebral steal phenomenon
  • Barbiturates are not cerebroprotective in global ischemia

explanation:
• Barbiturates cause cerebral vasoconstriction leading to a reduction in the cerebral blood flow.
  • Because barbiturate-induced cerebral vasoconstriction occurs only in normal areas, these agents tend to redistribute blood flow from normal to ischemic areas in the brain.
  • The cerebral vasculature in ischemic areas remains maximally dilated because of ischemic vasomotor paralysis.
  • Thus Thiopentone sodium causes preferential perfusion of the focal ischemic areas in the brain, which is known as robin hood/ reverse cerebral steal phenomenon.
  • But Barbiturates are not cerebroprotective in global ischemia.

Reference: Morgan and Mikhail’s clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 174, 591.

question_text: All are the early clinical signs of Malignant hyperthermia except;
option_d: Rapid increase in core body temperature
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Malignant Hyperthermia (MH):
    • Triggering Agents: Induced by volatile halogenated anaesthetics or depolarizing neuromuscular blockers (e.g., succinylcholine).
    • Genetic Basis: Linked to mutations in the type 1 ryanodine receptor (RyR1) and L-type calcium channel (CACNA1S).
    • Significance: A pharmacogenetic clinical syndrome that can lead to life-threatening complications if not recognized and treated promptly.
    • Early Clinical Signs:
      • Tachycardia: Increased heart rate is often one of the first signs (Option A)
      • Increased EtCO2: Elevated end-tidal carbon dioxide reflects increased metabolism and hypercapnia (Option B).
      • Mottling of Skin: Can indicate altered circulation and perfusion (Option C)
    • Core Body Temperature: A rapid increase in core body temperature is a late signof malignant hyperthermia, occurring after other symptoms have manifested. It indicates a severe reaction but does not present early in the syndrome.

Key Takeaways:

  • Recognizing early signs of malignant hyperthermia is critical for timely intervention.
  • A rapid increase in core body temperature signifies a later stage in the condition's progression.

question_text:
Which of the following is TRUE for Propofol

option_b: Sentence 1 and 2 both are True but 2 is not the correct reason for 1

explanation:
• Compared with other induction drugs, Propofol produces the most pronounced decrease in systemic blood pressure; this is a result of profound vasodilation in both arterial and venous circulations leading to reductions in preload and afterload. question_text: Which of the following general anaesthetic Agent should not be used in patient with Acute intermittent porphyria?

• Thiopental and methohexital undergo hepatic metabolism, mostly by oxidation but also by N -dealkylation, desulfuration, and destruction of the barbituric acid ring structure.
    • Barbiturates should not be administered to patients with acute intermittent porphyria because they increase the production of porphyrins through stimulation of aminolevulinic acid synthetase.
    • Methohexital has a shorter elimination half-time than thiopental due to its larger plasma clearance, leading to a faster and more complete recovery after bolus injection. Although thiopental is metabolized more slowly and has a long elimination half-time, recovery after a single bolus injection is comparable to that of methohexital and Propofol because it depends on redistribution to inactive tissue sites rather than on metabolism. However, if administered through repeated bolus injections or continuous infusion, recovery will be markedly prolonged because elimination will depend on metabolism under these circumstances

question_text: Gas cylinder valves on the anaesthesia machine with a pipeline supply should be kept closed for the following reasons:
option_b: So that a pipeline pressure failure will be recognized early
option_c: To prevent gas from flowing retrograde into the pipeline system
option_d: To prevent pressure alterations in the pipeline from drawing down the cylinder contents
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Valve Management:
    • After attaching the cylinder to the yoke, thevalve should be closedunless it's the primary gas supply.
    • Keeping the valve closed prevents gas from inadvertently escaping from the cylinder during pressure fluctuations in the anaesthesia machine.
  • Awareness of Pipeline Issues:
    • If the valve remains open and pipeline pressure fails, gas may flow from the cylinder without the user realizing it.
    • This can lead to the cylinder becoming empty before the user notices the loss of pipeline supply, leaving them without gas when needed.
  • While gas management is crucial, this reason isnot the primary focusfor keeping valves closed to prevent fires (Option A)
  • To prevent gas from flowing retrograde into the pipeline system, this is less of a concern with modern systems, as valves and safety features are designed to prevent retrograde flow (Option C).
  • To prevent pressure alterations in the pipeline from drawing down the cylinder contents this is less relevant because the main goal is to ensure the user recognizes when the pipeline pressure is lost (Option D).

Key Takeaways:

  • Keeping gas cylinder valvesclosedensures awareness of any pipeline pressure failures.
  • This practice prevents the unintended depletion of gas supplies during anaesthesia administration.

question_text: Best method to treat a large port-wine hemangioma is?
explanation: Pulsed dye Laser REF: Roxburgh's common Skin Diseases 17th edition page 194 & 205, Clinical Dermatology by John Hunter, John Savin & Mark Dahl 3' edition page 275 "Selective Photothermolysis or Pulsed dye laser is the treatment of choice for Portwine hemangioma" Port-wine stains are crimson blotches in which there is marked capillary dilatation compared to a capillary angioma, which is a red nodule or plaque containing proliferating endothelial cells. The latter tend to flatten and disappear at puberty. Larger ones may cause problems from bleeding and/or erosion. Cavernous haemangiomata are larger and compressible, containing large vascular spaces. Occasionally a port-wine stain of the trigeminal area is associated with a vascular malformation of the leptomeninges on the same side, which may cause epilepsy or hemiparesis (the Sturge​Weber syndrome), or with glaucoma. Excellent results have been obtained with careful and time- consuming treatment with a 585-nm flashlamp-pumped pulsed dye laser. Treatment sessions can begin in babies and anaesthesia is not always necessary. If a trial patch is satisfactory, 40-50 pulses can be delivered in a session and the procedure can be repeated at 3-monthly intervals.

question_text: A patient who is under general anaesthesia shows the following finding on the ETCO2 monitor. What condition can lead to the given capnograph show?
explanation:
Bronchospasm or airway obstruction can cause increased resistance to airflow during expiration, which leads to abnormalities in the capnograph waveform.

  • Phase III of the capnograph represents alveolar plateau, where the CO2 concentration is steady. In cases of bronchospasm, this phase shows an increased upslope and the characteristic "shark fin" appearance due to increased resistance from narrowed airways. This is the hallmark of bronchospasm (such as in asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), or when there is a partially obstructed endotracheal tube or breathing circuit.

Incorrect Options:

  • A) Malignant hyperthermia:
    • Malignant hyperthermia is a hypermetabolic reaction to volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine. It leads to an increase in temperature, heart rate, and metabolic demand, but it does not cause the characteristic "shark fin" appearance of the ETCO2 waveform. Instead, malignant hyperthermia may cause increased CO2 levels over time and increased oxygen consumption, but the waveform will typically show a steady rise in CO2 without the typical sharp increases seen in bronchospasm.
  • C) Rebreathing:
    • Rebreathing typically occurs when there is a problem with the unidirectional valves in the breathing circuit or the CO2 absorber. This can cause increased CO2 levels in the exhaled gas, but it does not specifically cause the "shark fin" appearance. Instead, rebreathing would show a normal capnograph waveform with an elevated baseline CO2 concentration.
  • D) Accidental extubation:
    • Accidental extubation occurs when the endotracheal tube is displaced from the trachea, leading to impaired ventilation and dropped or very low ETCO2 The waveform would not show a shark fin pattern, but rather, it may show minimal or no CO2 due to lack of exhalation.

Key Takeaway:

  • A "shark fin" appearance on the ETCO2 capnograph is classic for bronchospasm or airway obstruction, where increased resistance to airflow leads to a sharp upslope in phase III of the capnograph.
  • Malignant hyperthermia, rebreathing, and accidental extubation do not produce this characteristic waveform and should be differentiated based on other clinical findings.

question_text: A patient has sustained a road traffic accident and is bleeding profusely. He is hypotensive and requires large-volume replacement with intravenous fluids. What cannula gauge should be used in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

A 14 G cannula has the largest diameter and a flow rate of approximately 250-300 mL/min. It is orange colour-coded and is the preferred choice when rapid, large-volume IV fluid replacement is required, such as in trauma or massive hemorrhage. The wider bore allows for faster infusion rates, which is critical in resuscitative settings.

Explanation of other options:

13 G (Option B): A 13 G cannula does not exist in standard medical practice.

16 G (Option C): A 16 G cannula is grey colour-coded and commonly used for emergency fluid replacement, but its flow rate is lower than that of a 14 G. It can be used when slightly smaller bore access is acceptable.

18 G (Option D): An 18 G cannula is green colour-coded and used for routine IV access or moderate-volume fluid replacement. It can be used in emergencies but is slower than 14 G or 16 G for rapid transfusion or resuscitation.

Key takeaways:

  • 14 G (orange): Used for massive fluid resuscitation.
  • 16 G (grey): Used for emergency fluid replacement.
  • 18 G (green): Used for routine IV access.
  • 13 G cannula: Not available in standard use.

References:  https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9226746/

question_text: A 45-year-old man is rescued from a house fire and brought to the ER. He is noted to have major burns involving 45% of his body, with singed skin on the forehead and tip of his nose and painful burned hands. His blood pressure is 185/90 mm Hg, and his heart rate is 130. He complains of phlegm in his throat, has trouble phonating, and is coughing dark black material. The greatest need for this patient is
explanation:
Three main risk factors for death from burns include inhalation injury, burn size (> 40%), and age (> 60 years). Patients who have sustained major burns from a fire can rapidly deteriorate. Areas of concern include airway management, carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning, pain, edema, fluid management, intravenous access, maintenance of body temperature and prevention of infections. Because upper airway swelling can rapidly lead to airway obstruction and death, securing the airway with an endotracheal tube (0.5-1 mm internal diameter smaller than normal) is advised in patients with major burns. High-inspired oxygen concentrations are often required to prevent tissue hypoxia, as well as to reduce the half-life of CO in the blood. The half-life of CO is 4 hours when breathing room air, 60 to 90 minutes when breathing 100% oxygen, and 20 to 30 minutes in a hyperbaric chamber.

Reference: Anaesthesia Review a Comprehensive Texbook 5th Edition Chapter 22 Page No 196, 197.

question_text:

explanation:

question_text: Which of the following structures is tested to check for patency of a Bain's Circuit?
explanation:
• The integrity of the inner tube can be confirmed → activating the oxygen flush → observing the bag

To check the integrity of the inner tube

Flush high flow into the circuit and occlude the patent end until the reservoir bag is filled

The patient end is then opened, and circuit is then flushed with oxygen

If inner tubing is intact, the Venturi effect occurs at the patient end, causing decrease in pressure within the circuit and bag deflates

If there is leak in inner tubing, fresh gas will escape in the expiratory limb and the bag will inflate

question_text: The granular size of soda lime used in clinical practice is between:
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Optimal Granular Size: The granular size of soda lime in clinical use is between4 and 8 mesh. This range optimizes both theabsorptive surface areaand theresistance to flow, facilitating effective CO2 absorption.
  • Understanding Mesh Size: Mesh size refers to the number of openings per linear inch in a sieve. A4 to 8 meshsize means the granules are small enough to allow for efficient gas exchange while maintaining adequate flow.
  • Chemical Reactions Involved:Soda lime absorbs CO2 through a series ofchemical reactions, not merely physical absorption:
    • Formation of Carbonic Acid: CO2 + H2O ⇔H2CO3
    • Reaction with Hydroxides:H2CO3 + 2NaOH (or KOH) ⇔Na2CO3 (or K2CO3) + 2H2O + Heat
    • Formation of Calcium Carbonate: Na2CO3 (or K2CO3) + Ca (OH)2 ⇔CaCO3 + 2NaOH (or KOH)
  • Absorption Capacity: The maximum CO2 absorption capacity of soda lime is26 L of CO2 per 100 g of absorbent. This indicates its efficiency in clinical settings.

Key Takeaways:

  • Soda lime granular sizefor CO2 absorption in clinical practice is4 to 8 meshfor optimal performance.
  • Theabsorption processinvolves chemical reactions, resulting in efficient CO2 removal during anaesthesia.

question_text: While checking the Bain's circuit, the trainee performs the Pethik's test, during which there is collapse of the bag, ensuring that the inner tube of the circuit is patent. This test is based on which principle of physics?
explanation:
• Venturi effect is used in checking the integrity of the inner tube of the Bain's Circuit. The integrity of the inner tube is very essential, as any leak in that can result in large apparatus dead space. One of the tests used for the same is PETHIK'S TEST.
  • In this test, after keeping 3 liters of flow of O2, closing the expiratory valve and the outer tube with the thumb, one should make sure that the reservoir bag is full.
  • Then O2 flush is activated and simultaneously the thumb occluding the outer tube is released. If the inner tube does not have any leak, then the reservoir bag will collapse.
  • This is due to Venturi effect, because at the opening of the inner tube into the outer tube due to the rapid flow of 30-70 liters of O2 after activation of the O2 flush, a sudden fall in the pressure occurs, sucking the O2 from the bag & collapsing it.
  • If there is any leak in the inner tube, then the reservoir bag will not collapse.
  • Hagen-Poissuille's law: is applied for laminar flow. It states that the flow through the tube is directly proportional to the pressure gradient and 4th power of radius and inversely proportional to the length of the tube and viscosity of the gas. Used in selecting proper sized endotracheal tubes, insertion of large bore iv cannula etc.
  • Graham's law for turbulent flow: States that flow rate is directly proportional to the square root of the pressure gradient on either sides of the tube and inversely proportional to the square root of the density of the fluid. Used in flowmeters of anaesthesia machines, airway connectors with smooth bends, etc.
  • Coanda effect is the tendency of the fluid jet to be attached to a nearby surface. This phenomenon is also called as wall attachment.

Reference: race 2020 chapter 1 physics of flow.

question_text: Pressure gauge used on the cylinders are generally of type

question_text:
About the given equipment, chose the option
a. if A, B, and C are correct
b. if A and C are correct
c. if B and D are correct
d. if A, B, C, and D are correct.
option_a: There is no need to discontinue ventilation or positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) while using it.
option_b: It is not necessary to hyper oxygenate the patient prior to usage
option_d: Increased incidence of accidental extubation with its use
explanation:
• Given image is that of a closed suction catheter. A closed suction system offers several advantages over an open system (attaching a catheter to a vacuum source, disconnecting the patient from the ventilator, inserting the catheter through the tracheal tube, suctioning, then reconnecting the patient to the ventilator).
  • There is no need to discontinue ventilation or positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) while suctioning, although both the minute volume and end-expiratory pressure will be somewhat lowered.
  • Oxygenation is usually superior to the open suction technique. Closed suctioning may make it unnecessary to hyper oxygenate prior to suctioning.
  • Because the catheter is enclosed within a sterile closed system, contamination from accidental breaches in sterile technique should not occur. Rates of nosocomial infection have been found to be less than or comparable to rates associated with open suctioning.
  • Extra weight may pull on the airway, causing trauma or accidental extubation. It is important that the system be supported to prevent these problems.

Reference: Understanding Anaesthesia Equipment (Jerry A. Dorsch, Susan E. Dorsch) 5th edition pg 63,64

question_text: Which of the following is an advantage of a fenestrated tracheostomy tube over a non-fenestrated tube?
option_b: Can be used in positive pressure ventilation
explanation:
• Fenestrations in a tracheostomy tube are used to allow exhalation through the glottis as part of the weaning process, and in particular to permit speech.

Disadvantages

  • Positive pressure ventilation will result in air leak and should be avoided where possible.
  • There is a risk of surgical emphysema in patients with newly formed tracheostomies.
  • Granuloma formation may occur around the fenestrations.

Reference: Equipment in Anaesthesia and Critical Care, Daniel Aston, Angus Rivers, Asela Dharmadasa, pg 71.

question_text: Bernoulli's principle is used in anaesthesia during all of the following scenarios except:
explanation:
• Bernoulli's principle: When a gas flowing through a tube encounters a constriction, at that point the pressure drops and the velocity increases i.e. kinetic energy increases and the potential energy decreases. This is called as Bernoulli's principle.
  • Second stage pressure regulators use the Bernoulli's principle to reduce the pressure.
  • Bernoulli's principle is used in checking the integrity of the inner tube of the Bain's Circuit. (Pethick's test)
  • Measurement of cardiac output is based on FICK PRINCIPLE.
  • Fick principle states that "the total uptake of (or release of) a substance by the peripheral tissues is equal to the product of the blood flow to the peripheral tissues and the arterial-venous concentration difference (gradient) of the substance".
  • Venturi oxygen masks are designed to mix a predictable amount of oxygen (running through the oxygen tubing) with air (entrained through the orifice). The air is entrained because, the high velocity of oxygen causes a reduction in pressure inside the valve due to the Bernoulli principle.

Reference: RACE 2020 Ramachandra Anesthesia Continuing Education pg 10.

question_text: Dibucaine number reflects?
explanation:
• It is important to recognize that the dibucaine number reflects quality of cholinesterase enzyme (ability to hydrolyse succinylcholine) and not the quantity of the enzyme that is circulating in the plasma
  • In case of the usual butyrylcholinesterase genotype → the dibucaine number is 70 or higher
  • Homozygousfor the atypicalgene → the dibucaine number is less than 30
  • In individuals with the heterozygousatypical variant → the dibucaine number is in the range of 40 to 60

Reference: E Book of Miller's Anaesthesia 9th Edition Chapter 27 Page No 795, 796.

question_text: Which of the following medications is used to reverse the effects of anaesthesia?
explanation:
Explanation:

Neostigmine is the most widely used agent for reversing neuromuscular blockade after anesthesia.

About Neostigmine:

  • Type: Cholinesterase inhibitor
  • Mechanism of Action: Inhibits acetylcholinesterase, increasing acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, thereby restoring muscle activity.

Clinical Uses:

  • Myasthenia Gravis: Enhances muscle strength by improving neuromuscular transmission.
  • Reversal of Neuromuscular Blockade: Commonly used at the end of surgeries to reverse the effects of non-depolarizing muscle relaxants.
  • Postoperative Urinary Retention: Stimulates bladder contraction.
  • Anticholinergic Toxicity: Used in select cases.

Side Effects:

  • Muscarinic Effects: Bradycardia, hypotension, increased salivation, nausea, and diarrhea.
  • Nicotinic Effects: Muscle cramps, twitching, and possible respiratory issues in overdose.
  • Cholinergic Crisis: Excessive dosing can lead to muscle weakness and respiratory failure.

Explanation for other options:

  • Atropine & Glycopyrrolate (Options B & C): These are anticholinergic agents used to counteract the muscarinic side effects of Neostigmine, not to reverse muscle paralysis.
  • Midazolam (Option D): A benzodiazepine used for sedation and anesthesia, but not for reversal.

question_text: Remifentanil is an ideal drug for Total intravenous anesthesia. This is because of the property:
explanation:
Due to its ester linkages, it is susceptible to hydrolysis by blood and tissue nonspecific esterases resulting in rapid metabolism. This allows rapid termination is effect and referral from anesthesia.

  • Highly lipid soluble.
  • Pharmacokinetics uninfluenced by liver and renal failure.
  • It is not a substrate for hydrolysis by pseudocholinesterase
  • Context sensitive half time is around 4 minutes and is independent of the duration of infusion.

Reference: Comparative pharmacology for Anesthetist, page no 35

question_text: How does chronic liver disease affect the drugs used in anesthesia? Which of the following drugs can be used in a liver patient?
explanation:
• Benzodiazepines: Metabolism impaired and effects enhanced. These drugs should be avoided.
  • Opiates: Metabolism impaired and effects enhanced. Use with caution in reduced doses.
  • Barbiturates: Metabolism impaired, though their effects are terminated by redistribution.
  • Suxamethonium: Duration of action prolonged as decreased plasma cholinesterase.
  • Muscle relaxants: Effects enhanced as usually highly protein bound.
  • Fluid: Extreme care should be used in administering intravenous fluids as oedema and fluid overload are likely. Also avoid lactate-containing fluids, e.g., Hartmann’s as lactate metabolism will be impaired.

Reference: FRCA A TO Z, page no 358

question_text: A patient, after receiving succinylcholine, has remained apneic for 45 minutes post injection. How can this situation be manage?
explanation:
• Patients who are atypical homozygotes for pseudocholinesterase remain apneic for 1–2 hours after receiving the drug and develop a phase II block during this period (fresh frozen plasma may be used to provide a source of plasma cholinesterase under these circumstances).
  • Use of anticholinesterases is not recommended.

Reference: Drugs in Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, Edward Scarth, Susan Smith 5th edition pg 382.

question_text: A 75-year-old woman is scheduled for mitral valve repair. High-dose fentanyl is used to induce anesthesia. In order to counteract the bradycardia caused by fentanyl, Pancuronium is administered. Pancuronium blocks the bradycardia caused by fentanyl by acting on which of the following?
explanation:
• Pancuronium causes an increase in the heart rate, blood pressure, and cardiac output, secondary to a vagolytic action.
  • The systemic vascular resistance remains unchanged after the administration of the drug.
  • A slight fall in central venous pressure may occur.

Reference: Drugs in Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, Edward Scarth, Susan Smith 5th edition pg 295.

question_text: Contribution of the following scientist to anesthesia:

  • Davy undertook a series of experiments on the effects of breathing of N2O. Once he had a severe inflammation of his gum with acute pain
  • During an experiment with this pain, he breathed three large doses of N2O
  • The pain was diminished and then Davy had suggested the probable use of N2O as analgesic with definite advantages during surgical operations

question_text:
Assertion(A): It is impossible to maintain anaesthesia using Nitrous Oxide as the sole inhalational agent.
Reasoning(R): Nitrous oxide needs a higher MAC for the desired effect, that practically is not possible without Oxygen.
option_a: Both Assertion(A) and reasoning(R) are true ; But reasoning(R) does not explain assertion(A)
option_b: Both Assertion(A) and reasoning(R) are true ; and reasoning(R) explains assertion(A)
option_c: Both Assertion(A) and reasoning(R) are not true ; and reasoning(R) does not explain assertion(A)
option_d: Both Assertion(A) and reasoning(R) are not true ; But reasoning(R) explains assertion(A)
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Assertion(A): Nitrous oxide (N2O) is not sufficient as a sole agent for maintaining anaesthesia due to itslow potency.
  • Reasoning(R):
    • TheMinimum Alveolar Concentration (MAC)of nitrous oxide is approximately105%, which means achieving effective anaesthesia with N2O alone is impractical because it exceeds the 100% concentration that can be delivered.
    • Nitrous oxide is typically used as asecond gasalongside agents like isoflurane or desflurane to help reduce their MAC requirements and enhance the overall anaesthetic effect.

Key Takeaways:

  • N2Ocannot maintain anaesthesia alone due to its high MAC.
  • It is effectively used with other inhalational agents, enhancing their efficacy while reducing required concentrations.

question_text: ____ is a measure of the volatility of the liquid?
explanation:
• At equilibrium, the number of molecules entering and leaving the vapor phase is constant
  • As the temperature rises, more molecules enter the vapor phase and the partial pressure increases
  • The maximum partial pressure that can be achieved at any given temperature is called the Saturated vapor pressure (SVP) at that temperature
  • Saturated vapor pressure is a measure of the volatility of the liquid
  • Higher SVP denotes greater volatility
  • Desflurane is very volatile (SVP of 664 mm Hg at 20°C)

Reference: Anaesthesia Review a Comprehensive Texbook 5th Edition Chapter 44 Page No .423 to 425

question_text: Match the PIN index:
explanation:
Explanation:

  • PIN Index System (PISS):A safety mechanism designed to prevent the incorrect attachment of gas cylinders.
  • Each gas cylinder has a unique PIN configuration that fits only the corresponding yoke on the anaesthesia machine or regulator:
    • Air:Pins at positions1,5.
    • Oxygen:Pins at positions2,5.
    • Nitrous Oxide:Pins at positions3,5.
    • Heliox:Pins at positions2,4.

Key takeaways:

This system significantly reduces the risk of attaching the wrong cylinder, especially critical for oxygen, ensuring safe and correct administration of gases.

question_text:
Which of the following statements about thiopentone are true?
1. Thiopentone has a rapid onset of action due to high lipid solubility.
2. Rapid elimination is the reason for its short duration of action.
3. It causes significant analgesia during anesthesia.
4, Thiopentone acts by potentiating GABA-A receptor activity.
5. It is primarily metabolized by the kidneys
explanation:
Explanation:

Thiopental or Thiopentone is an Ultra-short acting barbiturate. It has rapid onset of action as it is highly lipid soluble, allowing it to cross the blood-brain barrier quickly, producing anesthesia within 20-30 seconds (Statement 1). Its action ends not by elimination but by redistribution from the brain to muscle/fat compartments (Statement 2).

Mechanism: Thiopental enhances inhibitory transmission via the GABA-A receptor complex, prolonging chloride channel opening and hyperpolarizing neurons (Statement 4).

Analgesic effect: Thiopental has poor analgesic properties and may even cause hyperalgesia (Statement 3 Ruled out)

Metabolism: It is metabolized in the liver, not the kidneys (Statement 5 ruled out).

question_text: Not true about commercial preparation of thiopentone?
option_a: Reconstituted with water to form a 10% solution
option_b: Available as a pale hygroscopic yellow powder
option_c: It is suspended in an atmosphere of nitrogen
option_d: Contains 500 mg or 1000 mg per vial
explanation:
• Thiopental (also referred to as thiopentone and Pentothal) is a barbiturate, supplied as a hygroscopic (attracts moisture from the atmosphere) pale yellow powder
  • Vials commonly contain 500mg of sodium thiopental with 6% sodium carbonate in an inert atmosphere of nitrogen
  • Reconstituted with 20ml of water this yields a 2.5% solution (25mg/ml) with a pH of 10.8

Reference: Stoelting's pharmacology and physiology in anesthetic practice 3th edition

question_text: The shortest acting benzodiazepine is?
explanation:
• The shortest acting benzodiazepine is midazolam
  • The benzodiazepines used in anaesthesia are classified according to their metabolism and plasma clearance as:
    • Short-acting agent (midazolam)
    • Intermediate-acting agents (lorazepam, temazepam)
    • Long-acting agent (diazepam)
  • Midazolam is the benzodiazepine of choice for induction of anaesthesia
  • The onset of anaesthesia is within 30 to 60 seconds

Reference: Stoelting's pharmacology and physiology in anesthetic practice 5th edition

question_text: Long term infusion of Propofol is usually avoided as it can result in Propofol infusion syndrome. This is characterised by
explanation:
Propofol infusion syndrome.

  • Progressive myocardial failure (often with resistant bradycardia), metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia and evidence of muscle damage in the absence of other causes, in children and adults receiving infusions of propofol.
  • Typically associated with hyperlipidemia at high infusion rates of propofol (> 4 mg/kg/h) for prolonged periods (> 2 days), it is thought to be related to exacerbation of poor tissue oxygenation and impaired cellular utilization of glucose, perhaps involving respiratory chain dysfunction.
  • Treatment is supportive and includes withdrawal of propofol;
  • Hemodialysis has been used successfully.
  • Mortality is high.

Reference: FRCA A TO Z, page no 483

question_text: Identify the given agent. What is not true about the agent?
option_a: Should be discarded in 6 hours after opening
explanation:
• The given agent is Propofol -presented as an oil-water emulsion:
  • 1% (presented in 20 ml ampoules, 50/100 ml vials and 50 ml prefilled syringes) or 2% (for infusion only and presented in 50 ml vials and 50 ml prefilled syringes), containing 10% soya bean oil, 1.2% egg phosphatide and 2.25% glycerol.
  • A new formulation containing medium- chain triglycerides causes less pain on injection; in addition, some formulations contain either 0.005% EDTA or sulphite as a preservative.
  • Fospropofol is the phosphate prodrug of propofol and as such has a slower onset of action; it is licensed in the USA for 'light sedation'.
  • Aquafol is a newly developed emulsification of propofol in water, which has similar properties to the parent agent but causes more pain on injection.

Reference: FRCA A TO Z, page no 482

question_text: If the internal diameter of an intravenous catheter were doubled, flow through the catheter would be
explanation:
Factors that influence the rate of laminar flow of a substance through a tube is described by the Hagen-Poiseuille law of friction.

The mathematical expression of the Hagen-Poiseuille law of friction is as follows:

where V. is the flow of the substance, r is the radius of the tube, ΔP is the pressure gradient down the tube, L is the length of the tube, and μ is the viscosity of the substance.

Note that the rate of laminar flow is proportional to the radius of the tube to the fourth power. If the diameter of an intravenous catheter is doubled, flow would increase by a factor of 2 raised to the fourth power (i.e., a factor of 16)

Reference: Ehrenwerth: Anesthesia Equipment: Principles and Applications, pg 225.

question_text: Post- operative nausea and vomiting(PONV) is a common post-operative complication. Methods to prevent this include
explanation:
• Decreased risk after benzodiazepines and clonidine, increased risk after opioids
  • Type of anaesthesia:
    • Volatile anaesthesia is associated with a 2-fold increase in riskof PONV, with risk increasing in a dose-dependent manner. No significant difference between different volatile agents
    • N2O increases the relative risk of PONV by 1.4
    • Intra-operative and post-operative opioid use increases the risk of PONV in a dose-dependent manner. Opioids reduce muscletone and peristaltic activity, thereby delaying gastric emptying, inducing distension, and triggering the vomiting reflex. the use of a short-acting opioid, like remifentanil, does not decrease the incidence of PONV

Reference: Oxford handbook of anesthesia, edition 4, page no 1087

question_text: A 60-year-old man undergoing an inguinal hernia repair is induced with propofol. Which of the following is most likely to be observed?
explanation:
• Hypotension and apnoea are the most common side effects of propofol
  • Options A, B and D are incorrect
  • Propofol does NOT cause hyperthermia
  • In fact, it is the anaesthetic of choice in patients at risk for malignant hyperthermia
  • Propofol is associated with a fast emergence, which is also an advantage of the drug

Reference: Stoelting's Pharmacology & Physiology in Anesthetic Practice, 5th Edition, Page Number-168.

question_text: A patient who was under sedative infusion in the intensive care unit developed greenish urine and green discoloration of hair. Which sedative agent must have been most likely used in this patient?
explanation:
• Propofol is used for sedation in intensive care unit apart from being an induction agent for anesthesia
  • Propofol is rapidly metabolized in the liver → undergoing conjugation to an inactive glucuronide (49–73%), or metabolized to a quinol → which is excreted as sulfate and glucuronide conjugates of the hydroxylated metabolite via cytochrome P450
  • The quinol metabolites of propofol may occasionally cause → green discoloration of the urine and hair.

Reference: Drugs in Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, Edward Scarth, Susan Smith 5th edition Pg. 326

question_text: A patient has been induced with a bolus dose of propofol for general anesthesia. After how long is the patient expected to wake up from this single bolus dose of propofol?
explanation:
• Propofol is administered intravenously in a bolus dose of 2–2.5 mg/kg for induction of anesthesia
  • Consciousness is lost in about 30–40 seconds, with emergence occurring approximately after 10 minutes (fast emergence) from a single dose
  • Plasma concentrations of 2–6 micrograms/ml and 5–1.5 micrograms/ml are associated with hypnosis and sedation, respectively

Reference: Drugs in Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, Edward Scarth, Susan Smith 5th edition Pg. 326

question_text: A 48 years old female is being induced for general anesthesia with propofol. Which of the following effects is least expected with the induction?
explanation:
• Propofol produces a
    • 15-25% decrease in the blood pressure (Option A)
    • Systemic vascular resistance, without a compensatory increase in the heart rate
    • The cardiac output decreases by 20%
    • Profound bradycardia, possibly through resetting of the baroreceptor reflex, and asystole may complicate the use of the drug (Correct Answer: Option B is False)

Wrong Answers:

Option C:

  • Pain on injection occurs in up to 28% of subjects
  • The incidence may be reduced by:
    • Addition of lidocaine (1 ml of 1%)
    • Cooling the drug
    • Use of large veins
  • Addition of lidocaine in quantities >20 mg lidocaine per 200 mg propofol results in emulsion instability and increases in globule size, which have been associated with reduced anesthetic potency in animals

Option D:

  • Bolus administration of propofol produces
    • apnea of variable duration (30 to ≥60 seconds)
    • suppression of laryngeal reflexes
  • Infusion of the drug produces a decrease in the tidal volume, tachypnoea, and a depressed ventilatory response to hypercarbia and hypoxia

Reference: Drugs in Anesthesia and Intensive Care, Edward Scarth, Susan Smith 5th edition Pg. 326

question_text: Thiopentone can be reconstituted with all except?
explanation:
• Thiopentone should not be reconstituted with ringer lactate because ringer lactate has an acidic pH decreases the alkalinity of the solution and the calcium present in ringer lactate can result in precipitation of thiopentone
  • Thiopentone and other barbiturates are prepared as sodium salts (mixed with 6% by weight anhydrous sodium carbonate) and can be reconstituted with water, glucose 5% or normal saline to produce a 5% solution of thiopental
  • After reconstitution:
    • Thiobarbiturates (thiopentone, thiamylal) - stable if refrigerated for 1 week
    • Methohexital - stable if refrigerated for 6 weeks

Reference: Stoelting's pharmacology and physiology in anesthetic practice 5th edition

question_text: True about mechanism of action of benzodiazepines is?
option_b: Bind to gamma subunit of GABA receptor
explanation:
• Benzodiazepines appear to produce all their pharmacologic effects by facilitating the actions of GABA at the GABAA chloride ionophore
  • Benzodiazepines do not activate GABAA receptors directly but bind to a specific site then act allosterically to enhance the affinity of the receptors for GABA
  • Benzodiazepines interact with a site located between the alpha and gamma subunits of the GABAA receptor

question_text: Which of the following techniques is LEAST effective in the treatment of pruritus from administration of neuraxial opiates?
explanation:
The treatment of pruritus, the most common side effect of neuraxial opiates, is primarily with opioid antagonists, mixed opioid agonist-antagonists, and antihistamine drugs (by their sedating effects). Nalbuphine is a mixed opioid agonist-antagonist; diphenhydramine has antihistamine properties. Propofol at very low doses (e.g., 10 mg) has been useful to treat pruritus, not only induced by neuraxial opiates but also the pruritus associated with cholestatic liver disease. Propofol does not affect analgesia, whereas opioid antagonists and mixed agonist-antagonists may reverse some or all of the analgesia, depending on dose. Dexmedetomidine is a highly selective α2-receptor agonist that has a faster onset and shorter duration of action compared with clonidine. Dexmedetomidine has analgesic properties, can potentiate neuraxial analgesia when injected spinally, and can perhaps decrease the incidence of pruritus by reducing the amount of opioid dose used. It does not treat pruritus.

Reference: Miller: Miller's Anesthesia, ed 8, pp 2986-2987.

question_text: Propofol infusion syndrome is associated with all except?

question_text: A 24-year male with patient with traumatic brain and spine injury and quadriplegia was on MV support was sedated with propofol infusion as he was irritable, also there is ventilator asynchrony. He is receiving propofol infusion for more than 48 hours. On review you find that patient has rhabdomyolysis with metabolic acidosis and you suspect the condition as propofol infusion syndrome. All are the clinical features of Propofol Infusion Syndrome (PRIS) except;
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Propofol Infusion Syndrome (PRIS):
    • A rare but serious condition linked to high dose propofol infusions (≥ 4 mg/kg/h for > 48 hours).
    • Initially identified in children but also observed in critically ill adults.
  • Clinical Features of PRIS:
    • Hyperkalemia (Option A): Elevated potassium levels due to muscle injury.
    • Bradycardia leading to Asystole (Option D): Acute refractory bradycardia is a hallmark, which can progress to asystole.
    • Hyperlipidaemia (Option C) : Increased lipid levels in the blood due to impaired fat metabolism.
    • Metabolic Acidosis: Indicated by a significant base deficit (>10 mmol/L).
    • Rhabdomyolysis: Muscle breakdown releases toxic substances into the bloodstream.
    • Cardiomyopathy: Acute cardiac failure may occur.
    • Enlarged or Fatty Liver: Hepatomegaly can be observed.
    • Tachycardiais generally not a feature of PRIS; instead,bradycardia is more common, which can lead to asystole.
    • Other potential symptoms include skeletal myopathy and lipemia.

Key Takeaways:

  • PRIS is characterized by: Hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperlipidaemia, and bradycardia leading to possible asystole.
  • Tachycardia is not a typical featureof PRIS, making option B the correct answer.
  • Monitor Patients: Particularly those on prolonged propofol infusions for signs of metabolic derangements and cardiac irregularities.

question_text: Following the attack on Pearl Harbor, which intravenous anesthetic agent was controversially blamed for causing profound hypotension and cardiovascular collapse in hypovolemic trauma patients?
explanation:
Explanation:

After Thiopentone sodium's introduction in 1934, Thiopentone became popular for its rapid induction. However, its use in shocked, hypovolemic casualties at Pearl Harbor led to disastrous outcomes.

Pathophysiology:

Thiopentone is a potent vasodilator and myocardial depressant. In a patient with hemorrhagic shock, the body is already compensating with intense peripheral vasoconstriction to maintain blood pressure. Administering a standard dose of Thiopentone to such a patient blocks this compensation, causing a sudden, catastrophic drop in blood pressure and cardiovascular collapse. This critical lesson in trauma anesthesia was learned tragically during WWII.

Timeline of IV Anesthetics:

Explanation of Other Options:

Methohexital (Option A): This is another barbiturate with similar hemodynamic effects, but it was introduced much later, in 1957.

Ketamine (Option B): Ketamine was introduced in the 1960s. Critically, it has the opposite effect of Thiopentone; it stimulates the sympathetic nervous system and is known to maintain or increase blood pressure, making it an ideal induction agent for trauma and shock patients.

Propofol (Option C): Propofol was introduced in the 1970s and was not available during World War II. It also causes significant vasodilation and hypotension.

question_text: Sedative of choice for premedication in children is?

question_text: Which intravenous anesthetic among the following acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist?
explanation:
Explanation:

Ketamine acts as an NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) receptor antagonist.

Mechanism of Action:

  • It blocks NMDA receptors (Option A), affecting the central nervous system.
  • Produces dissociative anesthesia, where patients seem conscious but cannot process sensory information.
  • Modulates endogenous pain-relief pathways.
  • Has high lipid solubility (5 to 10 times greater than thiopental) and low protein binding (around 12%).
  • The S(+) isomer of ketamine (Ketanest) is 3 to 4 times more potent as an analgesic and causes fewer psychomimetic side effects.
  • Despite its analgesic effects, the S(+) isomer may cause cognitive impairment and slowed reaction times.
  • The S(+) isomer has greater affinity for NMDA receptors and increased potency.

Pharmacokinetics:

  • Administered mainly intravenously or intramuscularly, reaching peak blood levels within 10-15 minutes.
  • Due to its high lipid solubility, it rapidly crosses into the brain, with a distribution half-life of 10-15 minutes.
  • Metabolized in the liver into active metabolites; repeated use can lead to tolerance.
  • Excreted primarily through the kidneys, with an elimination half-life of about 2 hours.

Explanation for other options:

Propofol and Thiopentone (Options B and C): act as direct agonists of the GABA-A receptor, enhancing the inhibitory effects of GABA.

Midazolam (Option D): a benzodiazepine, works by increasing GABA's effect through modulation of the receptor, making it more responsive to GABA.

  • The needle should not be removed, and saline is administered via the same needle todilute the drug (Option B)
  • Administering heparin to prevent thrombosis (Option C)
  • Brachial plexus block or stellate ganglion block to relieve vasospasm (Option D)

question_text: Initial dose of Flumazenil is?
explanation:
The recommended initial dose is 0.2 mg IV (8 to 15 mg/kg IV), which typically reverses the CNS effects of benzodiazepine agonists within about 2 minutes.

If required, further doses of 0.1 mg IV (to a total of 1 mg IV) may be administered at 60-second intervals.

The duration of action of flumazenil is 30 to 60 minutes, and supplemental doses of the antagonist may be needed to maintain the desired level of consciousness. An alternative to repeated doses of flumazenil to maintain wakefulness is a continuous low-dose infusion of flumazenil, 0.1 to 0.4 mg per hour.
