question_text: Each of the following drugs has been used to treat neuropathic pain. Selective inhibition of serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake is the mechanism of which drug?
explanation:
Many drugs have been used to treat neuropathic pain, including analgesics (NSAIDs and opioids), first-generation antiepileptic drugs (e.g., carbamazepine and phenytoin), second-generation antiepileptic drugs (e.g., gabapentin, pregabalin), topical agents (e.g., lidocaine, capsaicin), antiarrhythmics (e.g., mexiletine), and tricyclic antidepressants (e.g., amitriptyline, nortriptyline, desipramine), as well as other antidepressants (e.g., duloxetine, venlafaxine). Duloxetine (Cymbalta) is a selective serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) that is used for major depressive disorders, generalized anxiety disorders, fibromyalgia, and neuropathic pain. Mexiletine is an orally effective amine analog of lidocaine and may be effective in decreasing neuropathic pain when other drugs have failed. Gabapentin, a structural analog of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), works by increasing the synthesis of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA. Carbamazepine (Tegretol) is an anticonvulsant with specific analgesic properties for trigeminal neuralgia. Carbamazepine seems to reduce polysynaptic responses by an unknown mechanism.

Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 8, pp 1620-1621.

question_text: Which of the hepatic cytochrome enzymes is involved with hydroxylation of ropivacaine?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Metabolism of Amides:
    • Amide local anaesthetics, including ropivacaine, undergometabolism primarily in the liver.
  • Key Enzymes Involved:
    • CYP1A2andCYP3A4are significant enzymes in the metabolism of local anaesthetics.
    • RopivacaineundergoesN-dealkylation(primarily by CYP3A4) andhydroxylation(primarily by CYP1A2).
    • Other amides, such asbupivacaine, also follow similar metabolic pathways.
  • Additional Context:
    • Lidocaine is primarily metabolized byCYP1A2andCYP3A4to its metabolites, monoethyl glycine xylidide and glycine xylidide.
    • Esters, in contrast, undergorapid hydrolysisin blood through nonspecific esterases, leading to different metabolic pathways compared to amides.
  • CYP2D6 (Option B):Primarily involved in the metabolism of certain drugs, not significantly related to ropivacaine.
  • CYP3A4 (Option C):While it is involved in N-dealkylation of ropivacaine, it does not primarily mediate its hydroxylation.
  • CYP2C9 (Option D):Involved in the metabolism of various drugs but not in the metabolism of ropivacaine.

Key Takeaways:

  • CYP1A2is crucial for thehydroxylationof ropivacaine, whileCYP3A4handles itsN-dealkylation.
  • Understanding these metabolic pathways is essential for predicting drug interactions and individual responses to local anaesthetics.

question_text: A junior resident on duty , asks a doubt about the baricity of the drug to the anesthesiologist in operating room to explain, what is the right explanation
option_a: Milligram dose of an equipotent drug
option_b: Minimum concentration required to reach clinical effect
option_d: Ratio of specific gravity of drug to a reference specific gravity
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Definition of Baricity:
    • Baricityrefers to thespecific gravityof a local anesthetic (LA) solution relative to the specific gravity of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
  • Calculation:
    • Baricity is calculated as theratio of the specific gravity of the local anesthetic (numerator)to thespecific gravity of CSF (denominator).
  • Categories of Baricity:
    • Hyperbaric:Baricity > 1 (denser than CSF).
    • Isobaric:Baricity = 1 (same density as CSF).
    • Hypobaric:Baricity < 1 (less dense than CSF).
  • Importance of Baricity:
  • Influences thedistributionof local anesthetic based on gravity:
  • Hyperbaric solutionsspread to dependent areas of the spinal canal.
  • Hypobaric solutionsspread to nondependent areas.
  • Isobaric solutionsare not significantly influenced by gravity.
  • Clinical Application:
    • Altering the baricity of local anesthetic solutions (e.g., by adding dextrose for hyperbaric and sterile water for hypobaric) allows anaesthesiologists to predictably control the anesthetic spread by positioning the patient.
  • Milligram dose of an equipotent drug (Option A):Not related to baricity; refers to dosage.
  • Minimum concentration required to reach clinical effect (Option B):Relates to potency, not baricity.
  • Half-life of the local anaesthetics (Option C):Indicates duration of action, irrelevant to baricity.

Key Takeaways:

  • Baricity is crucial for determining how local anaesthetics distribute in the spinal canal, influencing the effectiveness and predictability of anaesthesia during procedures.
  • Understanding and manipulating baricity enhances patient safety and efficacy of anaesthesia.

question_text: How many hours should elapse before performing a single-shot spinal anesthetic in a patient who is receiving 1 mg/kg enoxaparin (Lovenox) twice a day for the treatment of a deep vein thrombosis?
explanation:
Enoxaparin, dalteparin, and ardeparin are low-molecular-weight heparins (LMWHs). Because of the possibility of spinal and epidural hematoma in the anticoagulated patient with neuraxial blockade, caution is advised. The plasma half-life of LMWH is two to four times longer than standard heparin. These drugs are commonly used for prophylaxis for deep vein thrombosis. These drugs are also used at high doses for treatment of deep vein thrombosis and (off label) as "bridge therapy" for patients chronically anticoagulated with warfarin (Coumadin). In these patients who are being prepared for surgery, Coumadin is discontinued and LMWH started. With high-dose enoxaparin administration (1 mg/kg twice daily), it is recommended to wait at least 24 hours before administration of a single-shot spinal anesthetic.

Reference: Miller: Miller's Anesthesia, ed 8, p 1691; Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 7, p 929; Third Consensus Conference on Neuraxial Anesthesia and Anticoagulation, Jan-Feb 2010; http://www.asra.com/publications-anticoagulation-3rd-edition-2010.php.

question_text: A 95-year-old woman has persistent and prolonged thoracic pain after a herpes zoster infection. Which of the treatments below would be the LEAST efficacious in the treatment of her pain?
explanation:
Acute herpes zoster is due to the reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus. Acute treatment includes symptomatic pain treatment and antiviral drugs (e.g., acyclovir, famciclovir, or valacyclovir). It is typically a benign and self limiting disease in patients younger than 50 years of age. As one gets older, the incidence of postherpetic neuralgia (PHN), defined as pain persisting for more than 3 months after resolution of the rash, increases. The incidence of PHN is about 30% to 50% in patients older than 50 years, although current vaccination to varicella-zoster will hopefully decrease incidence over time. Treatment of established PHN has been shown to be resistant to interventions and, thus, can be difficult. However, proven therapies include tricyclic antidepressants, anticonvulsants, opioids, topical local anesthetics (e.g., 5% lidocaine patch), topical capsaicin, and TENS. Sympathetic blocks can provide excellent analgesia but are most useful during the more acute stages of the disease rather than during the late chronic stages. Sympathetic blocks in the acute stages may decrease the incidence of PHN. Oral clonidine, which is used to treat hypertension and opioid withdrawal, has not been shown to be an effective treatment for PHN.

Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 8, p 1616

question_text: During the second stage of labor, complete pain relief can be obtained with
option_b: Neuraxial block with fentanyl and morphine
option_d: Lumbar epidural block with bupivacaine and no narcotic
explanation:
The first stage of labor starts with the onset of labor and ends with complete cervical dilation (10 cm). It is visceral pain, associated with uterine contractions and dilation of the cervix, and is transmitted via the autonomic nervous system through the sympathetic fibers that pass through the paracervical region and enter the CNS at T10-L1 segments. The second stage of labor includes these pathways and adds the somatic fibers of the birth canal that are transmitted via the pudendal nerve entering the CNS at S2-S4. Neuraxial block (spinal and/or epidural) with only narcotics can be useful for first-stage pain; however, the somatic pain is not well treated with narcotics alone. A local anesthetic-induced lumbar epidural block with or without narcotics can produce complete anesthesia during both first and second stage of labor pain. If a low spinal or saddle block is performed with local anesthetics (covering only sacral areas), the uterine contraction pain still will be felt. Paracervical blocks block only the first-stage pain. Pudendal blocks block the somatic component during the second stage but not the visceral pain of uterine contractions.

Reference: Chestnut: Chestnut's Obstetric Anesthesia, ed 5, pp 412-415, 459-480, 518-527; Suresh: Shnider and Levinson's Anesthesia for Obstetrics, ed 5, pp 119-133.

question_text: A 70 year old male patient with history of chronic hypertension, undergoes surgery for benign prostatic hypertrophy, under spinal anaesthesia. In the middle of the surgery patient develops TURP syndrome, the following are manifestations of TURP syndrome except
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Hyperglycemia (not hypoglycemia) is a relevant concern, particularly with the absorption of glycine-based irrigating solutions during transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP).
  • TURP Syndrome is characterized by:
    • Circulatory fluid overload.
    • Water intoxication.
    • Toxicity from solutes in the irrigating fluid.

  • Incidence: Less than 1%. Symptoms can manifest intraoperatively or postoperatively and can be rapidly fatal.
  • Hypoosmolality (Option B) is a typical manifestation due to fluid overload.
  • Hyponatremia (Option C) occurs as a result of dilution from absorbed irrigation fluids.
  • Hypothermia (Option D)can occur due to prolonged surgical procedures, especially in a regional anaesthesia context.

Key Takeaways:

  • TURP syndrome results from systemic absorption of irrigation fluid during prostate surgeries, leading to severe complications.
  • Understanding the signs and symptoms is crucial for early identification and management to prevent severe outcomes.
  • Preventative measures include using isotonic solutions, monitoring fluid absorption, and limiting irrigation time and pressure to reduce risks associated with TURP syndrome.

question_text: How do local anaesthetics work?
explanation:
Explanation:

Local anaesthetics act by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels in the neuronal cell membrane. This inhibits the influx of sodium ions during depolarization, preventing the generation and propagation of action potentials along the nerve fibers. As a result, the transmission of pain and sensory signals is interrupted, leading to localized loss of sensation without affecting consciousness.

This mechanism is reversible and depends on factors such as drug concentration, pH, and fiber type (smaller and myelinated fibers are blocked first).

Explanation of other options:

Block potassium channels (Option B): Potassium channels help in repolarizing the nerve membrane after depolarization. While important for nerve conduction, they are not the primary targets of local anaesthetics.

Block calcium channels (Option C): Calcium channels regulate neurotransmitter release at synapses but are not blocked by local anaesthetics. Drugs like calcium channel blockers (e.g., verapamil) act here instead.

Block chloride channels (Option D): Chloride channels maintain resting membrane potential and contribute to inhibitory neurotransmission, but they are not affected by local anaesthetics.

Key takeaways:

  • Local anaesthetics block sodium channels, preventing depolarization and action potential propagation.
  • Smaller and myelinated fibers are more sensitive to local anaesthetic action.
  • The effect is dose- and pH-dependent.
  • Other ion channels (K+, Ca2+, Cl-) are not significantly affected.

question_text: Rate of local anesthetic absorption from a particular injection site from highest to lowest rate is:

option_b: Epidural, intercostals, subcutaneous tissue brachial plexus
option_c: Brachial plexus, epidural, subcutaneous tissue, intercostals

explanation:
Explanation:

  • Highest Absorption:Local anaesthetics are absorbed most rapidly fromintercostal nerve blocksdue to their high vascularity.
  • Followed by Epidural:Epiduralinjections follow, as the caudal epidural space allows for substantial absorption.
  • Brachial Plexus and Subcutaneous Tissue:Brachial plexusinjections absorb next, whilesubcutaneous tissuehas the slowest absorption rate.
  • Factors Influencing Absorption:Absorption rate is influenced by:
    • Site of Injection:Highly vascular sites absorb faster.
    • Dosage and Volume:Larger volumes can lead to increased absorption.
    • Vasoconstrictor Use:Adding vasoconstrictors can decrease absorption.
    • Pharmacologic Profile:The specific local anesthetic used also affects absorption characteristics.

Key Takeaways:

  • Intercostal nerve blockshave the highest rate of local anesthetic absorption, followed byepiduralandbrachial plexusinjections, withsubcutaneous tissuebeing the slowest.
  • The vascularity of the injection site plays a crucial role in determining absorption rates.
  • Understanding these rates is essential to avoidlocal anesthetic toxicity, especially when using large doses in highly vascular areas.
  • Different sites may require careful consideration of dosage to prevent adverse effects based on absorption rates.

question_text: Local anesthetics acts by blocking
explanation:
• Local anesthetics function by blocking voltage gated sodium channels.
  • Recent studies show that local anesthetics also block potassium, chloride and calcium channels.

Local anesthetics work by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels. This inhibits the influx of sodium ions into the nerve cell during depolarization, thereby preventing the propagation of action potentials and blocking the transmission of nerve signals. This is the primary mechanism by which local anesthetics provide their numbing effect.

Incorrect Options:

  • B (Decreasing resting membrane potential): Local anesthetics do not primarily work by decreasing the resting membrane potential. Instead, they inhibit the depolarization of the nerve cell, which prevents nerve conduction.
  • C (Activating sodium channel): Local anesthetics do the opposite by blocking sodium channels, not activating them.
  • D (Inhibiting nicotine receptor): Local anesthetics do not primarily affect nicotine receptors. This option pertains more to the action of certain drugs like neuromuscular blockers, not local anesthetics.

Key Takeaway: Local anesthetics primarily block sodium channels, which prevents nerve conduction and leads to their anesthetic effect.

question_text: Each of the following items describes pain in the abdominal viscera EXCEPT
option_a: Pain is transmitted via the vagus nerve
option_b: The nerve fibers are type C
option_c: Pain is characterized by a dull aching or burning sensation
option_d: Distention of the transverse colon causes more pain than surgical transection
explanation:
Virtually all pain arising in the thoracic or abdominal viscera is transmitted via the sympathetic nervous system in unmyelinated type C fibers. Visceral pain is dull, aching, burning, and nonspecific. Visceral pain is caused by any stimulus that excites nociceptive nerve endings in diffuse areas. In this regard, distention of a hollow viscus causes a greater sensation of pain than does the highly localized damage produced by transecting the gut. Although the vagus nerve has a large number of afferent fibers, they do not include pain fibers.

Reference: Miller: Miller's Anesthesia, ed 8, p 2975; Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 8, p 336.

Assertion(A): Whitacre or pencil point tip spinal needles have lower incidence of Post dural puncture headache.

question_text: Which of the following is the best example of neuropathic pain?
explanation:
Neuropathic pain is persistent pain that occurs following damage or disease of the somatosensory nervous system. Three unique characteristics of neuropathic pain are spontaneous pain (absence of a stimulus), hyperalgesia (exaggerated pain to a mild painful stimulus) and allodynia (pain that occurs with a nonpainful stimulus such as light touch). The forms of neuropathic pain include PHN, diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN), Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS), human immunodeficiency virus neuropathy, and phantom limb pain. Fibromyalgia is chronic widespread musculoskeletal pain accompanied by other symptoms such as excessive fatigue, sleep disturbances, and trouble with memory but may have a partial peripheral neuropathic component. Nociceptive pain, also called physiologic pain, has two main types: radicular pain (e.g., disk herniation) and somatic pain (e.g., facet or hip joint arthritic pain)

Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 8, pp 1611-1618; Miller: Basics of Anesthesia, ed 7, pp 770-776.

question_text: Each of the following is associated with an increased incidence of PDPHs EXCEPT
explanation:
Younger adults have a higher incidence of PDPH than older adults or children. Women have a slightly higher incidence than men. Pregnant women have a higher incidence than nonpregnant women. Since the incidence and severity of PDPH relate to the amount of CSF leakage through the dural hole, it makes sense that the larger the needle and the more holes in the dura, the greater the incidence of PDPH. In addition, the shape of the tip of the needle is important: A cutting needle (e.g., Quincke) has a greater incidence of PDPH than a noncutting needle (e.g., Whitacre, Sprotte). The incidence of headache has been shown to be less when the dural fibers are split longitudinally than when they are cut, while the needle is held in a transverse direction. The timing of ambulation relative to dural puncture has not been shown to affect the incidence of postspinal headache. The block should wear off before ambulation is attempted.

Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 8, p 938; Miller: Miller's Anesthesia, ed 8, pp 1694-1695

question_text: Postdural puncture headaches (PDPHs)
option_a: Usually occur immediately following dural puncture
option_b: Are relieved 8 to 12 hours after an epidural blood patch is performed
option_c: Occur more frequently in nonpregnant patients compared with pregnant patients
option_d: Can be associated with neurologic deficits
explanation:
PDPHs typically appear within 12 to 48 hours of a dural puncture, but may be immediate and occasionally have become delayed for several days or months after a dural puncture. The headaches are characterized by dull or throbbing frontal or occipital pain, which worsens with sitting and improves with reclining. Postspinal headaches may be associated with neurologic symptoms such as diplopia, tinnitus, and reduced hearing acuity. Very rarely, a subdural hematoma will develop. The etiology of postspinal headaches is believed to be due to a reduction in CSF pressure and resulting tension on meningeal vessels and nerves (which results from leakage of CSF through the needle hole in the dura mater). Factors associated with an increased incidence of postspinal headaches include pregnancy, needle size (larger needles leave bigger holes than smaller needles), type of needle used to perform the block (cutting Quincke needles are more commonly associated with PDPH than pencil-point Whitacre or bullet-shaped Sprotte needles), and the number of dural punctures. They occur more frequently in young adults, compared with children and elderly persons. Conservative therapy for a postspinal headache includes bed rest, analgesics, and oral and IV hydration. If conservative therapy is not successful after 24 to 48 hours, an epidural "blood patch" with 10 to 20 mL of the patient's blood can be performed. An epidural blood patch usually provides prompt relief of the postspinal headache.

Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 8, pp 938-939.

question_text: In addition to the postural component of a postdural puncture headache (PDPH), signs and symptoms may include any of the following EXCEPT
explanation:
PDPHs are positional headaches (exacerbated by sitting or standing and relieved with recumbency) that usually present within 48 hours of a dural puncture (but could take up to a week to present) and typically resolve in 2 to 14 days. They are bilateral and typically located in the frontal or occipital regions. In one prospective series of nonobstetric patients with PDPH, symptoms included nausea (60%), vomiting (24%), neck stiffness (43%), ocular changes (photophobia, diplopia, difficulty in accommodation) (13%), and auditory changes (hearing loss, hyperacusis, tinnitus) (12%). Although postpartum seizures have been associated with PDPH, other etiologies are more likely. Seizures, lethargy, fever, nuchal rigidity, focal neurologic deficits (other than listed above), and a unilateral location suggest other headache etiologies.

Reference: Chestnut: Chestnut's Obstetric Anesthesia, ed 5, pp 713-721; Suresh: Shnider and Levinson's Anesthesia for Obstetrics, ed 5, pp 425-430.

question_text:
Assertion(A): Glycopyrrolate is preferred over atropine as antisialogogues in the adult population.
Reason(R): The quaternary ammonium compound exerts only peripheral effects, devoid of central effects.
option_a: Both Assertion(A) and Reason(R) are true, but Reason(R) does not explain Assertion(A)
option_b: Both Assertion(A) and Reason(R) are true, and Reason(R) explains Assertion(A)
option_c: Both Assertion(A) and Reason(R) are not true
option_d: Both Assertion(A) and Reason(R) are not true, but Reason(R) explains Assertion(A)
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Glycopyrrolate is preferred as an antisialogogue because it reduces salivary and airway secretions without producing central anticholinergic toxicity.
  • This directly results from its structure as a quaternary ammonium compound, which prevents it from crossing the blood-brain barrier.
  • The reason therefore accurately explains why glycopyrrolate is favored over atropine.
  • Peripheral action: Glycopyrrolate does not enter the CNS due to its quaternary structure, avoiding central side effects such as confusion and agitation. (Supports Assertion and Reason)
  • Comparison: Atropine, a tertiary amine, crosses the blood-brain barrier and may produce tachycardia, restlessness, and central toxicity.
  • Clinical preference: Glycopyrrolate is ideal for reducing secretions during anesthesia while maintaining hemodynamic stability.
  • Glycopyrrolate is commonly paired with neostigmine during neuromuscular block reversal because their durations of action are well matched.
  • Reduced central effects make it safer in elderly patients or those with cognitive impairment.
  • Produces less tachycardia compared to atropine, improving intraoperative stability.

Key Takeaways:

  • Glycopyrrolate is preferred over atropine as an antisialogogue in adults because it is a quaternary ammonium compound.
  • It does not cross the blood-brain barrier, preventing central anticholinergic effects such as sedation or confusion.
  • It produces effective peripheral antimuscarinic effects with fewer adverse reactions compared to atropine.
  • Its pharmacologic profile makes it suitable in patients where CNS side effects must be avoided.

  • Secondary hyperalgesia is manifested by the triple response of Lewis: a red flush around the site of injury (flare), local tissue edema, and sensitization to noxious stimuli.
  • It is diminished by injection of a local anesthetic.
  • Capsaicin applied topically in a gel, cream, or patch depletes substance P, diminishes neurogenic inflammation, and is useful for some patients with post-herpetic neuralgia.

Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 1059.

question_text: Which of the following structures does the needle not pass through during epidural anesthesia?
explanation:
Explanation:

During epidural anesthesia, the dura mater is not pierced.

The local anesthetic is administered through a Tuohy needle into the epidural space, which is located between the dura mater and the ligamentum flavum. The anesthetic acts on the nerve roots in this space.

Structures pierced to reach epidural space:

Skin------subcutaneous tissue------supraspinous ligament------infraspinous ligament------ligamentum flavum-----epidural space

(Options A, B, and C)

question_text: Which nerve block is shown in the image given below?
explanation:
• The inter-costobrachial nerve originates in the upper thorax (T2) and becomes superficial on the medial upper arm.
  • It supplies cutaneous innervation to the medial aspect of the proximal arm and is not anesthetized with a brachial plexus block.
  • The patient should be supine with the arm abducted and externally rotated. Starting at the deltoid prominence and proceeding inferiorly, a field block is performed in a linear fashion using 5 mL of local anesthetic, extending to the most inferior aspect of the medial arm

Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 1022.

question_text: While performing a peripheral nerve block in an awake patient, access and/or use of all of the following should be considered mandatory, except
option_c: Access to resuscitation medications and equipment
option_d: Immediate access to a mechanical ventilator
explanation:
Immediate access to a functioning anesthesia ventilator is not always necessary while administering regional anaesthesia.

Regional anesthesia should be administered in a monitored location where standard ASA monitors.

Supplemental oxygen along with resuscitative medications and equipment should be readily accessible and immediately available.

Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 999.

question_text: You are performing an axillary brachial plexus block using the instrument given below. At 0.5 mA current, you can see the motor response. Which is the next best step?
option_c: Administer local anaesthetic at this point
explanation:
• Given image is that of a peripheral nerve stimulator used for performing nerve stimulator guided blocks of peripheral nerves.
  • Occurrence of a motor response at 0.5 mA (0.1 ms) indicates needle-nerve contact or intraneural needle placement.
  • Such an occurrence should prompt caution. The practitioner should stop advancing the needle, withdraw the needle by 1 mm, and inject 1 mL of local anesthetic (assuming the opening pressure is less than 15 psi) to determine the needle tip position and adjust the needle and injection process accordingly.

Reference: Hadzic's textbook of regional anaesthesia and acute pain management, 2nd edition, pg 195

question_text: After administering which of the following nerve blocks would you expect the highest blood levels of local anaesthetic per local anaesthetic dose injected?
explanation:
The intercostal block has one of the highest complication rates of any peripheral nerve block due to the close proximity of the intercostal artery and vein (intravascular local anesthetic injection), as well as underlying pleura (pneumothorax).

Intercostal blocks result in the highest blood levels of local anesthetic per local anesthetic dose injected of any nerve block procedure, and if multiple blocks will be performed care must be taken to avoid toxic levels of local anesthetic.

Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 1040.

question_text: Match the following labels with the levels of brachial plexus blocks:
explanation:
• An interscalene brachial plexus block is indicated for procedures involving the shoulder and upper arm. Roots C5-7 are most densely blocked with this approach.
  • A supraclavicular brachial plexus block can provide dense anesthesia for procedures at or distal to the elbow at the level of the divisions.
  • An infraclavicular brachial plexus block at the level of the cords
  • Provides excellent anesthesia for procedures at or distal to the elbow
  • An axillary brachial plexus block is administered at the lateral border of the pectoralis minor muscle where the cords of the brachial plexus form large terminal 6 branches.

Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 1005-14.

question_text: You are administering ankle block to a patient for great toe amputation. Which of the following nerves also has a motor nerve supply, as opposed to the others that are pure sensory nerves?
explanation:
• The saphenous nerve is a terminal branch of the femoral nerve and the only innervation of the foot that is not a part of the sciatic system. It supplies superficial sensation to the anteromedial foot and is most constantly located just anterior to the medial malleolus.
  • The sural nerve is a branch of the tibial nerve and enters the foot between the Achilles tendon and the lateral malleolus to provide sensation to the lateral foot.
  • Superficial peroneal nerve, a branch of the common peroneal nerve, descends toward the ankle in the lateral compartment, giving motor branches to the muscles of eversion. It enters the ankle just lateral to the extensor digitorum longus and provides cutaneous sensation to the dorsum of the foot and toes.
  • Other 2 nerves blocked in the ankle block are the deep peroneal nerve and the posterior tibial nerve.

Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 1038.

question_text: A spinal neuraxial anesthetic was given 20 minutes earlier to a 28-year-old G3P2 parturient scheduled for repeat cesarean section. Alcohol swab exam revealed that she has lost temperature sensation up to T2 level. At what level do you anticipate the block will reach to provide adequate pain control?
explanation:
A manifestation of relative sensitivity or susceptibility of nerve fibres to the effects of local anesthetics is the observed differences in the peak block height (highest or most cephalad level of anesthesia) according to each sensory modality, which is termed differential sensory blockade.

For example, the level of anesthesia to cold sensation (also an approximate level of sympathetic blockade) is most cephalad and is on average one to two spinal segments higher than the level of pinprick anesthesia which in turn is one to two segments higher than the level of touch anesthesia.

In this spinal block, alcohol swab tested the level of sensory/sympathetic blockade.

Reference: Miller's anesthesiology 9th edition pg 1417.

question_text: The correct statement for human neuraxial anatomy is
option_a: Adult spinal cord ends at L2
option_b: Spinal cord in children ends at L3
option_c: The dural sac and subarachnoid space in adults end at S1
option_d: The dural sac and subarachnoid space in children end at S2
explanation:
The spinal cord typically ends around L1 in adults, and around L3 in children. This is the reason why neuraxial blocks are performed below these levels and carry a lower risk of direct spinal cord injury.

The dural sac and subarachnoid spaces end at S2 in adults and S3 in children.

Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 965.

question_text: The correct order of susceptibility of nerve fibers to local anesthetic agents
option_a: A gamma > A delta > A alpha > B > C
option_b: A alpha > B > C > A gamma > A delta
option_c: B > C >A gamma > A delta > A alpha
option_d: C >A gamma > A delta > A alpha > B
explanation:
• Sensitivity of nerve fibers to inhibition by local anesthetics is influenced by axonal diameter, myelination, and other factors.
  • In comparing nerve fibers of the same type (myelinated versus unmyelinated), smaller diameter associates with increased sensitivity to local anesthetics.
  • Thus, larger, faster-conducting Aα fibers are less sensitive to local anesthetics than smaller, slower- conducting Aδ fibers.
  • Larger unmyelinated fibers are less sensitive than smaller unmyelinated fibers.
  • On the other hand, small unmyelinated C fibers are relatively resistant to inhibition by local anesthetics as compared with larger myelinated fibers.
  • In a human peripheral nerve, the onset of local anesthetic inhibition generally follows this sequence: autonomic before sensory before motor.

Reference: Morgan anesthesia, edition 6, page no 264

question_text: Which of the following causes an increase in heart rate?
explanation:
• In general, opioids have few direct effects on the heart
  • Meperidine tends to increase heart rate (it is structurally like atropine and was originally synthesized as an atropine replacement)
  • Whereas larger doses of Morphine, Fentanyl, Sufentanil, Remifentanil, and Alfentanil are associated with a vagus nerve-mediated bradycardia (Option A, B & C)

Reference: Stoelting's pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 5th edition

question_text: Opioid with predominant peripheral action is?
explanation:
• Methyl naltrexone is a peripheral mu opioid receptor antagonist
  • It is a quaternary ammonium compound and hence cannot cross the blood brain barrier
  • Thus, it can reverse the effects of opioid mediated by peripheral opioid receptors, since it cannot cross the blood brain barrier, it does not affect the opioid effects mediated by opioid receptors in the CNS, such as analgesia
  • It was introduced in the treatment of opioid induced constipation refractory to other measures
  • Alvimopan is a similar acting peripheral mu opioid receptor antagonist

Reference: Stoelting's pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 5th edition

question_text: Vomiting is a common side effect following use of opioids. This is attributed to all of the following mechanisms except
explanation:
Gastric emptying time is slowed via central and peripheral mechanisms.

Increased tone and decreased propulsive action of both small and large intestine results into constipation.

Vomiting is induced by following mechanisms

  • CTZ stimulations.
  • Decreased gastrointestinal motility.
  • Prolonged gastric emptying time.

Reference: Comparative pharmacology for Anesthetist, page no 42

question_text: A 68-year-old male presents to his primary care physician's office with a major complain of back pain radiating into the gluteal region and pain in the distribution of the plantar surface of the foot on the same side. The patient's physical examination reveals decreased plantar flexion of the foot. An MRI will most commonly show a herniated disk at
explanation:
• Disk herniation at L5-S1 is the most common location of vertebral disk pathology presenting as back pain (affects the S1 nerve root).
  • Patients often have associated gluteal pain and numbness along with pain/paresthesia in the posterior thigh, posterolateral calf, lateral dorsum, and undersurface of the foot.
  • Physical examination will also identify a diminished plantar flexion of the ankle on the affected side.

Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 1068.

question_text: A 43-year-old female presents to the pain clinic with electric shock like pain on the right side of the face. All of the following are treatment options except:
option_b: Balloon compression of the otic ganglion
option_d: Microvascular decompression of the trigeminal nerve
explanation:
• The given case scenario with a middle aged female presenting with unilateral shock like pain on the face points towards trigeminal neuralgia.
  • Common causes of trigeminal neuralgia include compression of the nerve by the superior cerebellar artery as it exits the brainstem, multiple sclerosis, and cerebellopontine angle tumor.
  • The drug of choice for treatment is carbamazepine, although it carries a risk of agranulocytosis. Phenytoin or baclofen may be added, particularly if patients do not tolerate the required doses of carbamazepine.
  • More invasive treatments for patients who do not respond to drug therapy include glycerol injection, radiofrequency ablation, balloon compression of the gasserian ganglion, and microvascular decompression of the trigeminal nerve.

Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 1075.

question_text: Activation of which of the following mechanisms and/or pathways best describes "central sensitization" at the level of the spinal cord?
explanation:
Modulation of pain occurs peripherally at the nociceptor (Peripheral Modulation) and in the spinal cord, and supra-spinal structures (Central Modulation).

Central sensitization is an enhancement in the function of neurons and circuits in nociceptive pathways, caused by increases in membrane excitability and synaptic efficacy as well as reduced inhibition and is a manifestation of the plasticity of the somatosensory nervous system in response to activity, inflammation, and neural injury.

At least three mechanisms are responsible for central sensitization in the spinal cord:

  1. Wind-up and sensitization of second-order neurons.
  2. Receptive field expansion of dorsal horn neutrons.
  3. Hyper-excitability of flexion reflexes.

Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 1059.

question_text: You are administering gasserian ganglion block in a patient with neuralgia. Gasserian ganglion block is most commonly used for neuropathic pain located in which of the following nerve distributions?
explanation:
• The two principal indications for trigeminal nerve block are trigeminal neuralgia and intractable facial cancer pain
  • Depending on the site of pain, these blocks may be performed on the gasserian ganglion itself, on one of the major divisions (ophthalmic, maxillary, or mandibular), or on one of their smaller branches.

Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 1085.

question_text: A 40-year-old female presents to you with shock like pain on the right side of the face. The block of which of the following ganglia given below is shown in the image for the above mentioned condition?
explanation:
The above mentioned condition is trigeminal neuralgia and the ganglion to be blocked is gasserian ganglion blocked.

The rootlets of cranial nerve V arise from the brainstem and join one another to form a crescent-shaped sensory (gasserian) ganglion in Meckel's cave.

Reference: Morgan and Mikhail's clinical anesthesiology 6th edition pg 1085.

question_text: Select the one TRUE statement concerning phantom limb pain.
option_a: The incidence of phantom limb pain increases with more distal amputations
option_b: Most amputees do not experience phantom limb pain
option_c: Nerve blocks may be used to decrease the incidence of phantom limb pain
option_d: Traumatic amputees have a much higher incidence of phantom limb pain than nontraumatic amputees
explanation:
The incidence of phantom limb pain is estimated to be up to 80% after an amputation. This pain may be immediate but, in many cases, will develop within a few days of the amputation. The pain also may not be present all the time but only a few days a month. The incidence of phantom limb pain does not differ between traumatic and nontraumatic amputees. The incidence of phantom pain increases with more proximal amputation. About 50% of patients will have a decrease in pain over time; the rest have no change or an increase in pain with time. Although very difficult to treat, nerve blocks are commonly used in the perioperative setting to decrease the incidence of phantom limb pain. Oral agents such as opioids, antidepressants, and gabapentin are commonly used, as well as TENS units, spinal cord stimulators, and biofeedback methods.

Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 8, p 1618.

question_text: The mechanism of low-frequency transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) units in relieving pain is
option_a: Direct electrical inhibition of type A-δ and C fibers
explanation:
TENS produces a tingling or vibratory sensation in the area in which pads are placed. Although the exact mechanism is unclear, it is thought that TENS units produce analgesia by releasing endogenous endorphins, since its effects are partially blocked by naloxone. These endorphins have an inhibitory effect at the spinal cord level and augment descending inhibitory pathways.

Reference: Miller: Miller's Anesthesia, ed 8, pp 2339, 2991.

question_text: In addition to C nerve fibers, which nerve fibers carry pain impulses?
explanation:
Peripheral nerves are classified according to the fiber size and physiologic properties, such as the presence or absence of myelin, conduction velocity, location, and function. All type A fibers are myelinated. These fibers are subclassified into four groups based on their diameter, location, and function. A-alpha (Aα) and A-beta (Aβ) fibers are 6 to 22 μm in diameter and have conduction velocities of 30 to 120 m/sec. Aα fibers are efferent to the skeletal muscles. Aβ fibers are afferent from the skin and joints to provide touch and proprioception sensations. A-gamma (Aγ) fibers are 3 to 6 μm in diameter, have conduction velocities of 15 to 35 m/sec, and are efferent to the muscle spindles to provide muscle tone. A-delta (Aδ) fibers are 1 to 4 μm in diameter and have conduction velocities of 5 to 25 m/sec and are afferent fibers, which provide sharp localized pain and temperature and touch sensations. B fibers are myelinated, preganglionic sympathetic nerve fibers that are less than 3 μm in diameter, have medium conduction velocities 3 to 15 m/sec, and are involved with various autonomic nervous system control. C fibers are nonmyelinated, postganglionic sympathetic nerves that are 0.3 to 1.3 μm in diameter and have slow conduction velocities of 0.1 to 2 m/sec. C fibers are afferent sensory nerves involved with nonlocalized pain, temperature, and touch sensations.

Reference: Miller: Miller's Anesthesia, ed 8, pp 1013-1014

question_text: The following are the elements of pain except;
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The process of pain involves four key elements:
    • Transduction (Option A):
      • Involves the conversion of noxious thermal, chemical, or mechanical stimuli into an action potential.
      • This initial step is crucial for the perception of pain.
    • Transmission (Option B):
      • Refers to the conduction of action potentials through the nervous system via first-order, second order, and third-order neurons.
      • These neurons have cell bodies located in the dorsal root ganglion, dorsal horn, and thalamus, respectively.
    • Modulation (Option D):
      • Refers to the alteration of afferent neural transmission along the pain pathway.
      • This can either amplify or dampen the pain experience depending on various factors.
    • Sensitization:
      • While related to pain processing, sensitization itself is not considered a core element of the pain pathway.
      • It refers to neuroplastic changes resulting from tissue injury, leading to peripheral and central sensitization.
      • This can manifest clinically as hyperalgesia (exaggerated response to painful stimuli) and allodynia(painful response to normally non-painful stimuli).
      • These phenomena are consequences of altered pain processing rather than elements of the pain pathway itself.

Key Takeaways:

  • The primary elements of pain processing include transduction, transmission, and modulation.
  • Sensitization, although important in the context of pain perception, is not a direct element of pain processing but rather a consequence of it.

question_text: All are true regarding phantom limb pain except?
option_a: Behavioural intervention is probably the most effective approach
option_b: Peripheral mechanisms include increase in A delta-fiber activity
option_c: Central mechanisms include abnormal firing of spinal internuncial neurons
option_d: The onset of pain may be immediate but commonly occurs within the first few days following amputation
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Mechanisms of Phantom Limb Pain:
    • Peripheral Mechanisms:
      • Involves factors such as neuromas (nerve growths), increased C-fiber activity (not A delta-Fiber), and sodium channel activation.
      • A delta fibers are primarily associated with sharp, acute pain, not specifically linked to phantom pain.
    • Central Mechanisms (Option C): Includes abnormal firing of spinal internuncial neurons and changes in the central nervous system due to the development of new synaptic connections in the cerebral cortex.
    • Treatment Approaches:
      • Nonpharmacologic measures include transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, spinal cord stimulators, and biofeedback.
      • A combination of pharmacologic treatment with physical, psychological, or behavioural interventions is often the most effective strategy for managing phantom limb pain.
  • Phantom Limb Pain (PLP):
    • Nearly all patients with amputated limbs experience nonpainful sensations in the absent limb, with around 60% experiencing pain.
    • The onset of phantom limb pain may occur immediately or typically within the first few days after amputation (Option D)
    • Over time, approximately 50% of patients may experience a decrease in pain, while others report no change or an increase.
  • Behavioural intervention is probably the most effective approach (Option A): Behavioural interventions are indeed effective, often as part of a multimodal treatment strategy.

Key Takeaways:

  • Phantom limb pain arises from a combination of peripheral and central mechanisms, with peripheral mechanisms not primarily involving A delta-fiber activity but rather C-fiber activity and neuromas.
  • The onset of pain can be immediate or delayed, with various treatment options available that emphasize a multimodal approach for effective management.

question_text: A patient undergoes parotid gland removal under general anesthesia. Each of the following assesses facial nerve function EXCEPT
explanation:
The facial nerve (seventh cranial nerve) runs within the substance of the parotid gland and might become damaged during parotid surgery. The facial nerve innervates the lacrimal, submandibular, and sublingual glands, is sensory to the anterior two thirds of the tongue, and innervates all of the muscle of facial expression (including the orbicularis oculi-close the eyelids; orbicularis oris-purse the lips; frontalis-raise the eyebrows). The trigeminal nerve (fifth cranial nerve) innervates the muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial, and lateral pterygoids), which are used to clench the teeth.

Reference: Miller: Basics of Anesthesia, ed 6, p 497; Orient: Sapira's Art and Science of Bedside Diagnosis ed 4, pp 533-537.

question_text: A 35-year-old woman undergoes a total thyroidectomy. Post-operatively, a fiberoptic laryngoscopy is performed to assess laryngeal nerve integrity. The image below is captured while the patient is asked to take a deep breath in. Based on this view, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• The patient was asked to take a deep breath in. The normal physiological response to deep inspiration is the abduction (opening) of both vocal cords to widen the glottic airway.
  • The image shows that the vocal cords have failed to abduct and remain in the paramedian (or near-midline) position.
  • This failure of both vocal cords to open on command for inspiration is the classic and life-threatening presentation of bilateral abductor palsy, most commonly caused by iatrogenic injury to both recurrent laryngeal nerves (RLNs). This condition results in a critically narrowed airway and stridor.

Explanation of Other Options:

Normal vocal cord function (Option A): Normal vocal cords would have visibly abducted (moved apart) from the midline during a deep breath, creating a wide, open airway.

Unilateral adductor palsy (Option C): In an adductor palsy, the affected cord would be fixed laterally. On inspiration, the other (healthy) cord would still abduct normally. The image shows both cords are immobile.

Superior laryngeal nerve palsy (Option D): Injury to the superior laryngeal nerve affects vocal cord tension and pitch control. It leads to an inability to reach high-pitched sounds and results in a weak, breathy voice. The visual appearance on laryngoscopy can be subtle, often showing a "bowed" or wavy appearance of the affected cord.

Reference: Oxford handbook of Anesthesia, edition 4, Page Number:577

question_text: Which of the following peripheral nerves is MOST likely to become injured in patients who are under general anesthesia?
explanation:
The principal mechanism of peripheral nerve injury is ischemia caused by stretching or compression of the nerves. Anesthetized patients are at increased risk for peripheral nerve injuries because they are unconscious and unable to complain about uncomfortable positions that an awake patient would not tolerate and because of reduced muscle tone that facilitates placement of patients into awkward positions. The ulnar nerve in particular is vulnerable because it passes around the posterior aspect of the medial epicondyle of the humerus. The ulnar nerve may become compressed between the medial epicondyle and the sharp edge of the operating table, leading to ischemia and possible nerve injury, which may be transient or permanent

Reference: Miller: Basics of Anesthesia, ed 6, pp 310-312

question_text: A 32-year-old army officer is unable to oppose the left thumb and left little finger after an 8-hour exploratory laparotomy under general anesthesia. He had an IV induction through a peripheral IV and had a second IV placed in the antecubital fossa after he was asleep. Damage to which of the following nerves would MOST likely account for this deficit?
explanation:
The median nerve is most frequently injured at the antecubital fossa by extravasation of IV drugs that are toxic to neural tissue, or by direct injury caused by the needle during attempts to can[1]nulate the medial cubital or basilic veins. The median nerve provides sensory innervation to the palmar surface of the lateral three and one-half fingers and adjacent palm, and motor function to the abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis, and opponens pollicis muscles

Reference: Miller: Basics of Anesthesia, ed 6, p 313.

question_text: A 47-year-old morbidly obese patient develops bilateral blindness (only able to perceive light) after a 6-hour, three-segment laminectomy and fusion. The patient received 6 units of blood and 5 L of lactated Ringer solution. A mean arterial blood pressure was maintained at 50 to 60 mm Hg. The MOST likely structure involved in this visual loss is
explanation:
Perioperative visual loss associated with nonocular surgery is rare and may result from corneal trauma, retinal artery occlusion, retinal vein occlusion, optic nerve ischemia, or cortical disease. Although overall it is a rare problem, it may develop in up to 1% of prone spinal surgical cases and is most commonly due to ischemic optic neuropathy. The cause is unknown and multifactorial. Associated factors include prolonged intraoperative hypotension, anemia (Hgb

Reference: E Book of Morgan and Mikhail’s 6th Edition Chapter 36 Page No 1308 to 1326.

question_text: A 21-year-old woman has had a laparoscopic salpingectomy for an ectopic pregnancy. She received a total of 50 mg of atracurium during the procedure. At the end of the operation, a nerve stimulator is used to assess depth of neuromuscular blockade. Which of the following nerves best reflects the extent of neuromuscular blockade of the diaphragm?
explanation:
During reversal a peripheral muscle, such as adductor pollicis should be monitored which is supplied by ulnar nerve. As the peripheral muscles have a slower recovery time, the recovery of the peripheral muscles would indicate the respiratory muscles have recovered to a greater degree. This provides a larger margin of safety.

Reference: objective anaesthesia review 4th edition nerve locator and peripheral nerve stimulator pg 490.

question_text: A 40-year-old male is undergoing ankle surgery under a subgluteal sciatic nerve block. During preparation for the procedure, which of the following drug therapies must be readily available to manage potential local anesthetic systemic toxicity?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST):
    • LAST is alife-threatening conditionthat can occur following local anesthetic administration via various routes.
    • Thehigh volumeused in epidural anesthesia and peripheral nerve blocks (PNBs) increases the risk of LAST.
  • Mechanism of Toxicity:
    • Supratherapeutic plasma concentrations of local anaesthetics can cause significantadverse effectson thecentral nervous system (CNS)andcardiovascular system (CVS).
  • Symptoms:
    • Initial signs includeperioral numbness,tinnitus,agitation,dysarthria, andconfusion.
    • Severe CNS effects may includeseizuresandcoma.
    • Cardiovascular effects typically present ashypertensionandtachycardia, progressing tobradycardia,hypotension,ventricular arrhythmias, andasystole.
  • Onset:
    • Most adverse events occur within1 minuteof local anaesthetic injection, but delayed onset (over1 hour) can also occur.
  • Treatment:
    • Early recognition- STOP injection of local anesthetic immediately.
    • Airway & oxygenation
    • Control of seizures (Benzodiazepenes)
    • Circulatory support
    • Specific therapy- Intravenous Lipid Emulsion (ILE)
  • Adrenaline (Option A):While it can prolong the duration of anaesthesia and reduce systemic absorption, it does not treat LAST directly.
  • Bretylium (Option B):This is an antiarrhythmic agent but is not a first-line treatment for LAST and is rarely used in current practice.
  • Phenylephrine (Option D):This vasopressor can manage hypotension but does not address the broader systemic effects of LAST.

Key Takeaways:

  • 20% lipid emulsionis the primary therapy for LAST, as it helps to"lipid rescue"by binding and sequestering local anaesthetics, thus reducing toxicity.
  • Awareness of LAST symptoms is crucial for prompt intervention to mitigate severe complications.

question_text: Scopolamine should not be given as a premedication in patients with which of the following neurologic diseases?
explanation:
The principal feature of Alzheimer disease is progressive dementia. The onset typically occurs after age 60 years and may affect as many as 20% of patients older than age 80 years. In addition to age, other risk factors include history of serious head trauma (e.g., boxing), Down syndrome, and presence of the disease in a parent or sibling. One biochemical feature of this disease is a decrease in the enzyme choline acetyltransferase in the brain. There is a strong correlation between reduced enzyme activity and decreased cognitive function. Interestingly, administration of the anticholinergic drugs scopolamine or atropine (but not glycopyrrolate, which does not cross the blood-brain barrier) causes confusion similar to that seen in the early stages of Alzheimer disease. Conversely, administration of anticholinesterase drugs capable of penetrating the blood-brain barrier, such as donepezil (Aricept), galantamine, rivastigmine (Exelon), and tacrine are used to treat patients with Alzheimer disease. Physostigmine may have beneficial effects in some patients as well. Scopolamine is therefore a poor choice for premedication in patients with Alzheimer disease.

Reference: Hines: Stoelting's Anesthesia and Co-Existing Disease, ed 6, p 245; Butterworth: Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology, ed 5, pp 619-620

question_text: Oxygen therapy is indicated in all the following conditions excepts:
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Oxygen Therapy: Aims to increase the fraction of inspired oxygen concentration (FiO2) to prevent cellular hypoxia resulting from hypoxemia.
  • Primary Goals: Prevent irreversible damage to vital organs by maintaining adequate oxygen levels in the blood.
  • Main Indications for Oxygen Therapy:
    • Hypoxia (Option B): Diminished blood oxygen levels (oxygen saturation <92%).
    • Hypoxemia (Option C): Acute and chronic conditions with PaO2 <65 mm Hg (e.g., pneumonia, shock, asthma).
    • Myocardial Ischemia/Infarction: Administered if associated with hypoxemia; caution with high levels in ischemic heart disease/stroke.
    • Low Cardiac Output: Can contribute to metabolic acidosis (HCO3 <18 mmol/L).
    • Chronic Type II Respiratory Failure: Addresses both hypoxia and hypercapnia.
    • Acute Gastrointestinal Blood Loss: Oxygenation support during acute bleeding.
    • Carbon Monoxide Poisoning: Oxygen therapy aids in displacing CO from haemoglobin.
  • Metabolic Acidosis (Option D): Can benefit from oxygen therapy to support tissue oxygenation despite potential acid-base imbalance.

Key Takeaways:

  • Acid Inhalational Poisonings not a direct indication for oxygen therapy as it can lead to lung injury and inflammation, potentially making oxygen therapy less effective or even harmful.
  • Oxygen therapy is critical in conditions causing hypoxia and hypoxemia but should be used cautiously in certain situations like metabolic acidosis.

question_text: A 39-year-old male patient with moderate degree burns before 1 week is to be anaesthetised. Use of which of the following anaesthetic drugs can be safely used for this patient?
explanation:
• In patients with significant burns (>20% TBSA), injury and disruption of neuromuscular end plates occurs, followed by up regulation of acetylcholine receptors.
  • Beyond 15-48 h after significant burn injury, succinylcholine can produce lethal hyperkalemia.
  • This risk for succinylcholine-induced hyperkalemia persists for up to 2 years following burn injury.
  • Options a, b: Propofol and atracurium have no contraindications, and opioids (option d) should be used with caution as burns patients require frequent procedures and thus can land in opioid tolerance.
  • Ketamine used for burns dressings can also lead to tolerance and increased dose requirements if used frequently.

Reference: Morgan and mikhail’s clinical anaesthesiology 6th edition pg 837.

question_text: The most epileptogenic inhalational anaestheticis?
explanation:
• Enflurane is the most epileptogenic inhalational anaesthetic especially in the presence of cerebral injury and hypocapnia
  • So enflurane is contraindicated in patients with a
    • Known history of seizures
    • Cerebrovascular disease
    • In head injuries as seizure activity can increase the cerebral metabolism manifold
  • Besides enflurane increases cerebrospinal fluid secretion and decreases its absorption which is deleterious in those with poor intracranial compliance
  • Seizures have been associated with the use of sevoflurane in high concentrations, especially in the paediatric population.

Epileptogenic Potential : Enflurane >>> Sevoflurane

Reference: Drugs in Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, Edward Scarth, Susan Smith 5th edition

question_text: "Concentration effect" is associated with?
explanation:
• Nitrous oxide has a low blood-gas solubility compared with most other volatile agents. This ensures rapid equilibration
  • However, it is still much more soluble in blood than nitrogen, and because of the concentrations generally used this has several implications, especially during induction and recovery
  • When a patient changes from breathing a high concentration of nitrogen to breathing a high concentration of nitrous oxide, the concentration of nitrous oxide in the alveoli rises rapidly → Because nitrous oxide is more soluble in blood than nitrogen, the volume of nitrous oxide taken up by the blood is greater than the volume of nitrogen entering the alveoli from the blood → The alveoli therefore get smaller, and the fractional concentration of the remaining gases in the alveoli increases → If another anaesthetic agent is given with nitrous oxide, the relative concentration of this will also increase → This phenomenon is referred to as the "second gas effect"
  • It has been demonstrated that the higher the inspired concentration of nitrous oxide, the more rapidly the alveolar concentration approaches the inspired concentration
  • This has been referred to as the "concentration effect".

Reference: Stoelting's pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 3th edition

question_text: The second gas effect is seen with which anaesthetic?
explanation:
• Second Gas Effect is seen when nitrous oxide is administered with another inhaled anaesthetic
  • This is the result of another phenomenon called concentration effect which is usually seen with nitrous oxide as it is given in high concentration (66%)
  • Uptake of nitrous oxide from the alveoli into the blood results in a gradient which draws in more nitrous oxide from the anaesthetic machine (augmented inflow)
  • If another gas is simultaneously administered, nitrous oxide enhances the uptake of that gas as well. This is called the second gas effect

Reference: Drugs in Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, Edward Scarth, Susan Smith 5th edition

question_text: Pheochromocytoma would be MOST likely to coexist with which of the following?
explanation:
Pheochromocytoma is an endocrine tumor (with release of catecholamines) in which 90% of patients are hypertensive, 90% of the tumors originate in one adrenal medulla, and 90% of all pheochromocytomas are benign. This disease is rare (<0.1% of hypertension in adults), but when it occurs, it is often seen with a triad of diaphoresis, tachycardia, and headache in patients with hypertension. Other symptoms include palpitations, tremulousness, weight loss, hyperglycemia, hypovolemia, and in some cases dilated cardiomyopathy and CHF. Death as a result of pheochromocytoma is due to cardiac conditions (e.g., myocardial infarction, CHF) or an intracranial bleed. In about 5% of cases, pheochromocytomas show an autosomal dominant pattern and may coexist with other endocrine diseases such as medullary carcinoma of the thyroid and hyperparathyroidism. This combination is called multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) type II or IIA (Sipple syndrome). MEN type IIB consists of pheochromocytoma, medullary carcinoma of the thyroid, and neuromas of the oral mucosa. The von Hippel-Lindau disease consists of hemangiomas of the nervous system (i.e., retina or cerebellum), and 10% to 25% of these patients also have a pheochromocytoma. The average-sized pheochromocytoma contains 100 to 800 mg of norepinephrine.

Reference: Barash: Clinical Anesthesia, ed 7, pp 1339-1340; Hines: Stoelting's Anesthesia and Co-Existing Disease, ed 6, pp 392-395.

question_text: What is the diagnosis for a 23-year-old female presenting with a week-long fever and showing the following rhythm on the cardiac monitor?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The rhythm shown in the image is atrial fibrillation.
  • Atrial fibrillation is a cardiac arrhythmia marked by rapid, irregular electrical signals in the atria.
  • This causes the ventricles to beat in a fast and irregular manner, resulting in an irregular heart rate as seen on the monitor.

Atrial fibrillation

Explanation for other options:

Atrial flutter (Option B): usually presents with a regular, sawtooth pattern on the monitor, unlike the irregular pattern observed in this case.

Supraventricular tachyarrhythmia (Option C):

  • is a broad term that encompasses various rapid heart rhythms originating from above the ventricles.
  • It includes conditions like atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, and other supraventricular tachycardias. While atrial fibrillation is a type of supraventricular tachyarrhythmia, it is more specific than the general term used in this option.

Ventricular tachyarrhythmia (Option D): refers to fast, abnormal heart rhythms that start in the ventricles. This condition is marked by a wide QRS complex on the monitor, which differs from the narrow QRS complex usually observed in atrial fibrillation.

Reference:

https://cpr.heart.org/-/media/CPR-Files/CPR-Guidelines-Files/Algorithms/AlgorithmACLS_Tachycardia_200612.pdf?sc_lang=en

question_text: Opioid receptors belong to which class?
explanation:
• Opioids bind to specific receptors located throughout the central nervous system and other tissues
  • Four major opioid receptor types have been identified: mu, kappa, delta, and sigma
  • All opioid receptors couple to G proteins binding of an agonist to an opioid receptor causes membrane hyperpolarization
  • Acute opioid effects are mediated by inhibition of adenylyl cyclase (reductions in intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate concentrations) and activation of phospholipase C

Reference: Stoelting's pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 5th edition

question_text:
Which of the following statements about lumbar puncture are false?
1. Urgent indication if SAH is suspected with inconclusive CT.
2. Safe in platelet count above 10,000.
3. Post-tap headaches are more common in old.
4. Meningitis is an unusual complication.
explanation:
Explanation:

Lumbar puncture or Spinal tap is essential for the diagnosis of two treatable but potentially fatal conditions, central nervous system (CNS) infection and subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) with a negative computed tomography (CT) scan (Statement 1 is true). In SAH, LP is warranted to look for xanthochromia. LP can also be helpful in the differential diagnosis of other conditions including CNS malignancy, pseudotumor cerebri, and demyelinating diseases

LP is generally considered safe only if platelet count is ≥50,000-80,000. A count of 10,000 is grossly unsafe (Statement 2). Post-dural puncture headache (PDPH) or Post Tap Headache, occur within 5 days of a lumbar puncture, caused by cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage through the dural puncture. It is more common in young adults and females; it is less common in the elderly (Statement 3).

Infectious complications such as meningitis are rare but well documented (Statement 4).

question_text: When the patient complaints of abnormal sensation without an apparent stimulus, it is called as:
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Paraesthesia:
    • Refers to abnormal sensations such as tingling, prickling, or a "pins and needles" feeling without any external stimulus.
    • Often caused by nerve irritation, compression, or damage.
  • Radiculopathy (Option A): Involves pain, weakness, or numbness that follows the path of a nerve root due to compression or injury, typically associated with radicular pain.
  • Hyperpathia (Option B): A condition characterized by an exaggerated response to stimuli, often involving pain that is more intense than expected.
  • Allodynia (Option D): Refers to pain from stimuli that do not normally provoke pain, such as light touch.

Key Takeaways:

  • Paraesthesia is specifically defined as abnormal sensations without an apparent cause, distinguishing it from other conditions that involve pain or exaggerated responses.

question_text: A 54-year-old woman is having a bunionectomy under general anaesthetic. You perform an ankle block using the landmark technique. Which of the following nerves could a nerve stimulator be used to block?
explanation:

  • It requires blockade of the deep and superficial peroneal nerves, sural nerve, saphenous nerve and tibial nerve.
  • As the tibial nerve is the only one that has a motor component beyond the site of block, it is the only nerve that a nerve stimulator may identify.

question_text: Which of the following forms active metabolites?

question_text: Which of the following statements is false?
option_a: Naltrexone is an antagonist at Mu receptor
option_b: Nalbuphine is an agonist at k receptor

question_text: CNS effect of opioid is?
explanation:

question_text: Which of the following are features of opioid withdrawal?
explanation:
• Physical dependence on morphine usually requires about 25 days to develop but may occur sooner in emotionally unstable persons
  • When physical dependence is established, discontinuation of the opioid agonist produces a typical withdrawal abstinence syndrome
  • Initial symptoms of withdrawal include
    • Yawning
    • diaphoresis
    • lacrimation
    • coryza
    • Insomnia and restlessness are prominent
  • After 72 hours the following symptoms reach their peak and decline over the next 7-10 days
    • Abdominal cramps
    • Nausea
    • Vomiting
    • Diarrhoea
  • During withdrawal, tolerance to morphine is rapidly lost, and the syndrome can be terminated by a modest dose of opioid agonist

Reference: Stoelting's pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 5th edition

question_text: Which of the following opioids is to be avoided in patients on Monoamine oxidase inhibitors?
explanation:
• Meperidine (and methadone) inhibits the neuronal reuptake of serotonin -> serotonergic overactivity -> Serotonin Syndrome in patients receiving monoamine oxidase inhibitors (Option A)
  • The symptom complex includes
    • Fluctuations in blood pressure
    • Hyperthermia
    • Delirium
    • Convulsions
    • Coma
    • Death
  • Thus, it is not co-administered with mono amine oxidase inhibitors or is used 14 days after the discontinuation of mono amine oxidase inhibitors
  • Tramadol (and tapentadol) inhibits the reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin (Option B)
  • Besides, it is epileptogenic and can cause seizures in predisposed individuals and in those taking medications like monoamine oxidase inhibitors which can lower the seizure threshold
  • Dextromethorphan is a cough suppressant, an analogue of levorphanol. It inhibits the reuptake of serotonin and is thus not to be used in patients receiving monoamine oxidase inhibitors (Option C)
  • Other opioids like Morphine, Codeine, Oxycodone, Alfentanil, and Buprenorphine are free from such interactions

Reference: Stoelting's pharmacology and physiology in anaesthetic practice 5th edition

question_text: A 28-year-old G2P1L1, previous lower segment caesarean section, is brought to the hospital in an emergency with abdominal pain, haematuria, and vaginal bleeding. On examination, foetal bradycardia is seen, and the foetal heart rate tracing is non-reassuring. The anaesthetic technique of choice in this situation is?
explanation:
• A case of previous LSCS with symptoms of abdominal pain, haematuria and signs of foetal bradycardia, and a non-reassuring foetal heart rate tracing is suggestive of uterine scar dehiscence. So emergency caesarean section is indicated
  • General anaesthesia is the preferred choice considering the emergency nature of surgery and the possibility of hemodynamic instability of impending uterine rupture

Advantages of General anesthesia include:

  • A very rapid and reliable onset
  • Control over the airway and ventilation
  • More comfortable for parturient who have morbid fears of needles or surgery
  • Less incidence of hypotension as compared to regional anesthesia

General anesthesia is preferred in certain emergency conditions such as:

  • Massive bleeding (placenta previa or accreta, abruption placentae, or uterine rupture)
  • Coagulopathy
  • Hemodynamic instability
  • Severe foetal distress

Reference: E Book of Morgan and Mikhail's Clinical Anaesthesiology 6th Edition Chapter 41 Page No 1485

question_text: Who coined the term "balanced anaesthesia"?
explanation:
• Oliver Wendel Holmes coined the term Anaesthesia .
  • John snow- administered chloroform analgesia to Queen Victoria for the delivery of her eighth child. This was a success and led to medical and religious acceptance of obstetrical anesthesia. When cholera returned to London in 1853, John Snow undertook an epidemiological study and linked the outbreak in Golden Square to the water pump on Broad Street.
  • WTG Morton is considered as father of Anaesthesia
  • The concept of balanced anesthesia was introduced in 1926 by Lundy and others and evolved to include thiopental for induction, nitrous oxide for amnesia, an opioid for analgesia, and curare for muscle relaxation.
  • The term "spinal anesthesia" was coined in 1885 by Leonard Corning, a neurologist,and Augest Bier used cocaine for spinal anesthesia

question_text: Sevoflurane is preferred agent for inhaled induction in paediatric anaesthesia due to?
option_a: Sevoflurane appears to produce the least respiratory depression
option_b: Less likely than other volatile agents to irritate the airway
option_c: Sevoflurane appears to have a greater therapeutic index than halothane
explanation:
• Neonates, infants, and young children have relatively greater alveolar ventilation and reduced FRC compared with older children and adults
  • This greater minute ventilation-to-FRC ratio with relatively greater blood flow to vessel-rich organs contributes to a rapid increase in alveolar anaesthetic concentration and speeds inhalation induction
  • Furthermore, the blood/gas coefficients of volatile anaesthetics are reduced in neonates compared with adults, resulting in even faster induction times and potentially increasing the risk of accidental overdosage

So for lower flows it is laminar flow and for higher flows it is turbulent.
